{{Short description|System of psychotherapy}}
'''Compassion-focused therapy''' ('''CFT''') is a system of [[psychotherapy]] developed by [[Paul Gilbert (psychologist)|Paul Gilbert]] that integrates techniques from [[cognitive behavioral therapy]] with concepts from [[evolutionary psychology]], [[social psychology]], [[developmental psychology]], [[Buddhist psychology]], and [[neuroscience]]. According to Gilbert, "One of its key concerns is to use compassionate mind training to help people develop and work with experiences of inner warmth, safeness and soothing, via [[compassion]] and [[self-compassion]]."<ref name="Gilbert2009">{{cite journal |last=Gilbert |first=Paul |date=2009 |title=Introducing compassion-focused therapy |journal= Advances in Psychiatric Treatment|volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=199–208 |doi=10.1192/apt.bp.107.005264 |doi-access=free }}</ref>{{rp|199}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Beaumont |first1=Elaine |last2=Bell |first2=Tobyn |last3=McAndrew |first3=Sue |last4=Fairhurst |first4=Helen |date=2021-03-16 |title=The impact of compassionate mind training on qualified health professionals undertaking a compassion-focused therapy module |journal=Counselling and Psychotherapy Research |volume=21 |issue=4 |pages=910–922 |doi=10.1002/capr.12396 |issn=1473-3145}}</ref>

== Overview ==
A central therapeutic technique of CFT is compassionate mind training,<ref name=ci>{{Cite journal |last1=Irons |first1=Chris |last2=Heriot-Maitland |first2=Charles |date=September 2021 |title=Compassionate Mind Training: An 8-week group for the general public |url=https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/papt.12320 |journal=Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice |language=en |volume=94 |issue=3 |pages=443–463 |doi=10.1111/papt.12320 |pmid=33222375 |issn=1476-0835|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Matos |first1=Marcela |last2=Duarte |first2=Cristiana |last3=Duarte |first3=Joana |last4=Pinto-Gouveia |first4=José |last5=Petrocchi |first5=Nicola |last6=Basran |first6=Jaskaran |last7=Gilbert |first7=Paul |date=2017-12-01 |title=Psychological and Physiological Effects of Compassionate Mind Training: a Pilot Randomised Controlled Study |journal=Mindfulness |language=en |volume=8 |issue=6 |pages=1699–1712 |doi=10.1007/s12671-017-0745-7 |hdl=10316/46588 |issn=1868-8535|hdl-access=free }}</ref> which teaches the skills and attributes of [[compassion]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gilbert |first1=Paul |title=Compassion Focused Therapy: Clinical Practice and Applications |last2=Simos |first2=Gregoris |year=2022 |isbn= |language=English}}</ref> Compassionate mind training helps transform problematic patterns of cognition and emotion related to [[anxiety]], [[anger]], [[shame]] and [[self-criticism]].<ref name="Gilbert2009"/>{{rp|208}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kotera |first1=Yasuhiro |last2=Beaumont |first2=Julie |last3=Edwards |first3=Ann-Marie |last4=Cotterill |first4=Matthew |last5=Kirkman |first5=Ann |last6=Tofani |first6=Aiesha Carew |last7=McPhilbin |first7=Merly |last8=Takhi |first8=Simran |last9=Barnes |first9=Kristian |last10=Todowede |first10=Olamide |last11=Ingall |first11=Benjamin-Rose |last12=Asano |first12=Kenichi |last13=Arimitsu |first13=Kohki |date=2024-07-25 |title=A Narrative Review of Compassion Focused Therapy on Positive Mental Health Outcomes |journal=Behavioral Sciences |language=en |volume=14 |issue=8 |page=643 |doi=10.3390/bs14080643 |doi-access=free |issn=2076-328X |pmc=11351419 |pmid=39199039}}</ref>

Biological evolution forms the theoretical backbone of CFT. Humans have evolved with at least three primal types of emotion regulation system: the threat (protection) system, the drive (resource-seeking) system, and the soothing system.<ref name="Gilbert2009"/>{{rp|200}}<ref name="Gilbert2010">{{cite book |last=Gilbert |first=Paul |title=Compassion-focused therapy: distinctive features |year=2010 |series=The CBT distinctive features series |location=London; New York |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-0-415-44807-9 |oclc=463971957 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HhPHBQAAQBAJ}}</ref>{{rp|43}} CFT emphasizes the links between cognitive patterns and these three emotion regulation systems.<ref name="Gilbert2010"/>{{rp|59}} Through the use of techniques such as compassionate mind training and [[cognitive behavioral therapy]] (CBT), counseling clients can learn to manage each system more effectively and respond more appropriately to situations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rayner |first1=Gillian Clare |last2=Bowling |first2=Gosia |last3=Bluff |first3=Lisa |last4=Wright |first4=Karen |last5=Ashworth-Lord |first5=Anneliese |last6=Laird |first6=Catriona |date=September 2022 |title=A multi-method evaluation of a compassion-focused cognitive behavioural psychotherapy group for people who self-harm |journal=Counselling and Psychotherapy Research |language=en |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=569–582 |doi=10.1002/capr.12516 |issn=1473-3145|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Compassion-focused therapy is especially appropriate for people who have high levels of shame and self-criticism and who have difficulty in feeling warmth toward, and being kind to, themselves or others.<ref name="Gilbert2009"/> CFT can help such people learn to feel more safeness and warmth in their interactions with others and themselves.<ref name="Gilbert2009"/>

Numerous methods are used in CFT to develop a person's compassion. For example, people undergoing CFT are taught to understand compassion from the third person, before transferring these thought processes to themselves.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Horwood |first1=Victoria |last2=Allan |first2=Steven |last3=Goss |first3=Kenneth |last4=Gilbert |first4=Paul |date=June 2020 |title=The development of the Compassion Focused Therapy Therapist Competence Rating Scale |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/papt.12230 |journal=Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice |language=en |volume=93 |issue=2 |pages=387–407 |doi=10.1111/papt.12230 |pmid=31021509 |issn=1476-0835|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Gilbert |first1=Paul |last2=Irons |first2=Chris |date=2013 |chapter=Compassion-focused therapy |editor1-last=Dryden |editor1-first=Windy |editor2-last=Reeves |editor2-first=Andrew |title=The handbook of individual therapy |edition= 6th |location=Thousand Oaks, CA |publisher=[[SAGE Publications]] |pages=301–328 |isbn=978-1-4462-0136-7 |oclc=858825414 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Iu6GAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA301}}</ref>{{rp|317}}

== Core principles ==
CFT is an evolutionarily informed psychotherapy largely built on the idea that the evolution of caring behavior has major regulatory and developmental functions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Heriot-Maitland |first1=Charles |last2=Levey |first2=Valerie |date=August 2021 |title=A case report of compassion-focused therapy for distressing voice-hearing experiences |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jclp.23211 |journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology |language=en |volume=77 |issue=8 |pages=1821–1835 |doi=10.1002/jclp.23211 |pmid=34252979 |issn=0021-9762|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Psychosis">{{Cite book|title=Treating psychosis: a clinician's guide to integrating acceptance and commitment therapy, compassion-focused therapy, and mindfulness approaches within the cognitive behavioral therapy tradition|last=Jacobs|first=Andrew M.|date=2014|publisher=[[New Harbinger Publications]]|others=Hopton, Jennifer., Davies, David., Wright, Nicola P., Kelly, Owen P., Turkington, Douglas.|isbn=978-1-60882-408-3|location=Oakland|page=4|oclc=881571856}}</ref>{{rp|4}} The central focus of CFT is to concentrate on helping clients relate to their difficulties in compassionate ways, as well as provide them with effective tools to work with challenging circumstances and emotions they encounter.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Stroud |first1=James |last2=Griffiths |first2=Carys |date=September 2021 |title=An evaluation of compassion-focused therapy within adult mental health inpatient settings |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/papt.12334 |journal=Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice |language=en |volume=94 |issue=3 |pages=587–602 |doi=10.1111/papt.12334 |pmid=33629804 |issn=1476-0835|url-access=subscription }}</ref> CFT helps those learn tools to engage with their battles in accepting and encouraging ways, thereby aiding themselves to feel confident about accomplishing difficult tasks and dealing with challenging situations.<ref name=":0" />

This is facilitated by:

* Developing a positive therapeutic relationship that facilitates the process of engaging with one's challenges and development of skills to deal with them.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=The beginner's guide to counselling and psychotherapy|last1=Gilbert|first1=Paul|last2=Irons|first2=Chris|publisher=[[SAGE Publications]]|others=Palmer, Stephen, 1955-|year=2015|isbn=978-0-85702-234-9|edition= 2nd|location=Los Angeles|pages=3–5|chapter=Compassion Focused Therapy|oclc=905565554}}</ref>
* Developing non-blaming compassionate understandings into the nature of suffering.<ref name=":1" />
* Developing the ability to experience and cultivate compassionate attributes.<ref name=":1" />
* Developing the feeling of compassion for others, being open to compassion from others, and developing self-compassion.<ref name=":1" />

According to evolutionary analysis, there are three types of functional emotion regulation systems: drive, safety and threat. CFT is based on the relationship and interactions between these systems. One is born with each system but our surroundings implicate whether one utilizes and sustains the non-survival-based systems (drive and caregiving).<ref name=":1"/>

* Threat and self-protection focused system: evolved to alert and direct attention to detect and respond to threats. This system contains threat-based emotions (anger, anxiety, disgust), and threat-based behaviors (fight/flight, freezing).<ref name=":1" />
* Drive, seeking and acquisition focused system: pay attention and notice advantageous resources, experience drive and pleasure in securing them (positive system is activating).<ref name=":1" />
* Contentment, soothing and affiliative system: enables state of peacefulness when individuals are no longer focused on threats or seeking out resources (allows body to rest and digest and have open attention).<ref name=":1" />

Using CFT enriches the compassion-based soothing system, while withdrawing from the threat-focused emotional regulation system. In turn, this will augment the ability to activate (drive) and work towards valued goals.<ref name="Psychosis"/>{{rp|11}}

== Applications ==
Compassion-focused therapy has been investigated as a novel treatment for a wide variety of psychological disorders.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Garrett |first1=Charlotte |last2=Smith |first2=Debbie M. |last3=Wittkowski |first3=Anja |date=2025-02-27 |title=The acceptability of compassion-focused therapy in clinical populations: a metasynthesis of the qualitative literature |journal=Frontiers in Psychiatry |language=English |volume=16 |doi=10.3389/fpsyt.2025.1400962 |doi-access=free |issn=1664-0640 |pmc=11903422 |pmid=40084051}}</ref>
A 2012 randomized controlled trial showed CFT to be a safe and clinically effective treatment option for psychosis patients.<ref name=":7">{{cite journal |last1=Braehler |first1=Christine |last2=Gumley |first2=Andrew |last3=Harper |first3=Janice |last4=Wallace |first4=Sonia |last5=Norrie |first5=John |last6=Gilbert |first6=Paul |title=Exploring change processes in compassion-focused therapy in psychosis: Results of a feasibility randomized controlled trial |journal=Clinical Psychology |date=24 October 2012 |volume=52 |issue=2 |pages=199–214 |doi=10.1111/bjc.12009 |pmid=24215148 }}</ref> CFT was shown to be more effective than "treatment as usual", with particular efficacy in reducing depression symptoms.<ref name=":7" /> A further 2015 literature review of 14 different studies showed promising psychotherapeutic benefits of CFT, especially when treating mood disorders.<ref name=":8">{{cite journal |last1=Leaviss |first1=J |last2=Uttley |first2=L |title=Psychotherapeutic benefits of compassion-focused therapy: an early systematic review |journal=Psychological Medicine |volume=45 |issue=5 |pages=927–945 |doi=10.1017/S0033291714002141 |pmid=25215860 |pmc=4413786 |year=2015 }}</ref> A recent meta analysis found good support for CFT as a treatment for a variety of psychological difficulties.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Petrocchi |first1=Nicola |last2=Ottaviani |first2=Cristina |last3=Cheli |first3=Simone |last4=Matos |first4=Marcela |last5=Baldi |first5=Beatrice |last6=Basran |first6=Jaskaran K. |last7=Gilbert |first7=Paul |date=June 2024 |title=The impact of compassion-focused therapy on positive and negative mental health outcomes: Results of a series of meta-analyses. |journal=Clinical Psychology: Science and Practice |language=en |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=230–247 |doi=10.1037/cps0000193 |issn=1468-2850|doi-access=free }}</ref> However, further large-scale trials are necessary in order for CFT to become an accepted, "evidence-based" treatment for these disorders.<ref name=":8" /> For cancer patients, compassion-based interventions including CFT was shown to relieve depression and elevate self-compassion in this population.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fan |first1=Ya-Chi |last2=Hsiao |first2=Fei-Hsiu |last3=Hsieh |first3=Chia-Chen |date=June 2023 |title=The effectiveness of compassion-based interventions among cancer patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=Palliative and Supportive Care |language=en |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=534–546 |doi=10.1017/S1478951522001316 |pmid=36397274 |issn=1478-9515|doi-access=free }}</ref>

CFT has also been explored as a treatment for individuals with eating disorders. This slightly modified version of CFT, CFT-E, has had promising results in treating adult outpatients with restrictive eating disorders as well as with binging and purging disorders.<ref name=":9">{{cite journal |last1=Goss |first1=K |last2=Allan |first2=S |title=The development and application of compassion-focused therapy for eating disorders (CFT-E) |journal=British Journal of Clinical Psychology |date=21 February 2014 |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=62–77 |doi=10.1111/bjc.12039 |pmid=24588762 }}</ref> A 2014 literature review found CFT-E to be a particularly effective treatment for eating disorders due to the fact that it confronts the "high levels of shame and self‐criticism" that patients often experience.<ref name=":9" /> More recent primary studies have further proved CFT-E to be a safe and effective intervention for eating disorders.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kelly |first1=Allison Catherine |last2=Lucene |first2=Wisniewski |last3=Ellen |first3=Hoffman |title=Group-based compassion-focused therapy as an adjunct to outpatient treatment for eating disorders: a pilot randomized controlled trial |journal=Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy |date=30 May 2016 |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=475–487 |doi=10.1002/cpp.2018 |pmid=27237928 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Millard |first1=L. A. |last2=Wan |first2=M. W. |last3=Smith |first3=D. M. |last4=Wittkowski |first4=A. |date=2023-04-01 |title=The effectiveness of compassion focused therapy with clinical populations: A systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=Journal of Affective Disorders |volume=326 |pages=168–192 |doi=10.1016/j.jad.2023.01.010 |pmid=36649790 |issn=0165-0327|doi-access=free }}</ref>

CFT is also being studied as a rehabilitation method for patients with acquired brain injuries (ABI). Preliminary, small-scale studies have shown CFT to be safe and beneficial in treating anxiety and depressive symptoms of ABI patients, although further large-scale studies are needed.<ref name=":10">{{cite journal |last1=Ashworth |first1=Fiona |last2=Clarke |first2=Alexis |last3=Jones |first3=Lisa |last4=Jennings |first4=Caroline |last5=Longworth |first5=Catherine |title=An exploration of compassion-focused therapy following acquired brain injury |journal=Psychology and Psychotherapy |date=15 August 2014 |volume=88 |issue=2 |pages=143–162 |doi=10.1111/papt.12037 |pmid=25123589 }}</ref>

As well as being a psychological therapy (for individuals and groups), Compassionate Mind Training (CMT) has been shown to be an effective approach for reducing psychological distress in the general public. A variety of studies have found that engaging in guided audios,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Matos |first1=Marcela |last2=Duarte |first2=Joana |last3=Duarte |first3=Cristiana |last4=Gilbert |first4=Paul |last5=Pinto-Gouveia |first5=José |date=2018-08-01 |title=How One Experiences and Embodies Compassionate Mind Training Influences Its Effectiveness |journal=Mindfulness |language=en |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=1224–1235 |doi=10.1007/s12671-017-0864-1 |hdl=10316/46590 |issn=1868-8535|hdl-access=free }}</ref> online courses,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Northover |first1=Clare |last2=Deacon |first2=Jack |last3=King |first3=John |last4=Irons |first4=Chris |date=2021-09-21 |title=Developing Self-Compassion Online: Assessing the Efficacy and Feasibility of a Brief Online Intervention |url=http://www.lidsen.com/journals/icm/icm-06-04-056 |journal=OBM Integrative and Complementary Medicine |volume=6 |issue=4 |page=1 |doi=10.21926/obm.icm.2104056|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=#1 Compassion Focused Therapy & Self-Compassion Resources |url=https://balancedminds.com/ |access-date=2024-06-08 |language=en-GB}}</ref> an 8-week group<ref name=ci/> and using an app (The Self-Compassion App) can lead to reductions in self-criticism, shame, attachment insecurity, depression and anxiety symptoms, as well as increasing self-compassion, positive emotions and wellbeing.

CMT has also been used as an effective approach in schools,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Compassion in the Classroom {{!}} Home |url=https://www.cmtschools.org/ |access-date=2024-06-08 |website=www.cmtschools.org}}</ref> with results suggesting a variety of benefits for teachers who engaged in an 8-week compassion training course.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Matos |first1=Marcela |last2=Albuquerque |first2=Isabel |last3=Galhardo |first3=Ana |last4=Cunha |first4=Marina |last5=Lima |first5=Margarida Pedroso |last6=Palmeira |first6=Lara |last7=Petrocchi |first7=Nicola |last8=McEwan |first8=Kirsten |last9=Maratos |first9=Frances A. |last10=Gilbert |first10=Paul |date=2022-03-01 |title=Nurturing compassion in schools: A randomized controlled trial of the effectiveness of a Compassionate Mind Training program for teachers |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=17 |issue=3 |article-number=e0263480 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0263480 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=8887735 |pmid=35231057|bibcode=2022PLoSO..1763480M }}</ref>

== Limitations ==
Beaumont and Hollins Martin (2015)<ref name=":88">{{cite journal |last1=Beaumont |first1=Elaine |last2=Hollins Martin |first2=Caroline |title=A narrative review exploring the effectiveness of Compassion-Focused Therapy |url=https://salford-repository.worktribe.com/output/1417906/a-narrative-review-exploring-the-effectiveness-of-compassion-focused-therapy |journal=Counselling Psychology Review |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=21–32 |date=2015|doi=10.53841/bpscpr.2015.30.1.21 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> examined narrative reviews of 12 research findings that has shown use of CFT to treat and experiment with psychological outcomes in clinical populations. The researchers found that overall, there are improvements of mental health issues with CFT intervention, especially when combined with approaches such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).<ref name=":88" />

Beaumont and Hollins Martin (2015) found a major limitation in the empirical studies are the small number of participants involved in each case. For instance, Gilbert and Proctor (2006) showed small reductions in depression, anxiety, self-criticism and shame, however their participant group involved only 6 members.<ref name=":33">{{cite journal |last1=Gilbert |first1=Paul |last2=Proctor |first2=Sue |title=Compassionate mind training for people with high shame and self-criticism: Overview and pilot study of a group therapy approach. |journal=  Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy|date=November 2006 |volume=13 |issue=6 |pages=353–379 |doi=10.1002/cpp.507}}</ref> The small number of participants can cause bias or facilitate a problem of generalization for the broader population. For instance, out of the twelve studies only two individually supported effectiveness of CFT. A study conducted by Lucre and Corten (2012)<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lucre |first1=K. |last2=Corten |first2=N. |title=An exploration of group compassion-focused therapy for personality disorder |journal= Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice|volume=86 |issue=4 |pages=387–400 |date=2012 |doi=10.1111/j.2044-8341.2012.02068.x|pmid=24217864 }}</ref> found CFT to be effective for treating patients with personality disorders, and another study by Heriot-Maitland et al. (2014)<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Heriot-Maitland |first1=C. |last2=Vidal |first2=J.B |last3=Ball |first3=S. |last4=Irons |first4=C. |title=A compassionate-focused therapy group approach for acute inpatients: Feasibility, initial pilot outcome data, and recommendations |journal= British Journal of Clinical Psychology|date=March 2014 |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=78–94 |doi=10.1111/bjc.12040 |pmid=24588763 }}</ref> found that treating clients in acute inpatient settings was effective.<ref name=":88" />

Subsequently, a meta-analysis<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Petrocchi |first=Nicola |last2=Ottaviani |first2=Cristina |last3=Cheli |first3=Simone |last4=Matos |first4=Marcela |last5=Baldi |first5=Beatrice |last6=Basran |first6=Jaskaran K. |last7=Gilbert |first7=Paul |date=June 2024 |title=The impact of compassion-focused therapy on positive and negative mental health outcomes: Results of a series of meta-analyses. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/cps0000193 |journal=Clinical Psychology: Science and Practice |language=en |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=230–247 |doi=10.1037/cps0000193 |issn=1468-2850|doi-access=free }}</ref> systematically examined all studies published up to 2024. By integrating data on 7,875 participants from 17 countries, the authors showed that CFT was effective in reducing overall negative mental health outcomes and improving compassion for self and others. The qualitative analysis of the studies also confirmed the need for larger-scale, higher-quality randomized controlled trials.

== Recommendations ==
The findings of Beaumont and Hollins Martin (2015) recommended that the effectiveness of CFT needs further extensive research in order to fully examine reductions in mental illnesses and overall improvements in quality of life.<ref name=":88" /> This study and a more recent met-analysis<ref name=":2" /> recommend for consideration of larger samples of participants in order to ensure that CFT can be independently effective without other psychotherapy interventions involved such as CBT.

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Couples therapy
======================================================================

{{Short description|Therapy for people in a couple relationship}}
{{Other uses}}
[[File:Noun Family Counseling 967309.svg|thumb|Couples therapy session ]]
'''Couples therapy''' (also known as '''couples' counseling''', '''marriage counseling''', or '''marriage therapy''') is a form of [[psychotherapy]] that seeks to improve intimate relationships, resolve interpersonal conflicts and repair broken bonds of love.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-05-14 |title=The secret to saving your relationship: eight lessons from a couples therapist |url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2022/may/14/secret-to-saving-your-relationship-eight-lessons-from-a-couples-therapist |access-date=2022-05-31 |website=the Guardian |language=en}}</ref> It may be used to address a variety of concerns, including communication difficulties, relationship distress, infidelity, mental health conditions, and major life transitions.

This article describes the history and development of couples therapy, its theoretical foundations and common therapeutic approaches, research in its effectiveness, applications with different populations, emerging practices and the training and qualifications of couples therapists.

==History==
Marriage counseling first gained recognition in [[Germany]] and [[Austria]] following [[World War I]].<ref name="Stone">{{Cite journal |last=Stone |first=Abraham |date=1949 |title=Marriage Education and Marriage Counseling in the United States |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/347032 |journal=Marriage and Family Living |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=38–50 |doi=10.2307/347032 |issn=0885-7059|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The first institutes for marriage counseling in the United States started in the 1930s, partly in response to Germany's medically directed, [[racial purification]] marriage counseling centers. It was promoted by prominent American eugenicists such as [[Paul Popenoe]], who directed the American Institute of Family Relations until 1976;<ref name="Lepore">{{Cite news |last=Lepore |first=Jill |date=2010-03-22 |title=The Marriage-Improvement Industry |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2010/03/29/fixed |access-date= |work=The New Yorker |language=en-US |issn=0028-792X}}</ref> [[Robert Latou Dickinson]], and by [[birth control]] advocates such as Abraham and Hannah Stone who wrote ''A Marriage Manual'' in 1935 and were involved with [[Planned Parenthood]],<ref name="Kline">{{Cite book |last=Kline |first=Wendy |title=Building a Better Race: Gender, Sexuality, and Eugenics from the Turn of the Century to the Baby Boom |date=November 21, 2005 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0520246744}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=August 2026}} as well as [[Lena Levine]] and [[Margaret Sanger]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lena Levine|url=https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/lena-levine|access-date=2021-06-19|website=www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org}}</ref>

It was not until the 1950s that therapists began treating [[psychological problem]]s within the context of the family.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite book |last=Nichols |first=Michael P. |title=Family Therapy: Concepts and Methods |last2=Schwartz |first2=Richard C. |date=July 28, 1997 |publisher= Allyn & Bacon |isbn=978-0205269839}}</ref> Relationship counseling as a distinct, professional service is thus a recent phenomenon. Until the late 20th century, relationship counseling was informally provided by close friends, family members, or local [[religious]] leaders. [[Psychiatrists]], [[psychologists]], [[counseling|counselors]] and [[social workers]] historically dealt primarily with individual psychological problems within a medical and psychoanalytic framework.<ref name="ReferenceA" />{{Page needed|date=August 2026}} In many cultures, the institution of the [[family]] or group [[elder (administrative title)|elder]]s fulfills the role of relationship counseling; marriage mentoring mirrors these cultures.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

With increasing modernization or [[westernization]] and the continuous shift towards isolated [[nuclear families]], the trend is towards trained and [[Accreditation|accredited]] relationship counselors or couple therapists. Sometimes [[Volunteering|volunteer]]s are trained by either the government or social service institutions to help those who need family or marital counseling. Many communities and government departments have their own teams of trained voluntary and professional relationship counselors. Similar services are operated by many universities and colleges, sometimes staffed by volunteers from among the student [[peer group]]. Some large companies maintain full-time professional counseling staff to facilitate smoother interactions between corporate employees and to minimize the negative effects that personal difficulties might have on work performance.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

There is an increasing trend toward professional certification and government registration of these services, in part due to [[duty of care]] issues and the consequences of the counselor or therapist's services being provided in a [[fiduciary]] relationship.<ref>Stewart v Layton (1992) 111 ALR 687</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=The current source is insufficiently reliable ([[WP:NOTRS]]).|date=August 2026}}

==Basic principles==
[[File:Beach couple 2352352.jpg|thumb|A happy couple at [[Punta del Este]], Uruguay]]
The stats show that around 40% of all married couples in the US have [[divorce|divorced]] in the recent years{{When|date=August 2026}},<ref>{{Cite web |title=Divorce in Decline: About 40% of Today’s Marriages Will End in Divorce |url=https://ifstudies.org/blog/divorce-in-decline-about-40-of-todays-marriages-will-end-in-divorce |access-date=2026-03-10 |website=Institute for Family Studies |language=en}}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=The current source is insufficiently reliable ([[WP:NOTRS]]).|date=August 2026}} and it has been estimated that approximately 20% of all married couples experience marital distress at any given time.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Wall |first=Denny |date=2021-03-10 |title=Marital Distress {{!}} Fact Sheet |url=https://www.abct.org/fact-sheets/marital-distress/ |access-date=2026-03-10 |website=ABCT - Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies |language=en-US}}</ref> These numbers vary between countries and over time; for example, in Germany, only 35.74% of marriages ended in divorce, half of those involving children under 18.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023 |title=Ehescheidungen und betroffene minderjährige Kinder |url=https://www.destatis.de/DE/Themen/Gesellschaft-Umwelt/Bevoelkerung/Eheschliessungen-Ehescheidungen-Lebenspartnerschaften/Tabellen/ehescheidungen-kinder.html }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024 |title=Scheidungsquote in Deutschland von 1960 bis 2023 |url=https://de.statista.com/statistik/daten/studie/76211/umfrage/scheidungsquote-von-1960-bis-2008/ |website=Statista}}</ref> Challenges with affection, communication, disagreements, and fears of divorce are some of the most common reasons couples seek help. Couples who are dissatisfied with their relationship may seek help from a variety of sources including online courses, self-help books, retreats, workshops, and couples' counseling.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Doss|first1=Brian D.|last2=Rhoades|first2=Galena K.|last3=Stanley|first3=Scott M.|last4=Markman|first4=Howard J.|date=January 2009|title=Marital Therapy, Retreats, and Books: The Who, What, When, and Why of Relationship Help-Seeking|url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1111/j.1752-0606.2008.00093.x|journal=Journal of Marital and Family Therapy|language=en|volume=35|issue=1|pages=18–29|doi=10.1111/j.1752-0606.2008.00093.x|pmid=19161581|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Before a relationship between individuals can be understood, it is important to recognize and acknowledge that each person, including the counselor, has a unique [[Personality type|personality]], [[perception]], [[opinion]]s, set of [[Value (ethics and social sciences)|values]], and history. Individuals in the relationship may adhere to different and unexamined value systems. Institutional and societal variables (like social or [[religion|religious]] groups and other collective factors) which shape a person's nature and behavior, are considered in counseling and therapy. A tenet of relationship counseling is that it is intrinsically beneficial for all the participants to interact with each other,and with society at large with optimal amounts of conflict. A couple's conflict resolution skills seem to predict divorce rates.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sternberg |first=Robert J. |title=Satisfaction in Close Relationships |last2=Hojjat |first2=Mahzad |date=June 27, 1997 |publisher= The Guilford Press |isbn=978-1572302174 |pages=344}}</ref>

Most relationships will experience strain at some point, resulting in a failure to function optimally and causing self-reinforcing, [[Maladaptation|maladaptive]] patterns to form, sometimes called "negative interaction cycles."<ref name=":0" /> There are many possible reasons for this, including insecure [[attachment theory|attachment]], [[Human ego|ego]], [[arrogance]], [[jealousy]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sullivan |first=Kieran T. |date=2021-07-16 |title=Attachment Style and Jealousy in the Digital Age: Do Attitudes About Online Communication Matter? |url=https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.678542/full |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |language=English |volume=12 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2021.678542  |doi-access=free|issn=1664-1078|pmc=8322522 }}</ref> [[anger]], [[greed]], poor communication/understanding or [[problem solving|problem-solving]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Mendelson |first=Drew |date=2024-01-22 |title="The Commitment of a Lifetime": The Role of Emotionally Focused Couple Therapy in Strengthening Attachment Bonds and Improving Relationship Health in Later-Life Couples—The Teletherapy Case of "Alice" and "Steve" |url=https://pcsp.nationalregister.org/index.php/pcsp/article/view/2150 |journal=Pragmatic Case Studies in Psychotherapy |language=en |volume=20 |issue=1 |doi=10.55818/pcsp.v20i1.2150 |issn=1553-0124|doi-access=free }}</ref> [[Disease|ill health]],<ref name=":0" /> and third parties.<ref name=":1" />

Changes in circumstances, like finances, physical health, and the influence of other family members can significantly influence the conduct, responses, and actions of the individuals in a relationship.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Peetz |first=Johanna |last2=Fisher-Skau |first2=Odin |last3=Joel |first3=Samantha |date=June 2024 |title=How individuals perceive their partner's relationship behaviors when worrying about finances |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11136612/ |journal=Journal of Social and Personal Relationships |volume=41 |issue=6 |pages=1577–1599 |doi=10.1177/02654075241227454 |issn=0265-4075 |pmc=11136612 |pmid=38828228}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ross |first=D. Bruce |last2=Gale |first2=Jerry |last3=Wickrama |first3=Kandauda K. A. S. |last4=Goetz |first4=Joseph |last5=Vowels |first5=Matthew |date=2019 |title=The Impact of Family Economic Strain On Work-Family Conflict, Marital Support, Marital Quality, and Marital Stability During the Middle Years |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8425486/ |journal=Journal of Personal Finance |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=9–24 |issn=2638-3217 |pmc=8425486 |pmid=34504410}}</ref>

Often, it is an interaction between two or more factors, and frequently, it is not just one of the people involved who exhibit such traits. Relationship influences are reciprocal: each person involved contributes to causing and managing problems.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

A viable solution to the problem and setting these relationships back on track, may be to reorient the individuals' [[perception]]s and [[emotion]]s—how one views or responds to situation, and how one feels about them. Perceptions of, and emotional responses to, a relationship are contained within an often unexamined mental map of the relationship, also called a 'love map' by [[John Gottman]]. These can be explored collaboratively and discussed openly. The core values they comprise can then be understood and respected, or changed when no longer appropriate. This implies that each person takes equal responsibility for awareness of the problem as it arises, awareness of their own contribution to the problem, and making fundamental changes in [[thought]] and [[feeling]]. The next step is to adopt [[Consciousness|conscious]], implement structural changes to the inter-personal relationships, and evaluate the effectiveness of those changes over time.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

==Basic practices==
{{promotional|section|date=December 2018}}
Two methods of couples therapy focus primarily on the process of communicating. The most commonly used method is [[active listening]], used by [[Carl Rogers]] and [[Virginia Satir]]. More recently, a method called "Cinematic Immersion" has been developed by [[Warren Farrell]]. Each describes a communication method intended to provide a structured environment in which partners can express and discuss their feelings.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} 

When the Munich Marital Study discovered active listening was not used in the long run,<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2_WiYestq0cC&pg=PA366 |title = Comprehensive Handbook of Psychotherapy, Cognitive-Behavioral Approaches|isbn = 978-0-471-21100-6|last1 = Kaslow|first1 = Florence W.|last2 = Patterson|first2 = Terence|date = 2004-01-30| publisher=John Wiley & Sons }}</ref> Farrell argued that active listening did a better job of creating a safe environment for the criticizer to criticize than for the listener to hear the criticism. Farrell suggested that the listener often felt overwhelmed by the criticism and tended to avoid future encounters. He hypothesized that people may be biologically predisposed to respond defensively to criticism, and therefore the listener needed in-depth training with mental exercises and methods to interpret criticism differently. His method is cinematic immersion.

After 30 years of research into marriage, [[John Gottman]] found that healthy couples almost never listen and echo each other's feelings naturally. Whether miserable or happy, couples said what they thought about an issue, and "they got angry or sad, but their partner's response was never anything like what we were training people to do in the listener/speaker exercise, not even close."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gottman |first=John M. |title=The Marriage Clinic: A Scientifically Based Marital Therapy |date=March 1, 1999 |isbn=9780393702828}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=August 2026}}

<blockquote>
Such exchanges occurred in less than 5 percent of marital interactions and they predicted nothing about whether the marriage would do well or badly. What's more, Gottman noted, data from a 1984 Munich study demonstrated that the (reflective listening) exercise itself was not associated with improvements in marital outcomes. To teach such interactions, Gottman concluded that it was ineffective as a therapeutic exercise.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://archives.his.com/smartmarriages/2000-March/msg00014.html |title=Smart Marriage Archives |access-date=2009-05-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060617145457/http://archives.his.com/smartmarriages/2000-March/msg00014.html |archive-date=2006-06-17 }}</ref>
</blockquote>

[[Emotionally focused therapy]] for couples (EFT-C) is based on attachment theory and focuses on emotion as a central mechanism of change. According to the model, emotions reflect patterns of interaction that develop over time. As one of its founders, Sue Johnson described EFT as emphasizing emotional attachment and secure bonding between partners rather than focusing primarily on communication techniques.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Johnson |first=Sue |title=Hold Me Tight: Seven Conversations for a Lifetime of Love |year=2008 |isbn=978-0316113007 |pages=6}}</ref> 

Additionally, one study examined the effectiveness of emotionally focused therapy for specific populations. A controlled study of infertile couples reported that participants receiving EFT experiences significant reductions in depression, anxiety, and stress compared to a control group, suggesting that attachment-based interventions were associated with improvement in both emotional well-being and relationship functioning.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Soltani |first=Marzieh |last2=Shairi |first2=Mohammad Reza |last3=Roshan |first3=Rasoul |last4=Rahimi |first4=Changiz Rahimi |date=c. 2014 |title=The impact of emotionally focused therapy on emotional distress in infertile couples |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3901179/ |journal=International Journal of Fertility & Sterility |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=337–344 |issn=2008-076X |pmc=3901179 |pmid=24520504}}</ref>

[[Imago Relationship Therapy]], developed by Harville Hendrix and Helen LaKelly Hunt in the 1980s, is another communication-focused approach. The term "Imago" ([[Latin]] for "image") refers to an unconscious composite image of one's primary caregivers that Hendrix theorizes influences partner selection. According to this model, individuals are drawn to partners who embody both positive and negative traits of their childhood caregivers, unconsciously seeking to heal early relational wounds through adult partnerships.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hendrix |first=Harville |title=Getting the Love You Want: A Guide for Couples |year=1988 |publisher=Henry Holt |location=New York |isbn=978-0805068955}}</ref>

The central technique of Imago therapy is the "Imago Dialogue," a structured communication process with three components: mirroring (reflecting back what the partner said without interpretation), validation (acknowledging the partner's perspective as understandable), and empathy (imagining the partner's emotional experience). This structured format is intended to facilitate structured communication by ensuring each partner feels heard before any response is offered. Hendrix and Hunt describe three relationship stages—romantic love, power struggle, and conscious partnership—with therapy aimed at helping couples move toward what the model describes as a conscious partnership."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hendrix |first1=Harville |last2=Hunt |first2=Helen LaKelly |title=Getting the Love You Want: A Guide for Couples |edition=Revised |year=2019 |publisher=St. Martin's Griffin |location=New York |isbn=978-1250310538}}</ref>

While these approaches differ in emphasis—Gottman focusing on behavioral patterns and interaction ratios, EFT targeting attachment emotions and relational cycles, and Imago exploring developmental origins of partner selection—some researchers and clinicians have described these approaches as complementary. [[Attachment theory]] has been proposed as an explanation for why humans need secure bonds; EFT applies attachment theory to therapeutic practice by accessing vulnerable emotions beneath defensive behaviors; Gottman's model emphasizes behavioral interventions for daily interactions; and Imago Relationship Therapy emphasizes how childhood experiences shape adult relationship patterns. Some contemporary couples therapists use integrative approaches that draw from multiple therapeutic frameworks based on client needs.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gottman |first1=John M. |last2=Gottman |first2=Julie Schwartz |title=10 Principles for Doing Effective Couples Therapy |year=2015 |publisher=W. W. Norton |location=New York |isbn=978-0393708356}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Science of Relationship Repair: A Complete Guide to Evidence-Based Couples Therapy Frameworks |url=https://lovefix.app/resources/relationship-repair-evidence-based-couples-therapy/ |website=LoveFix |access-date=2025-12-27}}</ref>

==Research on therapy==
The most researched approach to couples therapy is behavioral couples therapy.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Chapman | last2 = Compton | year = 2003 | title = From Traditional Behavioral Couple Therapy to Integrative Behavioral Couple Therapy: New Research Directions | url = | journal = The Behavior Analyst Today | volume = 4 | issue = 1| pages = 17–25 | doi = 10.1037/h0100007| doi-access = free }}</ref> It is a well-established treatment for marital discord.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = O'Donohue | first1 = W. | last2 = Ferguson | first2 = K.E. | year = 2006 | title = Evidence-Based Practice in Psychology and Behavior Analysis | url = | journal = The Behavior Analyst Today | volume = 7 | issue = 3| pages = 335–347 | doi = 10.1037/h0100155 | doi-access = free }}</ref> This form of therapy has evolved into [[integrative behavioral couples therapy]]. Integrative behavioral couples therapy appears to be effective for 69% of couples in treatment, while the traditional model was effective for 50–60% of couples.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Christensen | first1 = A | last2 = Atkins | first2 = DC | last3 = Yi | first3 = J | last4 = Baucom | first4 = DH | last5 = George | first5 = WH | year = 2006 | title = The couple and individual adjustment for 2 years following a randomized clinical trial comparing traditional versus integrative behavioral couple therapy | url = | journal = J Consult Clin Psychol | volume = 74 | issue = 6| pages = 1180–91 | doi = 10.1037/0022-006X.74.6.1180 }}</ref> At a five-year follow-up, the marital happiness of the 134 couples who had participated in either integrative behavioral couples therapy or traditional couples therapy showed that 14% of relationships remained unchanged, 38% deteriorated, and 48% improved or recovered completely.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Christensen | year = 2010 | title = Marital status and satisfaction five years following a randomized clinical trial comparing traditional versus integrative behavioral couple therapy | journal = Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology | volume = 78 | issue = 2| pages = 225–235 | doi=10.1037/a0018132| pmid = 20350033 |first=A.|last2=Baucom|first2=B.|last3=Atkins|first3=D.C.|last4=Yi|first4=J.}}</ref>

Recent research has expanded the evidence base for couples therapy across a variety of clinical populations. A 2018 systematic review by [[Cochrane (organisation)|Cochrane (organization)]] found that couples therapy can be a good option for treating depression when relationship problems are also present, but its not necessarily better than individual therapy. Although the authors concluded that the quality of evidence was low because of methodological limitations. The review suggested that couples therapy may provide benefits beyond symptom reduction by addressing relationship dynamics that contribute to mental health outcomes.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Barbato | first1 = A | last2 = D'Avanzo | first2 = B | last3 = Parabiaghi | first3 = A | year = 2018 | title = Couple therapy for depression | journal = Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2018 | issue = 6| article-number = CD004188 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD004188.pub3 | pmid = 29882960 | pmc = 6513419 }}</ref> 

There has also been research examining the effectiveness of couples therapy for situational intimate partner violence (IPV). A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that couples therapy significantly reduced violence among couples experiencing situational IPV. The authors noted that additional research is needed before findings can be generalized, especially to more diverse or severe IPV relationships.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Karakurt |first=Gunnur |last2=Whiting |first2=Kathleen |last3=van Esch |first3=Chantal |last4=Bolen |first4=Shari D. |last5=Calabrese |first5=Joseph R. |date=2016 |title=Couples Therapy for Intimate Partner Violence: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jmft.12178 |journal=Journal of Marital and Family Therapy |language=en |volume=42 |issue=4 |pages=567–583 |doi=10.1111/jmft.12178 |issn=1752-0606 |pmc=5050084 |pmid=27377617}}</ref>

A meta-analysis published in 2023, covering 48 studies of nonrandomized couples therapies, identified influencing factors on the efficiency of coupls therapy in real-world settings. These factors include the age of the partners, the length of the relationship, and the type of institution that provided therapy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Owen |first1=Jesse |last2=Sinha |first2=Sree |last3=Polser |first3=Geneva Crabtree |last4=Hangge |first4=Anna |last5=Davis |first5=Jasmine |last6=Blum |first6=Lena |last7=Drinane |first7=Joanna |date=September 2023 |title=Meta-analysis of couple therapy in non-randomized clinical trial studies: Individual and couple level outcomes |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/famp.12889 |journal=Family Process |language=en |volume=62 |issue=3 |pages=976–992 |doi=10.1111/famp.12889 |pmid=37114710 |issn=0014-7370|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Many studies about research on couples therapy can be found in [[Family Process|''Family Process Journal'']] and ''[[Journal of Marital and Family Therapy]]'', both published by Wiley.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

==Relationship counselor or couple's therapist==
Licensed couple therapists may refer to a [[psychiatrist]], clinical [[social work]]ers, counseling psychologists, clinical psychologists, [[Pastoral counseling|pastoral counselors]], marriage and family therapists, and [[Mental health nursing|psychiatric nurses]].<ref name="ReferenceB">Couples Therapy. The Harvard Mental Health Letter. Gale Group Inc. 2007</ref> The role of a relationship counselor or couples therapist is to listen, respect, understand, and facilitate better functioning between those involved.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

The basic principles for a counselor include:{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}
*Providing a confidential [[dialogue]], which normalizes and validates feelings
*Enabling each person to be heard and to hear themselves
*Providing a mirror with expertise to reflect the relationship's difficulties and the potential and direction for change
*Empowering the relationship to take control of its own destiny and make vital decisions
*Delivering relevant and appropriate information
*Changing the view of the relationship 
*Improving communication
*Setting clear goals and [[Strategic planning|objectives]]

As well as the above, the basic principles for a couples therapist also include:{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}
*Identifying the repetitive, negative interaction cycle as a [[pattern]].
*Understanding the source of reactive emotions that drive the pattern.
*Expanding and re-organizing key emotional responses in the relationship.
*Facilitating a shift in partners' interaction to new patterns of interaction.
*Creating new and positively bonding emotional events in the relationship
*Fostering a secure [[Attachment theory|attachment]] between partners.
*Helping maintain a sense of intimacy.

Common core principles of relationship counseling and couples therapy are:{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}
*[[Respect]]
*[[Empathy]]
*Tact
*[[Consent]]
*[[Confidentiality]]
*[[Accountability]]
*[[Expert]]ise
*[[Evidence-based medicine|Evidence based]]
*[[Certification]] and ongoing [[training]]

In both methods, the practitioner evaluates the couple's personal and relationship story as it is narrated, interrupts wisely, and facilitates both de-escalations of unhelpful conflict and the development of realistic, practical solutions. The practitioner may meet each person individually at first, but only if this is beneficial to both, it is [[Consent|consensual]], and it is unlikely to cause harm—individualistic approaches to couple problems can cause harm. The counselor or therapist encourages the participants to give their best efforts to reorient their relationship with each other. One of the challenges here is for each person to change their own responses to their partner's behavior. Other challenges to the process are disclosing controversial or shameful events and revealing closely guarded secrets. Not all couples put all of their cards on the table at first. This can take time, and requires patience and commitment to repairing the relationship.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

Many couples delay professional help despite experiencing significant relationship distress. A descriptive study of veteran couples found that communication difficulties, lack of trust and external life stressors are the most common reasons couples eventually seek therapy. Many participants waited several years before seeking treatment and even attempted self-directed strategies to improve their relationship before consulting a therapist. This suggests that barriers to treatment and delayed help-seeking are common among couples and can contribute to worsening relationship distress over time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jarnecke |first=Amber M. |last2=Ridings |first2=Leigh E. |last3=Teves |first3=Jenna B. |last4=Petty |first4=Karen |last5=Bhatia |first5=Vickie |last6=Libet |first6=Julian |date=c. 2020 |title=The path to couples therapy: A descriptive analysis on a veteran sample. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/cfp0000135 |journal=Couple and Family Psychology: Research and Practice |language=en |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=73–89 |doi=10.1037/cfp0000135 |issn=2160-410X |pmc=7351137 |pmid=32655982}}</ref>

==Novel practices==
A novel development involves introducing insights gained from [[affective neuroscience]] and [[psychopharmacology]] into clinical practice.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Atkinson B., Atkinson L., Kutz P.|display-authors=et al|year=2005|title=Rewiring Neural States in Couples Therapy: Advances from Affective Neuroscience|journal=Journal of Systemic Therapies|volume=24|issue=3|pages=3–16|doi=10.1521/jsyt.2005.24.3.3 |s2cid=143952777 }}</ref>

===Oxytocin===
There has been interest in using [[oxytocin (medication)|oxytocin]] during therapy sessions, although this is still largely experimental and somewhat controversial.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Resnikoff R | year = 2002 | title = Couples Therapy and Psychopharmacology | url = http://www.psychiatrictimes.com/Psychotherapy/showArticle.jhtml?checkSite=psychiatricTimes&articleID=175802181 | journal = Psychiatric Times | volume = 19 | issue = 7 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |pmc=3935449|year=2013|last1=Wudarczyk|first1=O. A.|title=Could intranasal oxytocin be used to enhance relationships? Research imperatives, clinical policy, and ethical considerations|journal=Current Opinion in Psychiatry|volume=26|issue=5|pages=474–484|last2=Earp|first2=B. D.|last3=Guastella|first3=A|last4=Savulescu|first4=J|doi=10.1097/YCO.0b013e3283642e10|pmid=23880593}}</ref><ref>Smith, D. [http://www.smh.com.au/news/science/clashing-couples-to-get-a-spray-of-love/2007/05/25/1179601669078.html# Clashing couples to get a spray of love.] ''Sydney Morning Herald'' May 26, 2007.</ref> Some researchers have argued oxytocin has a general enhancing effect on all social emotions, since intranasal administration of oxytocin also increases [[envy]] and ''[[Schadenfreude]]''.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Shamay-Tsoory SG, Fischer M, Dvash J, Harari H, Perach-Bloom N, Levkovitz Y | title = Intranasal administration of oxytocin increases envy and schadenfreude (gloating) | journal = Biological Psychiatry | volume = 66 | issue = 9 | pages = 864–70 | date = November 2009 | pmid = 19640508 | doi = 10.1016/j.biopsych.2009.06.009 | s2cid = 20396036 }}</ref> Also, oxytocin has the potential for abuse in [[confidence trick]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |pmc=3308927|year=2012|last1=Tennison|first1=M. N.|title=Neuroscience, Ethics, and National Security: The State of the Art|journal=PLOS Biology|volume=10|issue=3|article-number=e1001289|last2=Moreno|first2=J. D.|doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.1001289|pmid=22448146 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study involving couples affected by substance misuse found that oxytocin reduced physiological stress responses in women during conflict discussions but did not significantly improve conflict resolution behaviors or communication outcomes. These findings suggest that while oxytocin may influence stress regulation, additional research is needed before it can be considered an effective therapeutic intervention for couples therapy.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2018-02-01 |title=Effects of oxytocin on cortisol reactivity and conflict resolution behaviors among couples with substance misuse |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165178117304936 |journal=Psychiatry Research |language=en-US |volume=260 |pages=346–352 |doi=10.1016/j.psychres.2017.12.003 |issn=0165-1781 |pmc=5988859 |pmid=29232576}}</ref>

==Outside of heteronormativity ==
{{See also|Homosexuality and psychology|Sexual relationship disorder|List of transgender-related topics}}
Differing psychological theories play an important role in determining how effective relationship counseling is, especially when it concerns [[Homosexuality|gay]] and [[Bisexuality|bisexual]] clients. Some experts tout [[cognitive behavioral therapy]] as the tool of choice for intervention, while many rely on [[acceptance and commitment therapy]] or [[cognitive analytic therapy]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = Psychotherapies|url = https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/psychotherapies|website = www.nimh.nih.gov|access-date = 2015-11-27}}</ref> One major progress in this area is the fact that "marital therapy" is now referred to as "couples therapy" in order to include individuals who are not married or those who are engaged in same-sex relationships.<ref name="ReferenceB" /> Most relationship issues are shared equally among couples regardless of [[sexual orientation]], but [[LGBT]] clients additionally have to deal with [[heteronormativity]], [[homophobia]], [[biphobia]], and both socio-cultural and legal [[discrimination]].<ref name=":2" /> Individuals may experience relational ambiguity from being in different stages of the [[coming out]] process or having an [[HIV]] [[serodiscordant]] relationship. Often, same-sex couples do not have as many role models of successful relationships as opposite-sex couples. In many jurisdictions, committed LGBT couples desiring a family are denied access to [[Assisted reproductive technology|assisted reproduction]], [[adoption]] and [[Foster care|fostering]], leaving them [[Childlessness|childless]], feeling excluded, [[Other (philosophy)|other]], and [[Grief|bereaved]]. There may be issues with [[gender role]] socialization that do not affect opposite-sex couples.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Bigner |first=Jerry J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tIefcYvSQ5IC&dq=Buxton+2001+marriage&pg=PA95 |title=Relationship Therapy with Same-sex Couples |last2=Wetchler |first2=Joseph L. |date=2004 |publisher=Haworth Press |isbn=978-0-7890-2555-5 |language=en}}</ref>

A significant number of men and women experience conflict surrounding homosexual expression within a [[mixed-orientation marriage|mixed-orientation]] marriage⁣⁣.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Wolf TJ |title=Group psychotherapy for bisexual men and their wives |journal=J. Homosex. |volume=14 |issue=1–2 |pages=191–9 |year=1987 |pmid=3655341 |doi=10.1300/J082v14n01_14 }}</ref> Couple therapy may include helping the clients feel more comfortable and accepting of same-sex feelings and to explore ways of incorporating same-sex and opposite-sex feelings into life patterns.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Coleman E |title=Bisexual and gay men in heterosexual marriage: conflicts and resolutions in therapy |journal=J. Homosex. |volume=7 |issue=2–3 |pages=93–103 |year=1981 |pmid=7346553 |doi=10.1300/J082v07n02_11 }}</ref> Although a strong [[Gay|gay identity]] was associated with difficulties in marital satisfaction, viewing same-sex activities as compulsive facilitated commitment to the marriage and to [[monogamy]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Schneider JP, Schneider BH|title=Marital satisfaction during recovery from self-identified sexual addiction among bisexual men and their wives |journal=J Sex Marital Ther |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=230–50 |year=1990 |pmid=2079706 |doi=10.1080/00926239008405460}}</ref>

Research has also emphasized the importance of providing affirming and culturally competent therapy to clients in consensually non-monogamous (CNM) relationships. Studies indicate that therapists who demonstrate knowledge on CNM relationships and avoid pathologizing clients' relationship structures are associated with more positive therapeutic experiences. In contrast, biased and uninformed therapeutic practices have been linked to poorer treatment experiences and ending therapy early.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schechinger |first=Heath A. |last2=Sakaluk |first2=John Kitchener |last3=Moors |first3=Amy C. |date=c. 2018 |title=Harmful and helpful therapy practices with consensually non-monogamous clients: Toward an inclusive framework. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/ccp0000349 |journal=Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology |language=en |volume=86 |issue=11 |pages=879–891 |doi=10.1037/ccp0000349 |issn=1939-2117}}</ref>
