{{short description|Treatment method for anxiety disorders}}
{{cs1 config|name-list-style=vanc}}
'''Exposure therapy''' is a technique in behavior therapy to treat [[anxiety disorder]]s. Exposure therapy involves exposing the patient to the anxiety source or its context (without the intention to cause any danger). Doing so is thought to help them overcome their anxiety or distress.<ref name="Myers_2007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Myers KM, Davis M | title = Mechanisms of fear extinction | journal = Molecular Psychiatry | volume = 12 | issue = 2 | pages = 120–150 | date = February 2007 | pmid = 17160066 | doi = 10.1038/sj.mp.4001939 | doi-access = free }}</ref>{{rp|141–142}}<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Joseph JS, Gray MJ | year = 2008 | title = Exposure Therapy for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder | journal = Journal of Behavior Analysis of Offender and Victim: Treatment and Prevention | volume = 1 | issue = 4| pages = 69–80 | doi=10.1037/h0100457| doi-access = free }}</ref> Numerous studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in the treatment of disorders such as [[generalized anxiety disorder]], [[social anxiety disorder]], [[obsessive–compulsive disorder]] (OCD),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Huppert |first1=Jonathan D. |last2=Roth |first2=Deborah A. |title=Treating obsessive-compulsive disorder with exposure and response prevention. |journal=The Behavior Analyst Today |date=2003 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=66–70 |doi=10.1037/h0100012 |doi-access=free }}</ref> [[post-traumatic stress disorder]] (PTSD),<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://effectivehealthcare.ahrq.gov/topics/ptsd-adult-treatment-update/research-2018 |title=Psychological and Pharmacological Treatments for Adults With Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Systematic Review Update |last1=Forman-Hoffman |first1=Valerie |last2=Cook Middleton |first2=Jennifer |date=2018-05-17 |publisher=Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) |doi=10.23970/ahrqepccer207 |last3=Feltner |first3=Cynthia |last4=Gaynes |first4=Bradley N. |last5=Palmieri Weber |first5=Rachel |last6=Bann |first6=Carla |last7=Viswanathan |first7=Meera |last8=Lohr |first8=Kathleen N. |last9=Baker |first9=Claire|doi-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Depression (mood)|depression]], and [[specific phobias]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Böhnlein J, Altegoer L, Muck NK, Roesmann K, Redlich R, Dannlowski U, Leehr EJ | title = Factors influencing the success of exposure therapy for specific phobia: A systematic review | journal = Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews | volume = 108 | pages = 796–820 | date = January 2020 | pmid = 31830494 | doi = 10.1016/j.neubiorev.2019.12.009 | doi-access = free }}</ref> 

As of 2024, focus is particularly on exposure and response prevention (ERP or ExRP) therapy, in which exposure is continued and the resolution to refrain from the escape response is maintained at all times (not just during specific therapy sessions).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Himle |first1=Joseph A. |last2=Grogan-Kaylor |first2=Andrew |last3=Hiller |first3=Matthew A. |last4=Mannella |first4=Kristin A. |last5=Norman |first5=Luke J. |last6=Abelson |first6=James L. |last7=Prout |first7=Aileen |last8=Shunnarah |first8=Angela A. |last9=Becker |first9=Hannah C. |last10=Russman Block |first10=Stefanie R. |last11=Taylor |first11=Stephan F. |last12=Fitzgerald |first12=Kate D. |title=Exposure and response prevention versus stress management training for adults and adolescents with obsessive compulsive disorder: A randomized clinical trial |journal=Behaviour Research and Therapy |date=January 2024 |volume=172 |article-number=104458 |doi=10.1016/j.brat.2023.104458 |pmid=38103359 |s2cid=266285353 |pmc=11639395 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Song |first1=Yuqi |last2=Li |first2=Dongxu |last3=Zhang |first3=Shuyu |last4=Jin |first4=Zirong |last5=Zhen |first5=Yuanyuan |last6=Su |first6=Yiyang |last7=Zhang |first7=Muzi |last8=Lu |first8=Liuyang |last9=Xue |first9=Xiangrui |last10=Luo |first10=Jingyi |last11=Liang |first11=Meng |last12=Li |first12=Xiaoming |title=The effect of exposure and response prevention therapy on obsessive-compulsive disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=Psychiatry Research |date=November 2022 |volume=317 |article-number=114861 |doi=10.1016/j.psychres.2022.114861 |pmid=36179591 |s2cid=252530334 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-809324-5.05378-5 |chapter=Posttraumatic Stress Disorder |title=Reference Module in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Psychology |date=2017 |last1=Wynn |first1=G.H. |last2=Ursano |first2=R.J. |isbn=978-0-12-809324-5 }}</ref><ref name="auto2">{{Cite web|url=https://iocdf.org/about-ocd/treatment/erp/|title=International OCD Foundation &#124; Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP)}}</ref>

==Techniques==
Exposure therapy is based on the principle of [[respondent conditioning]] often termed Pavlovian extinction.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Marks IM |title=Cure and care of neuroses: theory and practice of behavioral psychotherapy |publisher=Wiley |location=New York |year=1981 |isbn=978-0-471-08808-0}}{{pn|date=February 2024}}</ref> The exposure therapist identifies the cognitions, emotions and physiological arousal that accompany a fear-inducing stimulus and then tries to break the pattern of escape that maintains the fear. This is done by exposing the patient to fear-inducing stimuli.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = De Silva P, Rachman S | title = Is exposure a necessary condition for fear-reduction? | journal = Behaviour Research and Therapy | volume = 19 | issue = 3 | pages = 227–232 | year = 1981 | pmid = 6117277 | doi = 10.1016/0005-7967(81)90006-1 }}</ref> 

This may be done:
* using progressively stronger stimuli. Fear is minimized at each of a series of steadily escalating steps or challenges (a [[Exposure hierarchy|hierarchy]]), which can be explicit ("static") or implicit ("dynamic" – see [[Method of Factors]]) until the fear is finally gone.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Miltenberger RG | title = Behavioral Modification: Principles and Procedures | publisher = [[Thomson/Wadsworth]] | date = 2008 | edition = 4th | page = 552 }}</ref> The patient is able to terminate the procedure at any time.
* using [[Flooding (psychology)|flooding therapy]], which exposes the patient to feared stimuli starting at the most feared item in a fear [[Exposure hierarchy|hierarchy]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = de Silva P, Rachman S | title = Exposure and fear-reduction | journal = Behaviour Research and Therapy | volume = 21 | issue = 2 | pages = 151–152 | year = 1983 | pmid = 6838470 | doi = 10.1016/0005-7967(83)90160-2 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cobb J | title = Behaviour therapy in phobic and obsessional disorders | journal = Psychiatric Developments | volume = 1 | issue = 4 | pages = 351–365 | year = 1983 | pmid = 6144099 }}</ref>

There are several types of exposure procedures:
* [[In vivo]] or "real life".<ref name="Kaplan_2021">{{Cite journal | vauthors = Kaplan JS, Tolin DF |title=Exposure Therapy for Anxiety Disorders|url=https://www.psychiatrictimes.com/view/exposure-therapy-anxiety-disorders|access-date=2021-09-22|journal=Psychiatric Times |date=6 September 2011 |volume=28 |issue=9}}</ref> This type exposes the patient to actual fear-inducing situations. For example, if someone fears public speaking, the person may be asked to give a speech to a small group of people. 
* [[Virtual reality]], in which technology is used to simulate in vivo exposure. Studies suggest that immersive virtual reality has the ability to mimic feared stimuli and patients actually perceive them as real threats.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ramsey |first1=Kesley A. |last2=Essoe |first2=Joey Ka-Yee |last3=Boyle |first3=Nathan |last4=Patrick |first4=Ainsley K. |last5=McGuire |first5=Joseph F. |date=2025-08-01 |title=Immersive Virtual Reality Exposures for the Treatment of Childhood Anxiety |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10578-023-01628-4 |journal=Child Psychiatry & Human Development |language=en |volume=56 |issue=4 |pages=1117–1128 |doi=10.1007/s10578-023-01628-4 |pmid=37985621 |issn=1573-3327|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* [[imagination|Imaginal]], where patients are asked to imagine a situation that they are afraid of. This procedure is helpful for people who need to confront feared thoughts and memories. 
* [[Narrative exposure therapy|Written exposure therapy]], where patients write down their account of the traumatic event 
* [[Interoceptive]], in which patients confront feared bodily symptoms such as increased heart rate and shortness of breath. This may be used for more specific disorders such as [[Panic disorder|panic]] or [[post-traumatic stress disorder]].
* Self Distancing- A cognitive strategy typically used alongside exposure therapy where an individual refers to themselves in third person allowing them take a step back and see the fearful stimulus through a less intimidating perspective.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bilek |first1=Emily L. |last2=Meyer |first2=Allison E. |last3=Tomlinson |first3=Rachel |last4=Chen |first4=Carol |date=2025-02-01 |title=Pilot Study of Self-Distancing Augmentation to Exposure Therapy for Youth Anxiety |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10578-023-01540-x |journal=Child Psychiatry & Human Development |language=en |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=153–165 |doi=10.1007/s10578-023-01540-x |issn=1573-3327 |pmc=10212740 |pmid=37231323}}</ref>
The various types of exposure may be used together or separately.<ref name="Foa">{{cite journal | vauthors = Foa EB | title = Prolonged exposure therapy: past, present, and future | journal = Depression and Anxiety | volume = 28 | issue = 12 | pages = 1043–1047 | date = December 2011 | pmid = 22134957 | doi = 10.1002/da.20907 | s2cid = 28115857 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/25067-exposure-therapy|title=Exposure therapy|website=Cleveland Clinic}}</ref><ref name="APA-PTSD" /> Discussion continues on how best to carry out exposure therapy, including on whether safety behaviors should be discontinued.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.psychologytools.com/resource/safety-behaviors|title=Safety Behaviors|website=Psychology Tools}}</ref><ref name="auto1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.psychologytools.com/articles/delivering-more-effective-exposure-therapy-in-cbt/|title=Delivering More Effective Exposure Therapy In CBT|website=Psychology Tools}}</ref> A 2024 literature review of studies of adults with PTSD compared in-person exposure therapies to digital and found comparable results between the two.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yoshikawa |first1=Mayu |last2=Narita |first2=Zui |last3=Kim |first3=Yoshiharu |date=2024 |title=Digital health–based exposure therapies for patients with posttraumatic stress disorder: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jts.23052 |journal=Journal of Traumatic Stress |language=en |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=814–824 |doi=10.1002/jts.23052 |pmid=38637958 |issn=0894-9867}}</ref>

===Exposure and response prevention (ERP) ===
In the exposure and response prevention (ERP or EX/RP) form of exposure therapy, the resolution to refrain from the [[escape response]] is to be maintained at all times (not just during specific practice sessions).<ref name="Hezel_2019">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hezel DM, Simpson HB | title = Exposure and response prevention for obsessive-compulsive disorder: A review and new directions | journal = Indian Journal of Psychiatry | volume = 61 | issue = Suppl 1 | pages = S85–S92 | date = January 2019 | pmid = 30745681 | pmc = 6343408 | doi = 10.4103/psychiatry.IndianJPsychiatry_516_18 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Thus, not only does the subject experience [[habituation]] to the feared stimulus, but they also practice a fear-incompatible behavioral response to the stimulus. The distinctive feature is that individuals confront their fears and discontinue their escape response.<ref name="Abramowitz_2011">{{cite book |last1=Abramowitz |first1=Jonathan S. |last2=Deacon |first2=Brett J. |last3=Whiteside |first3=Stephen P. H. |title=Exposure Therapy for Anxiety: Principles and Practice |date=2011 |publisher=Guilford Press |isbn=978-1-60918-017-1 }}{{pn|date=February 2024}}</ref>

While this type of therapy typically causes some short-term anxiety, this facilitates long-term reduction in obsessive and compulsive symptoms.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Ten Things You Need To Know To Overcome OCD|url=https://beyondocd.org/expert-perspectives/articles/ten-things-you-need-to-know-to-overcome-ocd|access-date=2020-08-17|website=Beyond OCD|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book | vauthors = Abramowitz JS, Deacon BJ, Whiteside SP | chapter = Treatment Planning II: Hierarchy Development and Treatment Engagement |title = Exposure Therapy for Anxiety: Principles and Practice| chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=pnoznH2c7esC&pg=PT103|publisher = Guilford Press|date = 2011-03-14|isbn = 978-1-60918-017-1}}</ref>{{rp|103}}<ref name="auto2"/> 

The American Psychiatric Association recommends ERP for the treatment of [[OCD]], citing that ERP has the richest empirical support.<ref name="AAP2007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Koran LM, Hanna GL, Hollander E, Nestadt G, Simpson HB | title = Practice guideline for the treatment of patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder | journal = The American Journal of Psychiatry | volume = 164 | issue = 7 Suppl | pages = 5–53 | date = July 2007 | pmid = 17849776 | url = http://psychiatryonline.org/pb/assets/raw/sitewide/practice_guidelines/guidelines/ocd.pdf }}</ref> {{As of|2019}}, ERP is considered a first-line psychotherapy for OCD.<ref name="Hezel_2019"/><ref>"The best treatment for OCD is CBT which typically includes exposure and response prevention (ERP) and some degree of more cognitive interventions." {{Cite web|url=https://iocdf.org/expert-opinions/expert-opinion-relapse-prevention/|title=Relapse Prevention in the Treatment of OCD}}</ref> A 2024 systematic review found that ERP is highly effective in treating pediatric OCD using both in-person and telehealth-based modailites<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://effectivehealthcare.ahrq.gov/products/obsessive-compulsive-disorder/research |title=Diagnosis and Management of Obsessive Compulsive Disorders in Children: A Systematic Review |last1=Steele |first1=Dale W. |last2=Caputo |first2=Eduardo L. |last3=Kanaan |first3=Ghid |last4=Zahradnik |first4=Michael L. |last5=Brannon |first5=Elizabeth |last6=Freeman |first6=Jennifer B. |last7=Balk |first7=Ethan M. |last8=Trikalinos |first8=Thomas A. |last9=Adam |first9=Gaelen P. |date=2024-12-06 |publisher=Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) |doi=10.23970/ahrqepccer276|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and a 2025 meta-analysis ranked exposure and response prevention among the top three treatments for children and adolescents with OCD, whether delivered in person or through telehealth.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Steele |first1=Dale W. |last2=Kanaan |first2=Ghid |last3=Caputo |first3=Eduardo L. |last4=Freeman |first4=Jennifer B. |last5=Brannan |first5=Elizabeth H. |last6=Balk |first6=Ethan M. |last7=Trikalinos |first7=Thomas A. |last8=Adam |first8=Gaelen P. |date=2025-03-01 |title=Treatment of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder in Children and Youth: A Meta-Analysis |journal=Pediatrics |language=en |volume=155 |issue=3 |article-number=e2024068992 |doi=10.1542/peds.2024-068992 |issn=0031-4005|doi-access=free |pmid=39639456 }}</ref>

Effectiveness is heterogeneous. Higher efficacy correlates with lower avoidance behaviours, and greater adherence to homework. Using [[SSRI]] meds whilst doing ERP does not appear to correlate with better outcomes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kim |first1=Hyunsik |last2=Wheaton |first2=Michael G. |last3=Foa |first3=Edna B. |last4=Simpson |first4=H. Blair |title=Identifying trajectories of symptom change in adults with obsessive compulsive disorder receiving exposure and response prevention therapy |journal=Journal of Anxiety Disorders |date=May 2023 |volume=96 |article-number=102711 |doi=10.1016/j.janxdis.2023.102711 |pmid=37148799 |pmc=10209477 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wheaton |first1=Michael G. |last2=Rosenfield |first2=Benjamin |last3=Rosenfield |first3=David |last4=Marsh |first4=Rachel |last5=Foa |first5=Edna B. |last6=Simpson |first6=H. Blair |title=Predictors of EX/RP alone versus EX/RP with medication for adults with OCD: Does medication status moderate outcomes? |journal=Journal of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders |date=October 2023 |volume=39 |article-number=100850 |doi=10.1016/j.jocrd.2023.100850 |pmid=38054078 |pmc=10695351 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Development of a Patient Adherence Scale for Exposure and Response Prevention Therapy|first1=Helen Blair|last1=Simpson|first2=Michael|last2=Maher|first3=Jessica R.|last3=Page|first4=Carly J.|last4=Gibbons|first5=Martin E.|last5=Franklin|first6=Edna B.|last6=Foa|date=March 10, 2010|journal=Behavior Therapy|volume=41|issue=1|pages=30–37|doi=10.1016/j.beth.2008.12.002|pmid=20171325|pmc=3949512}}</ref> Discussion continues on how to best conduct ERP.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ong |first1=Clarissa W. |last2=Petersen |first2=Julie M. |last3=Terry |first3=Carina L. |last4=Krafft |first4=Jennifer |last5=Barney |first5=Jennifer L. |last6=Abramowitz |first6=Jonathan S. |last7=Twohig |first7=Michael P. |title=The 'how' of exposures: Examining the relationship between exposure parameters and outcomes in obsessive-compulsive disorder |journal=Journal of Contextual Behavioral Science |date=April 2022 |volume=24 |pages=87–95 |doi=10.1016/j.jcbs.2022.03.009 |s2cid=247802575 |url=https://digitalcommons.usu.edu/psych_facpub/2058 }}</ref>

Generally, ERP incorporates a [[relapse prevention]] plan toward the end of the course of therapy.<ref name="Hezel_2019" /> This can include being ready to re-apply ERP if an anxiety does occur.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://iocdf.org/expert-opinions/expert-opinion-relapse-prevention/|title=Relapse Prevention in the Treatment of OCD}}</ref>

==Mechanism==
Mechanism research has been limited in the field.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Tolin DF, McKay D, Olatunji BO, Abramowitz JS, Otto MW | title = On the importance of identifying mechanisms and active ingredients of psychological treatments | journal = Behaviour Research and Therapy | volume = 170 | article-number = 104425 | date = November 2023 | pmid = 37913558 | doi = 10.1016/j.brat.2023.104425 | pmc = 11034847 | s2cid = 264571425 }}</ref>

[[Habituation]] was seen as a mechanism in the past, but is seen more recently as a model of therapeutic process.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Benito |first1=Kristen G. |last2=Walther |first2=Michael |title=Therapeutic process during exposure: Habituation model |journal=Journal of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders |date=July 2015 |volume=6 |pages=147–157 |doi=10.1016/j.jocrd.2015.01.006 |pmid=26258012 |pmc=4525711 }}</ref>

===Inhibitory learning===
As of 2022, the inhibitory learning model is the most common conjecture of the mechanism which causes exposure therapy efficacy. This model posits that in exposure therapy the unpleasant reactions such as anxiety (that were previously learned during fear conditioning) remain intact - they are not expected to be eliminated - but that they are now inhibited or balanced or overcome by new learning about the situation (for instance that the feared result will not necessarily happen).<ref name="auto1"/><ref name="Craske_2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Craske MG, Treanor M, Conway CC, Zbozinek T, Vervliet B | title = Maximizing exposure therapy: an inhibitory learning approach | journal = Behaviour Research and Therapy | volume = 58 | pages = 10–23 | date = July 2014 | pmid = 24864005 | pmc = 4114726 | doi = 10.1016/j.brat.2014.04.006 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book | vauthors = Sewart AR, Craske MG | chapter = Inhibitory learning. | veditors = Abramowitz JS, Blakey SM | title = Clinical handbook of fear and anxiety: Maintenance processes and treatment mechanisms | pages = 265–285 | publisher = American Psychological Association. | chapter-url=https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2019-52029-015 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://iocdf.org/expert-opinions/the-inhibitory-learning-approach-to-exposure-and-response-prevention/|title=The Inhibitory Learning Approach to Exposure and Response Prevention}}</ref> More research is needed.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lebois |first1=Lauren A.M. |last2=Seligowski |first2=Antonia V. |last3=Wolff |first3=Jonathan D. |last4=Hill |first4=Sarah B. |last5=Ressler |first5=Kerry J. |title=Augmentation of Extinction and Inhibitory Learning in Anxiety and Trauma-Related Disorders |journal=Annual Review of Clinical Psychology |date=7 May 2019 |volume=15 |pages=257–284 |doi=10.1146/annurev-clinpsy-050718-095634 |pmid=30698994 |pmc=6547363 }}</ref>

===Inhibitory retrieval===
This model posits that additional associative learning processes, such as counterconditioning and novelty-enhanced extinction may contribute to exposure therapy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Craske |first1=Michelle G. |last2=Treanor |first2=Michael |last3=Zbozinek |first3=Tomislav D. |last4=Vervliet |first4=Bram |title=Optimizing exposure therapy with an inhibitory retrieval approach and the OptEx Nexus |journal=Behaviour Research and Therapy |date=May 2022 |volume=152 |article-number=104069 |doi=10.1016/j.brat.2022.104069 |pmid=35325683 |s2cid=247487555 |url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechAUTHORS:20220318-999075000 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brevers |first1=Damien |last2=Philippot |first2=Pierre |title=An inhibitory retrieval approach for maximizing exposure therapy in elite sport |journal=Journal of Applied Sport Psychology |date=3 November 2023 |volume=35 |issue=6 |pages=941–959 |doi=10.1080/10413200.2023.2166154 |s2cid=255798306 |hdl=2078.1/274834 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Under-use and barriers to use==
Exposure therapy is seen as under-used in relation to its efficacy.<ref name="Becker-Haimes_2022">{{cite journal | vauthors = Becker-Haimes EM, Stewart RE, Frank HE | title = It's all in the name: why exposure therapy could benefit from a new one | journal = Current Psychology | volume = 42 | issue = 25 | pages = 21641–21647 | date = June 2022 | pmid = 35669210 | pmc = 9161762 | doi = 10.1007/s12144-022-03286-6 }}</ref> Barriers to use of exposure therapy by psychologists include it appearing antithetical to mainline psychology,<ref name="Becker-Haimes_2022"/> lack of confidence, and negative beliefs about exposure therapy.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Moses K, Gonsalvez CJ, Meade T | title = Barriers to the use of exposure therapy by psychologists treating anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and posttraumatic stress disorder in an Australian sample | journal = Journal of Clinical Psychology | volume = 79 | issue = 4 | pages = 1156–1165 | date = April 2023 | pmid = 36449416 | doi = 10.1002/jclp.23470 | s2cid = 254093759 }}</ref> 

==Uses==

===Phobia===
Exposure therapy is the most successful known treatment for phobias.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chambless DL, Ollendick TH | title = Empirically supported psychological interventions: controversies and evidence | journal = Annual Review of Psychology | volume = 52 | issue = 1 | pages = 685–716 | year = 2001 | pmid = 11148322 | doi = 10.1146/annurev.psych.52.1.685 | s2cid = 9487499 }}</ref> Several published meta-analyses included studies of one-to-three-hour single-session treatments of phobias, using imaginal exposure. At a post-treatment follow-up four years later 90% of people retained a considerable reduction in fear, avoidance, and overall level of impairment, while 65% no longer experienced any symptoms of a specific phobia.<ref name="Kaplan_2021" />

[[Agoraphobia]] and [[social anxiety disorder]] are examples of phobias that have been successfully treated by exposure therapy.<ref name="Vogele">{{cite journal | vauthors = Vögele C, Ehlers A, Meyer AH, Frank M, Hahlweg K, Margraf J | title = Cognitive mediation of clinical improvement after intensive exposure therapy of agoraphobia and social phobia | journal = Depression and Anxiety | volume = 27 | issue = 3 | pages = 294–301 | date = March 2010 | pmid = 20037922 | doi = 10.1002/da.20651 | s2cid = 21915062 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Post-traumatic stress disorder===

Exposure therapy in [[Post-traumatic stress disorder|PTSD]] involves exposing the patient to PTSD-anxiety triggering stimuli, with the aim of weakening the neural connections between triggers and trauma memories ({{aka}} [[desensitization (psychology)|desensitization]]). Exposure may involve:<ref name="APA-PTSD">{{cite web |url= https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline/patients-and-families/exposure-therapy |title=What Is Exposure Therapy? | publisher = American Psychological Association (APA) }}</ref>
* a real-life trigger ("in vivo")
* an imagined trigger ("imaginal")
* [[Virtual reality exposure therapy|Virtual reality exposure]]
* a triggered feeling generated in a physical way ("interoceptive"){{efn|For example, a person with [[panic disorder]] may be told to run in place, causing their heart to race, so that they can see that this feeling is not dangerous.}}

Forms include:

*[[Flooding (psychology)|Flooding]] – exposing the patient directly to a triggering stimulus, while simultaneously making them not feel afraid.
*[[Systematic desensitization]] ({{aka}} "graduated exposure") – gradually exposing the patient to increasingly vivid experiences that are related to the trauma, but do not trigger post-traumatic stress.
* [[Narrative exposure therapy]] - creates a written account of the traumatic experiences of a patient or group of patients, in a way that serves to recapture their self-respect and acknowledges their value. Under this name it is used mainly with refugees, in groups.<ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline/treatments/narrative-exposure-therapy|title=Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET) | publisher = American Psychological Association }}</ref> Written trauma accounts were part of the original protocol of [[cognitive processing therapy]]; a dismantling trial found a version without them to be at least as effective, though its authors cautioned against dropping the component on the evidence of a single study.<ref name="Resick2008">{{cite journal |vauthors=Resick PA, Galovski TE, Uhlmansiek MO, Scher CD, Clum GA, Young-Xu Y |title=A randomized clinical trial to dismantle components of cognitive processing therapy for posttraumatic stress disorder in female victims of interpersonal violence |journal=Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology |date=April 2008 |volume=76 |issue=2 |pages=243–258 |doi=10.1037/0022-006X.76.2.243 |pmid=18377121 |pmc=2967760}}</ref> Narrative exposure therapy is conditionally recommended for treatment of PTSD by the [[American Psychological Association]].<ref name="auto"/>
* [[Prolonged exposure therapy]] (PE) - a form of [[behavior therapy]] and [[cognitive behavioral therapy]] designed to treat [[post-traumatic stress disorder]], characterized by two main treatment procedures – imaginal and in vivo exposures. Imaginal exposure is a repeated 'on-purpose' retelling of the trauma memory. In vivo exposure is gradually confronting situations, places, and things that are reminders of the trauma or feel dangerous (despite being objectively safe). Additional procedures include processing of the trauma memory and breathing retraining. The [[American Psychological Association]] strongly recommends PE as a first-line psychotherapy treatment for PTSD.<ref>{{cite web |vauthors=Courtois CA, Sonis J, Brown LS, Cook J, Fairbank JA, Friedman M, Schulz P | title = Clinical practice guideline for the treatment of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in adults. | location = Washington, D.C. | publisher = American Psychological Association | date = 2017 | url = https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline/ptsd.pdf }}</ref>
* S.H.A.R.E (Survivors Healing from Abuse: Recovery through Exposure) – exposure-based group therapy that specifically focuses on providing services for previously incarcerated women that are at high risk of developing PTSD because of them being sexually assaulted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bull |first1=Chelsey |last2=Steely-Smith |first2=Mollee |last3=Bossard |first3=MeeSoh |last4=Karlsson |first4=Marie E. |last5=Bridges |first5=Ana J. |last6=Zielinski |first6=Melissa J. |date=February 2025 |title=To SHARE or not to SHARE: Exploring incarcerated women's decisions about enrolling in exposure-based group therapy. |journal=Psychological Services |language=en |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=81–91 |doi=10.1037/ser0000861 |issn=1939-148X|doi-access=free |pmid=38780557 |pmc=12989175 }}</ref>

Researchers began experimenting with [[Virtual reality therapy|Virtual reality exposure (VRE) therapy]] in PTSD exposure therapy in 1997 with the advent of the "Virtual Vietnam" scenario. Virtual Vietnam was used as a graduated exposure therapy treatment for Vietnam veterans meeting the qualification criteria for PTSD. A 50-year-old Caucasian male was the first veteran studied. The preliminary results concluded improvement post-treatment across all measures of PTSD and maintenance of the gains at the six-month follow up. Subsequent open clinical trial of Virtual Vietnam using 16 veterans, showed a reduction in PTSD symptoms.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rizzo |first1=Albert |last2=Rothbaum |first2=Barbara O |last3=Graap |first3=Ken |chapter=Virtual reality applications for combat-related posttraumatic stress disorder |pages=183–204 |editor1-last=Figley |editor1-first=Charles R. |editor2-last=Nash |editor2-first=William P. |title=Combat Stress Injury: Theory, Research, and Management |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-91933-7 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-66192-6_27 |id={{DTIC|AD1160293}} |chapter=Virtual Reality Applications for the Assessment and Treatment of PTSD |title=Handbook of Military Psychology |date=2017 |last1=Rizzo |first1=Albert |last2=Roy |first2=Michael J. |last3=Hartholt |first3=Arno |last4=Costanzo |first4=Michelle |last5=Highland |first5=Krista Beth |last6=Jovanovic |first6=Tanja |last7=Norrholm |first7=Seth D. |last8=Reist |first8=Chris |last9=Rothbaum |first9=Barbara |last10=Difede |first10=Joann |pages=453–471 |isbn=978-3-319-66190-2 }}</ref>

This method was also tested on several active duty Army soldiers, using an immersive computer simulation of military settings over six sessions. Self-reported PTSD symptoms of these soldiers were greatly diminished following the treatment.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Reger GM, Gahm GA | title = Virtual reality exposure therapy for active duty soldiers | journal = Journal of Clinical Psychology | volume = 64 | issue = 8 | pages = 940–946 | date = August 2008 | pmid = 18612993 | doi = 10.1002/jclp.20512 }}</ref> {{Dubious|date=July 2020}} Exposure therapy has shown promise in the treatment of [[co-morbid]] PTSD and [[substance abuse]].

In the area of PTSD, historic barriers to the use of exposure therapy include that clinicians may not understand it, are not confident in their own ability to use it, or more commonly, see significant [[Contraindication|contraindications]] for their client.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Becker CB, Zayfert C, Anderson E | title = A survey of psychologists' attitudes towards and utilization of exposure therapy for PTSD | journal = Behaviour Research and Therapy | volume = 42 | issue = 3 | pages = 277–292 | date = March 2004 | pmid = 14975770 | doi = 10.1016/S0005-7967(03)00138-4 | url = https://digitalcommons.trinity.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1006&context=psych_faculty }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Jaeger JA, Echiverri A, Zoellner LA, Post L, Feeny NC | title = Factors Associated with Choice of Exposure Therapy for PTSD | journal = International Journal of Behavioral Consultation and Therapy | volume = 5 | issue = 3–4 | pages = 294–310 | year = 2009 | pmid = 22545029 | pmc = 3337146 | doi = 10.1037/h0100890 }}</ref>

=== Obsessive–compulsive disorder ===
Exposure and response prevention (also known as exposure and ritual prevention; ERP or EX/RP) is a variant of exposure therapy that is recommended by the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP), the American Psychiatric Association (APA), and the Mayo Clinic as first-line treatment of [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder|OCD]] citing that it has the richest empirical support for both youth and adolescent outcomes.<ref name="AAP2007"/><ref name=AACAP2012>{{cite journal | title = Practice parameter for the assessment and treatment of children and adolescents with obsessive-compulsive disorder | journal = Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry | volume = 51 | issue = 1 | pages = 98–113 | date = January 2012 | pmid = 22176943 | doi = 10.1016/j.jaac.2011.09.019 | doi-access = free | vauthors = Geller DA, March J }}</ref>

ERP is predicated on the idea that a [[Psychotherapy|therapeutic]] effect is achieved as subjects confront their fears, but refrain from engaging in the escape response or ritual that delays or eliminates distress.<ref name="Abramowitz_2011"/> In the case of individuals with OCD or an anxiety disorder, there is a thought or situation that causes distress. Individuals usually combat this distress through specific behaviors that include avoidance or rituals. However, ERP involves purposefully evoking fear, anxiety, and or distress in the individual by exposing him/her to the feared stimulus.<ref name="Kaplan_2021" /> The response prevention then involves having the individual refrain from the ritualistic or otherwise compulsive behavior that functions to decrease distress. The patient is then taught to tolerate distress until it fades away on its own, thereby learning that rituals are not always necessary to decrease distress or anxiety. Over repeated practice of ERP, patients with OCD expect to find that they can have obsessive thoughts and images but not have the need to engage in [[Compulsive behavior|compulsive rituals]] to decrease distress.<ref name=AAP2007/><ref name=AACAP2012/>

The AACAP's practice parameters for OCD recommends cognitive behavioral therapy, and more specifically ERP, as first line treatment for youth with mild to moderate severity OCD and combination psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy for severe OCD.<ref name=AACAP2012/> The [[Cochrane (organisation)|Cochrane Review]]'s examinations of different randomized control trials echoes repeated findings of the superiority of ERP over waitlist control or pill-placebos, the superiority of combination ERP and pharmacotherapy, but similar effect sizes of efficacy between ERP or pharmacotherapy alone.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = O'Kearney RT, Anstey KJ, von Sanden C | title = Behavioural and cognitive behavioural therapy for obsessive compulsive disorder in children and adolescents | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2006 | issue = 4 | article-number = CD004856 | date = October 2006 | pmid = 17054218 | pmc = 8855344 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD004856.pub2 | hdl-access = free | hdl = 1885/50872 }}</ref>

===Generalized anxiety disorder===
There is empirical evidence that exposure therapy can be an effective treatment for people with [[generalized anxiety disorder]], citing specifically in vivo exposure therapy (exposure through a real-life situation),<ref name="Kaplan_2021" /> which has greater effectiveness than imaginal exposure in regards to generalized anxiety disorder. The aim of in vivo exposure treatment is to promote emotional regulation using systematic and controlled therapeutic exposure to traumatic stimuli.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Parsons TD, Rizzo AA | title = Affective outcomes of virtual reality exposure therapy for anxiety and specific phobias: a meta-analysis | journal = Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry | volume = 39 | issue = 3 | pages = 250–261 | date = September 2008 | pmid = 17720136 | doi = 10.1016/j.jbtep.2007.07.007 | s2cid = 6688068 }}</ref> Exposure is used to promote fear tolerance.<ref>"Instead of teaching patients to resist, control or "fix" their fear or anxiety, exposure is used to promote 'fear tolerance' given that fear and anxiety are universal, inevitable and safe." Exposure Therapy for Anxiety, Second Edition (2019), p18, Abramowitz, Deacon and Whiteside</ref>

Exposure therapy is also a preferred method for children who struggle with anxiety.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Whiteside SP, Deacon BJ, Benito K, Stewart E | title = Factors associated with practitioners' use of exposure therapy for childhood anxiety disorders | journal = Journal of Anxiety Disorders | volume = 40 | pages = 29–36 | date = May 2016 | pmid = 27085463 | pmc = 4868775 | doi = 10.1016/j.janxdis.2016.04.001 }}</ref> Researchers suggest that it is crucial for children to start this form of therapy from an early age to provide effective treatment that will follow them through adulthood.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ramsey |first1=Kesley A. |last2=Essoe |first2=Joey Ka-Yee |last3=Boyle |first3=Nathan |last4=Patrick |first4=Ainsley K. |last5=McGuire |first5=Joseph F. |date=2025-08-01 |title=Immersive Virtual Reality Exposures for the Treatment of Childhood Anxiety |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10578-023-01628-4 |journal=Child Psychiatry & Human Development |language=en |volume=56 |issue=4 |pages=1117–1128 |doi=10.1007/s10578-023-01628-4 |pmid=37985621 |issn=1573-3327|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Other possible uses of exposure therapy===

Use of exposure therapy for treating [[Depression (mood)|depression]] is comparable to [[cognitive behavioral therapy]] for depressive symptom reduction.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Grosse Holtforth |first1=Martin |last2=Krieger |first2=Tobias |last3=Zimmermann |first3=Johannes |last4=Altenstein-Yamanaka |first4=David |last5=Dörig |first5=Nadja |last6=Meisch |first6=Laurence |last7=Hayes |first7=Adele M. |date=2019-01-02 |title=A randomized-controlled trial of cognitive–behavioral therapy for depression with integrated techniques from emotion-focused and exposure therapies |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/10503307.2017.1397796 |journal=Psychotherapy Research |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=30–44 |doi=10.1080/10503307.2017.1397796 |issn=1050-3307 |pmid=29130400|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Researchers examined Exposure Based Cognitive Therapy (EBCT) as means of treatment and found although increase in symptoms may persist in early stage treatment, depressive symptoms did decrease over time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hayes |first1=Adele M. |last2=Feldman |first2=Greg C. |last3=Beevers |first3=Christopher G. |last4=Laurenceau |first4=Jean-Philippe |last5=Cardaciotto |first5=LeeAnn |last6=Lewis-Smith |first6=Jamie |date=2007 |title=Discontinuities and cognitive changes in an exposure-based cognitive therapy for depression. |journal=Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology |language=en |volume=75 |issue=3 |pages=409–421 |doi=10.1037/0022-006X.75.3.409 |issn=1939-2117 |pmc=6961653 |pmid=17563158}}</ref>

A form of exposure therapy, [[Narrative exposure therapy|Written Exposure Therapy]] (WET), has been studied as a treatment. WET can significantly decrease PTSD and depressive symptoms in comorbid cases of PTSD and [[Substance use disorder|Substance Use Disorder]] (SUD) in veterans.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Van Doren |first1=Natalia |last2=Chang |first2=Fang-Hsi |last3=Nguyen |first3=Amanda |last4=McKenna |first4=Kevin R. |last5=Satre |first5=Derek D. |last6=Wiltsey-Stirman |first6=Shannon |date=2025-02-10 |title=A pilot study of twice-weekly group-based written exposure therapy for veterans in residential substance use treatment: effects on PTSD and depressive symptoms |journal=Addiction Science & Clinical Practice |language=en |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=11 |doi=10.1186/s13722-024-00531-0 |doi-access=free |issn=1940-0640 |pmc=11809123 |pmid=39924479}}</ref> 

==History==

The 9th century Persian polymath [[Abu Zayd al-Balkhi]] wrote about 'tranquilizing fear' by 'forcing oneself to repeatedly expose one's hearing and sight to noxious things' and to 'moved again and again near the thing it is scared of until it becomes used to it and loses its fear.'<ref>Sustenance of the soul, al-Balkhi, p49</ref>

The use of exposure as a mode of therapy began in the 1950s, at a time when [[Psychodynamics|psychodynamic]] views dominated Western clinical practice and [[Behaviour therapy|behavioral therapy]] was first emerging. South African psychologists and psychiatrists first used exposure as a way to reduce pathological fears, such as phobias and anxiety-related problems, and they brought their methods to England in the [[Maudsley Hospital]] training program.<ref name="Abramowitz_2011" />

[[Joseph Wolpe]] (1915–1997) was one of the first psychiatrists to spark interest in treating psychiatric problems as behavioral issues. He sought consultation with other behavioral psychologists, among them James G. Taylor (1897–1973), who worked in the psychology department of the [[University of Cape Town]] in South Africa. Although most of his work went unpublished, Taylor was the first psychologist known to use exposure therapy treatment for [[anxiety]], including methods of situational exposure with response prevention—a common exposure therapy technique still being used.<ref name="Abramowitz_2011" />
Since the 1950s, several sorts of exposure therapy have been developed, including [[systematic desensitization]], [[Flooding (psychology)|flooding]], implosive therapy, [[prolonged exposure therapy]], in vivo exposure therapy, and imaginal exposure therapy.<ref name="Abramowitz_2011" />

Exposure and response prevention (ERP) traces its roots back to the work of psychologist [[Vic Meyer]] in the 1960s. Meyer devised this treatment from his analysis of [[Extinction (psychology)|fear extinguishment]] in animals via [[Flooding (psychology)|flooding]] and applied it to human cases in the psychiatric setting that, at the time, were considered intractable.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Meyer V | title = Modification of expectations in cases with obsessional rituals | journal = Behaviour Research and Therapy | volume = 4 | issue = 4 | pages = 273–280 | date = November 1966 | pmid = 5978682 | doi = 10.1016/0005-7967(66)90023-4 }}</ref> The success of ERP clinically and scientifically has been summarized as "spectacular" by prominent OCD researcher [[Stanley Rachman]] decades following Meyer's creation of the method.<ref name=":22">{{Cite web|url=http://www.ocdhistory.net/20thcentury/behaviortherapy.html|title=The history of obsessive-compulsive disorder|website=www.ocdhistory.net}}</ref>

==Possibly related psychological techniques==

===Mindfulness===
A 2015 review pointed out parallels between exposure therapy and [[mindfulness]], stating that mindful meditation "resembles an exposure situation because [mindfulness] practitioners 'turn towards their emotional experience', bring acceptance to bodily and affective responses, and refrain from engaging in internal reactivity towards it."<ref name=NRN2015>{{cite journal | vauthors = Tang YY, Hölzel BK, Posner MI | title = The neuroscience of mindfulness meditation | journal = Nature Reviews. Neuroscience | volume = 16 | issue = 4 | pages = 213–225 | date = April 2015 | pmid = 25783612 | doi = 10.1038/nrn3916 | s2cid = 54521922 }}</ref> Imaging studies have shown that the [[ventromedial prefrontal cortex]], [[hippocampus]], and the [[amygdala]] are all affected by exposure therapy; imaging studies have shown similar activity in these regions with mindfulness training.<ref name=NRN2015/>

===EMDR===
[[Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing]] (EMDR) includes an element of exposure therapy (desensitization), though whether this is an effective method or not, is controversial.<ref>{{Cite web |url= https://www.div12.org/treatment/eye-movement-desensitization-and-reprocessing-for-post-traumatic-stress-disorder/ |title=Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder | publisher = Society of Clinical Psychology |date=6 March 2017}}</ref>

===Other===
[[Desensitization (psychology)|Desensitization]] and [[Extinction (psychology)|extinction]] also involve exposure to a cause of disturbance.

===Research; Expectations violation===
Research has been undertaken on the therapy impact of a focus on the mismatch between threat expectancy before exposure and what actually occurs in exposure, but this has not produced clearly positive results.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/21677026221101379|title=Change of Threat Expectancy as Mechanism of Exposure-Based Psychotherapy for Anxiety Disorders: Evidence From 8,484 Exposure Exercises of 605 Patients|first1=Andre|last1=Pittig|first2=Ingmar|last2=Heinig|first3=Stephan|last3=Goerigk|first4=Jan|last4=Richter|first5=Maike|last5=Hollandt|first6=Ulrike|last6=Lueken|first7=Paul|last7=Pauli|first8=Jürgen|last8=Deckert|first9=Tilo|last9=Kircher|first10=Benjamin|last10=Straube|first11=Peter|last11=Neudeck|first12=Katja|last12=Koelkebeck|first13=Udo|last13=Dannlowski|first14=Volker|last14=Arolt|first15=Thomas|last15=Fydrich|first16=Lydia|last16=Fehm|first17=Andreas|last17=Ströhle|first18=Christina|last18=Totzeck|first19=Jürgen|last19=Margraf|first20=Silvia|last20=Schneider|first21=Jürgen|last21=Hoyer|first22=Winfried|last22=Rief|first23=Michelle
