misophonic and obsessive-compulsive symptoms: A systematic case study |journal=Journal of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders |date=July 2016 |volume=10 |pages=1–9 |doi=10.1016/j.jocrd.2016.04.009 }}</ref>

Due in part to the need for differential diagnosis with other psychiatric and audiological conditions, academic commentaries make various recommendations regarding misophonia assessment, including that misophonia diagnoses be made by multidisciplinary groups and draw upon multiple sources of data.<ref name="Ferrer-Torres_2022"/><ref name="Henry_2022"/><ref name="Campbell_2023">{{cite journal | vauthors=Campbell J | journal=Journal of the American Academy of Audiology | title=Misophonia: A Need for audiologic diagnostic guidelines | pages=a-2125-7645 | date=10 July 2023 | volume=34 | issue=7–08 | issn=2157-3107 | doi=10.1055/a-2125-7645| pmid=37429565 | pmc=11586086 }}</ref>

===Classification===
The diagnosis of misophonia is not recognized in the [[DSM-5-TR]] or the [[International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems|ICD-11]] and it is not classified as a [[audiological|hearing]] or [[psychiatric]] disorder.<ref name="Duddy_2014">{{cite journal |vauthors=Duddy DF, Oeding KA | year = 2014 | title = Misophonia: An Overview | journal = Semin Hear | volume = 35 | issue = 2| pages = 084–091 | doi = 10.1055/s-0034-1372525 | s2cid = 76090599 }}</ref>

The consensus among misophonia experts is that the relationship between misophonia and other conditions is unclear.<ref name="Swedo_2022" /> Scholars debate whether misophonia should be considered an audiological or psychiatric disorder, with some evidence favoring the latter view.<ref name="Plos2013"/><ref name="Taylor_2017"/>  It has been tentatively suggested that misophonia belongs to the spectrum of [[Obsessive–compulsive spectrum|obsessive–compulsive and related disorders]], although the authors of that proposal also describe it as "premature".<ref name="Plos2013"/>

===Measures===
Misophonia has generally been measured using adult self-report questionnaires.<ref name="Kula_2022">{{cite journal | last1=Kula | first1=Fatma Betul | last2=Cropley | first2=Mark | last3=Aazh | first3=Hashir | journal=Journal of the American Academy of Audiology | title=Hyperacusis and Misophonia: A Systematic Review of Psychometric Measures | volume=33 | issue=7/08 | pages=417–428 | date= July 2022 | issn=2157-3107 | doi=10.1055/a-1896-5032| pmid=35817311 | url=https://openresearch.surrey.ac.uk/view/delivery/44SUR_INST/12171940600002346/13171940590002346 }}</ref> A 2021 review of misophonia and hyperacusis measures found only three misophonia instruments with reported psychometric properties, all of which were adult self-report measures; the review called the evidence regarding the measures' psychometrics "limited".<ref name="Kula_2022"/> Psychometric properties of several additional adult self-report misophonia measures have since been reported in the scholarly literature.<ref name="Rosenthal_2021" /><ref name="Vitoratou_2021" /><ref name="Dibb_2021">{{cite journal | last1=Dibb | first1=B. | last2=Golding | first2=S.E. | last3=Dozier | first3=T.H. | journal=Journal of Psychosomatic Research | title=The development and validation of the Misophonia response scale | volume=149 | article-number=110587 | publisher=Elsevier Inc. | date= 2021 | issn=0022-3999 | doi=10.1016/j.jpsychores.2021.110587| pmid=34390941 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Naylor_2021">{{cite journal | last1 = Naylor | first1 = Jay | last2 = Caimino | first2 = Charlotte | last3 = Scutt | first3 = Polly | last4 = Hoare | first4 = Derek J. | last5 = Baguley | first5 = David M. | title = The Prevalence and Severity of Misophonia in a UK Undergraduate Medical Student Population and Validation of the Amsterdam Misophonia Scale | journal = The Psychiatric Quarterly | volume = 92 | issue = 2 | pages = 609–619 | date = June 2021 | pmid = 32829440 | pmc = 8110492 | doi = 10.1007/s11126-020-09825-3 }}</ref><ref name="Remmert_2022">{{cite journal | last1=Remmert | first1=N. | author2=Schmidt KMB | last3=Mussel | first3=P. | last4=Hagel | first4=M. L. | last5=Eid | first5=M. | editor-first1=Sónia | editor-last1=Brito-Costa | journal=PLOS ONE | title=The Berlin Misophonia Questionnaire Revised (BMQ-R): Development and validation of a symptom-oriented diagnostical instrument for the measurement of misophonia | volume=17 | issue=6 | article-number=e0269428 | date=21 June 2022 | issn=1932-6203 | doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0269428| doi-access=free | pmid=35727794 | pmc=9212156 | bibcode=2022PLoSO..1769428R }}</ref><ref name="Simner_2024B">{{cite journal | last1=Simner | first1=Julia | last2=Rinaldi | first2=Louisa J. | last3=Ward | first3=Jamie | journal=Assessment | title=An Automated Online Measure for Misophonia: The Sussex Misophonia Scale for Adults | volume=31 | issue=8 | pages=1598–1614 | date=27 February 2024 | issn=1552-3489 | doi=10.1177/10731911241234104| pmid=38414185 | pmc=11528938 }}</ref><ref name="Williams_ZJ_2022">{{cite journal | last1=Williams | first1=Zachary J. | last2=Cascio | first2=Carissa J. | last3=Woynaroski | first3=Tiffany G. | journal=Frontiers in Psychology | title=Psychometric validation of a brief self-report measure of misophonia symptoms and functional impairment: The duke-vanderbilt misophonia screening questionnaire | volume=13 | article-number=897901 | date=22 July 2022 | issn=1664-1078 | doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2022.897901| doi-access=free | pmid=35936331 | pmc=9355318 }}</ref> Further unvalidated misophonia questionnaires are available on the internet.<ref name="Ferrer-Torres_2022"/><ref name="Henry_2022"/><ref name="Siepsiak_2020">{{cite journal | last1=Siepsiak | first1=Marta | last2=Śliwerski | first2=Andrzej | last3=Łukasz Dragan | first3=Wojciech | journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health | title=Development and psychometric properties of MisoQuest — A new self-report questionnaire for misophonia | volume=17 | page=1797 | date= 2020 | issue=5 | doi=10.3390/ijerph17051797| doi-access=free | pmid=32164250 | pmc=7084437 | bibcode=2020IJERP..17.1797S }}</ref>

More recently, self-report and caregiver proxy-report measures to assess misophonia in children and youth have begun to appear in the scholarly literature.<ref name="Cervin_2023">{{cite journal | last1=Cervin | first1=Matti | last2=Guzick | first2=Andrew G. | last3=Clinger | first3=Jane | last4=Smith | first4=Eleanor E.A. | last5=Draper | first5=Isabel A. | last6=Goodman | first6=Wayne K. | last7=Lijffijt | first7=Marijn | last8=Murphy | first8=Nicholas | last9=Rast | first9=Catherine E. | last10=Schneider | first10=Sophie C. | last11=Storch | first11=Eric A. | journal=Journal of Affective Disorders | title=Measuring misophonia in youth: A psychometric evaluation of child and parent measures | volume=39 | pages=180–186 | date= May 2023 | issn=0165-0327 | doi=10.1016/j.jad.2023.05.093| pmid=37263358 | pmc=11165319 }}</ref><ref name="Rappoldt_2024">{{cite journal | last1=Rappoldt | first1=Lotte R. | last2=Kan | first2=Kees J. | last3=Dalmeijer | first3=Lenrine | last4=Rutten | first4=Sterre A. | last5=Van Horen | first5=Renske | last6=Van Der Pol | first6=Marthe M. | last7=De Wit | first7=Carola | last8=Denys | first8=Damiaan | last9=Vulink | first9=Nienke C. C. | last10=Utens | first10=Elisabeth M. W. J. | journal=Child Psychiatry & Human Development | title=Psychometric Validation of the New Misophonia Screening List—Child and Youth and AMISOS-Y (Dutch Child- and Parent-Report Versions) for Assessing Misophonia in Youth | date=14 November 2024 | volume=57 | issue=4 | pages=1195–1209 | issn=1573-3327 | doi=10.1007/s10578-024-01781-4 | pmid=39540976 | doi-access=free | pmc=13437573 }}</ref><ref name="Rinaldi_2022">{{cite journal | last1=Rinaldi | first1=Louisa J. | last2=Smees | first2=Rebecca | last3=Ward | first3=Jamie | last4=Simner | first4=Julia | journal=Frontiers in Psychology | title=Poorer Well-Being in Children With Misophonia: Evidence From the Sussex Misophonia Scale for Adolescents | volume=13 | article-number=808379 | date=6 April 2022 | issn=1664-1078 | doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2022.808379| doi-access=free | pmid=35465571 | pmc=9019493 }}</ref> At least one study uses [[psychiatric interview|interviews]] with caregivers, and sometimes their children, to assess misophonia in children and adolescents.<ref name="Michałowska_2023">{{cite journal | last1=Siepsiak | first1=Marta | last2=Turek | first2=Anna | last3=Michałowska | first3=Magdalena | last4=Gambin | first4=Małgorzata | last5=Dragan | first5=Wojciech Łukasz | journal=Child Psychiatry & Human Development | title=Misophonia in Children and Adolescents: Age Differences, Risk Factors, Psychiatric and Psychological Correlates. A Pilot Study with Mothers' Involvement | date=8 September 2023 | volume=56 | issue=3 | pages=758–771 | issn=0009-398X|eissn=1573-3327 | doi=10.1007/s10578-023-01593-y | pmid=37684420 | pmc=12095346 }}</ref>

Another relatively novel development in misophonia assessment is a [[psychoacoustics|psychoacoustic]] measure, which uses adults' self-reported ratings of the pleasantness of sounds to identify a set of sounds that appear to distinguish between people with and without misophonia.<ref name="Enzler_2021">{{cite journal | last1=Enzler | first1=Falco | last2=Loriot | first2=Céline | last3=Fournier | first3=Philippe | last4=Noreña | first4=Arnaud J. | journal=Scientific Reports | title=A psychoacoustic test for misophonia assessment | volume=11 | article-number=11044 | date= 2021 | issue=1 | issn=2045-2322 | doi=10.1038/s41598-021-90355-8 | doi-access=free| pmid=34040061 | pmc=8155015 | bibcode=2021NatSR..1111044E }}</ref>

Due to the difficulty of distinguishing misophonia from other psychiatric and audiological conditions, it is unclear whether any single tool can be relied upon to diagnose misophonia.<ref name="Ferrer-Torres_2022"/><ref name="Campbell_2023"/> It has been suggested that assessment should involve the collection of multiple sources of data, such as patient case histories, interviews, audiological examination, and self-report tools.<ref name="Ferrer-Torres_2022"/><ref name="Henry_2022"/><ref name="Campbell_2023"/>

==Management==
Despite high demand in the community,<ref name="Abraham_2025">{{cite journal | last1=Abraham | first1=Katherine L. | last2=Rast | first2=Catherine E. | last3=Storch | first3=Eric A. | last4=Guzick | first4=Andrew G. | journal=Personalized Medicine in Psychiatry | title=What's next for misophonia? Child and parent priorities for misophonia advocacy, treatment, and research | volume=51–52 | article-number=100160 | date= July 2025 | issn=2468-1717 | doi=10.1016/j.pmip.2025.100160}}</ref> there has been relatively limited research into misophonia treatment and intervention,<ref name="Rosenthal_2023"/><ref name="Mattson_2023"/> and few clinical providers have extensive knowledge of it.<ref name="Rosenthal_2023"/> People seeking misophonia treatment often rate it unsatisfactory.<ref name="Smith_2022">{{cite journal | vauthors = Smith EE, Guzick AG, Draper IA, Clinger J, Schneider SC, Goodman WK, Brout JJ, Lijffijt M, Storch EA | title = Perceptions of various treatment approaches for adults and children with misophonia | journal = Journal of Affective Disorders | volume = 316 | pages = 76–82 | date = November 2022 | pmid = 35970326 | pmc = 9884516 | doi = 10.1016/j.jad.2022.08.020 }}</ref> Indeed, no misophonia treatments or interventions currently qualify as evidence-based.<ref name="Rosenthal_2023"/> But several recent studies investigated [[cognitive behavioral therapy]] (CBT) as an option, and there are reports of other approaches, including [[tinnitus retraining therapy]] (TRT), [[exposure therapy]], [[cognitive behavioral therapy#Merger of behavioral and cognitive therapies|third-wave]] psychotherapies such as [[dialectical behavior therapy]] (DBT), and [[acceptance and commitment therapy]] (ACT), and some pharmacological treatments.<ref name="Mattson_2023"/>

CBT-based programs have the strongest evidentiary support of any misophonia treatment so far.<ref name="Mattson_2023"/> Trials of a group-based CBT program,<ref name="Schroder_2017">{{cite journal | last1=Schröder | first1=Arjan E. | last2=Vulink | first2=Nienke C. | last3=Van Loon | first3=Arnoud J. | last4=Denys | first4=Damiaan A. | journal=Journal of Affective Disorders | title=Cognitive behavioral therapy is effective in misophonia: An open trial | volume=217 | pages=289–294 | date= August 2017 | issn=0165-0327 | doi=10.1016/j.jad.2017.04.017 | pmid=28441620 }}</ref><ref name="Jager_2020">{{cite journal | last1=Jager | first1=Inge J. | last2=Vulink | first2=Nienke C. C. | last3=Bergfeld | first3=Isidoor O. | last4=Loon | first4=Arnoud J. J. M. | last5=Denys | first5=Damiaan A. J. P. | journal=Depression and Anxiety | title=Cognitive behavioral therapy for misophonia: A randomized clinical trial | volume=38 | issue=7 | pages=708–718 | date= 2020 | issn=1091-4269 | doi=10.1002/da.23127| pmid=33336858 | pmc=8359510 }}</ref> including a randomized clinical trial,<ref name="Jager_2020"/> have found reductions in misophonia symptoms, which appeared to be maintained one year later.<ref name="Jager_2020"/> Another randomized clinical trial evaluated a CBT-based mobile health app, which also appeared to reduce misophonia symptoms.<ref name="Podoly_2025">{{cite journal | last1=Podoly | first1=Tamar Yonit | last2=Even-Ezra | first2=Hadar | last3=Doron | first3=Guy | journal=Journal of Affective Disorders | title=A randomized controlled trial evaluating an mHealth intervention for anger-related cognitions in misophonia | volume=379 | pages=350–361 | date= June 2025 | issn=0165-0327 | doi=10.1016/j.jad.2025.03.060| pmid=40081589 }}</ref>

Several case reports on third-wave psychotherapies such as DBT or ACT have found preliminary evidence of possible benefits.<ref name="Mattson_2023"/> Additional research is needed to understand the potential utility of ACT and DBT approaches for misophonia intervention.<ref name="Mattson_2023"/>

Investigations of pharmacological treatments for misophonia have been limited to case studies,<ref name="Ferrer-Torres_2022"/> most frequently of [[selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor]]s (SSRIs) such as [[sertraline]] and [[fluoxetine]].<ref name="Mattson_2023"/> Other case reports discuss how misophonia symptoms may have been secondarily affected by [[propranolol]], [[risperidone]], or [[methylphenidate]] prescribed to address other conditions.<ref name="Mattson_2023"/> These case studies may provide directions for further research, such as understanding neurophysiological mechanisms and processes that could be targeted through medication<ref name="Mattson_2023"/> and conducting larger randomized controlled trials.<ref name="Ferrer-Torres_2022"/> No medications for misophonia can be considered evidence-based.<ref name="Rosenthal_2023"/>

Many approaches to misophonia treatment leverage the idea that negative evaluations of trigger sounds can be disrupted and replaced by more positive associations.<ref name="CBT_Protocol_2022"/><ref name="Jastreboff_2014"/> This is the main focus of TRT for misophonia,<ref name="Jastreboff_2014"/> and it has also been leveraged in CBT-based approaches.<ref name="Mattson_2023"/> A report from a clinical service suggests that most patients with misophonia benefited from TRT,<ref name="Jastreboff_2014"/> a result that has been called good or promising.<ref name="Rosenthal_2023"/><ref name="Ferrer-Torres_2022"/> But counterconditioning and stimulus manipulation—changing trigger sounds or pairing them with pleasant or humorous stimuli to disrupt negative affective evaluations—were infrequently used by participants in a misophonia CBT trial. The patients considered these less effective than other strategies used in the program.<ref name="CBT_Protocol_2022"/> Traditional habituation-based exposure therapy is not recommended for misophonia.<ref name="Rosenthal_2023"/>

Several studies report that a common approach to misophonia management is to amend one's lifestyle and avoid trigger sounds,<ref name="Cavanna_2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Cavanna AE, Seri S | title = Misophonia: current perspectives | journal = Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment | volume = 11 | pages = 2117–2123 | date = Aug 2015 | pmid = 26316758 | pmc = 4547634 | doi = 10.2147/NDT.S81438 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Guzick_2024"/><ref name="pmid23805089"/><ref name="Smith_2022"/> and people with misophonia generally perceive lifestyle changes as highly appropriate.<ref name="Smith_2022"/> [[Noise-cancelling headphones]] and passive sound protection are frequently used and rated by community members as highly appropriate.<ref name="Smith_2022"/> But there is clinical concern that avoidance might be dysfunctional and could even inadvertently tend to exacerbate some sound intolerance,<ref name="Cavanna_2015"/><ref name="Jastreboff_2014"/> although some evidence suggests people with misophonia who avoid triggers more often may later have fewer role limitations due to emotional problems,<ref name="Dibb_QOL">{{cite journal | last1=Dibb | first1=Bridget | last2=Golding | first2=Sarah E. | journal=Frontiers in Neuroscience | title=A longitudinal investigation of quality of life and negative emotions in misophonia | volume=16 | article-number=900474 | date=22 July 2022 | issn=1662-453X | doi=10.3389/fnins.2022.900474| doi-access=free | pmid=35937869 | pmc=9354518 }}</ref> which may suggest that at least some level of avoidance is beneficial. There are other approaches to management and coping; some people with misophonia mimic trigger sounds, either to retaliate or cancel them out in a way they can control.<ref name="pmid23805089"/> People with misophonia may attempt cognitive strategies such as self-talk and diverting their attention.<ref name="pmid23805089"/> Relaxation is also commonly attempted.<ref name="Smith_2022"/> Participants in a CBT program considered relaxation, training to shift attention away from triggers, and peer support the most successful parts of the intervention.<ref name="CBT_Protocol_2022"/>

Given the limited nature of the misophonia intervention evidence base, it has been suggested that providers work collaboratively and flexibly with patients to identify strategies that are useful to them.<ref name="Rosenthal_2023"/><ref name="Duddy_2014" /> It is speculated that treatment methods vary significantly in effectiveness from patient to patient.<ref name="Cavanna_2015"/> Where there are gaps in the misophonia-specific literature, transdiagnostic research on interventions found to be efficacious or effective for other conditions may be relevant.<ref name="Rosenthal_2023"/> Multidisciplinary treatment approaches, incorporating insights from diverse experts such as [[audiology#Audiologist|audiologists]], [[mental health professional]]s, and [[occupational therapist]]s, may also improve the quality of support.<ref name="Rosenthal_2023"/>

==Mechanism==
The mechanism of misophonia is not yet fully understood, and all proposed causes of the disorder are hypothesized based on a combination of clinical observation and the limited existing empirical research.<ref name="Palumbo_2018" /> Although misophonia is a disorder of sound tolerance, work to date has not typically demonstrated any peripheral audiologic abnormalities in people with the condition,<ref name="Muñoz_2024">{{Cite journal |last1=Muñoz |first1=Karen |last2=Woolley |first2=Mercedes G. |last3=Velasquez |first3=Doris |last4=Ortiz |first4=Diana |last5=San Miguel |first5=Guadalupe G. |last6=Petersen |first6=Julie M. |last7=Twohig |first7=Michael P. |date=2024-09-30 |title=Audiological Characteristics of a Sample of Adults With Misophonia |url=https://pubs.asha.org/doi/10.1044/2024_AJA-24-00111 |journal=American Journal of Audiology |volume=33 |issue=4 |language=en |pages=1202–1211 |doi=10.1044/2024_AJA-24-00111 |pmid=39348505 |issn=1059-0889|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Suraj_2024">{{Cite journal |last1=Suraj |first1=Urs |last2=Nisha |first2=Kavassery Venkateswaran |last3=Prabhu |first3=Prashanth |date=2024-04-01 |title=Normal linear and non-linear cochlear mechanisms and efferent system functioning in individuals with misophonia |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00405-023-08273-6 |journal=European Archives of Oto-Rhino-Laryngology |language=en |volume=281 |issue=4 |pages=1709–1716 |doi=10.1007/s00405-023-08273-6 |pmid=37837477 |issn=0937-4477|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="WilliamsDissertation_Ch5">{{Citation |last=Williams |first=Zachary James |title=Investigating the Nature of Decreased Sound Tolerance in Autistic and Non-autistic Adults |date=2024-06-21 |pages=197–249 |url=https://ir.vanderbilt.edu/items/a9e54a3e-61db-467b-b2cf-2eb0e9f8b977 |place=Nashville, TN, USA |publisher=Vanderbilt University |department=Neuroscience}}</ref> suggesting that any "auditory" abnormalities may be caused by a dysfunction of the [[central auditory system]] or other parts of the brain that govern "higher-order" perceptor or cognition, rather than the ears ''per se''.<ref name="Brout_2018" />

Some research has found evidence consistent with the idea that there are genetic contributions to misophonia, but more research is needed.<ref name="pmid23805089">{{cite journal | vauthors = Edelstein M, Brang D, Rouw R, Ramachandran VS | title = Misophonia: physiological investigations and case descriptions | journal = Frontiers in Human Neuroscience | volume = 7 | issue =  | page = 296 | date = 2013 | pmid = 23805089 | pmc = 3691507 | doi = 10.3389/fnhum.2013.00296 | doi-access = free }}</ref> An unpublished study suggests a genetic locus is associated with responses to a single question asking about the misophonic symptom of experiencing rage to sounds of people chewing.<ref name="23andme">{{Citation | vauthors=Fayzullina S, Smith RP, Furlotte N, Hu Y, Hinds D, Tung JY | year=2015 | title=Genetic Associations with Traits in 23andMe Customers | publisher=23andMe | url=https://permalinks.23andme.com/pdf/23-08_genetic_associations_with_traits.pdf | access-date=3 January 2025}}</ref>

==="Neurophysiological" (Jastreboff) model===
The first mechanistic theory of misophonia, proposed by Jastreboff and Jastreboff in 2014,<ref name="Jastreboff_2023">{{Cite journal |last1=Jastreboff |first1=Pawel J. |last2=Jastreboff |first2=Margaret M. |date=2023-03-23 |title=The neurophysiological approach to misophonia: Theory and treatment |journal=Frontiers in Neuroscience |volume=17 |article-number=895574 |doi=10.3389/fnins.2023.895574 |doi-access=free |issn=1662-453X |pmc=10076672 |pmid=37034168}}</ref><ref name="Jastreboff_2014">{{Cite journal |last1=Jastreboff |first1=Pawel |last2=Jastreboff |first2=Margaret |date=2014-04-29 |title=Treatments for Decreased Sound Tolerance (Hyperacusis and Misophonia) |url=http://www.thieme-connect.de/DOI/DOI?10.1055/s-0034-1372527 |journal=Seminars in Hearing |language=en |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=105–120 |doi=10.1055/s-0034-1372527 |issn=0734-0451|url-access=subscription }}</ref> is based on the authors' clinical experience and little empirical data. This model, which the authors call the "neurophysiological model",<ref name="Jastreboff_2023"/> seeks to contrast misophonia with [[hyperacusis]], another disorder of sound tolerance that primarily manifests as excessive [[loudness]] perception (or the experience of [[physical pain]] in one's ears or head) in response to soft or moderate-intensity everyday sounds.<ref name="Henry_2022"/><ref name="Salvi_2022">{{Cite journal |last1=Salvi |first1=Richard |last2=Chen |first2=Guang-Di |last3=Manohar |first3=Senthilvelan |date=2022-12-01 |title=Hyperacusis: Loudness intolerance, fear, annoyance and pain |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0378595522002167 |journal=Hearing Research |language=en |volume=426 |article-number=108648 |doi=10.1016/j.heares.2022.108648|pmid=36395696 }}</ref> The Jastreboffs' neurophysiological model posits that the fundamental difference between misophonia and [[hyperacusis]] is that decreased sound tolerance in hyperacusis is closely coupled to the physical properties of the sound stimulus (i.e., [[Sound intensity|intensity]], [[frequency]]) while, in misophonia, decreased tolerance of "trigger" sounds has little to do with acoustic properties (beyond louder sounds perhaps being easier to perceive and respond to)<ref name="Jastreboff_2023"/> and arguably depends almost exclusively on the [[Meaning (non-linguistic)|meaning]] of the sounds to a given person.<ref name="Jastreboff_2014"/><ref name="Jastreboff_2023"/><ref name="Jastreboff_2024">{{Citation |last=Jastreboff |first=Pawel J. |chapter=The Neurophysiological Model of Tinnitus and Decreased Sound Tolerance |date=2024 |title=Textbook of Tinnitus |pages=231–249 |editor-last=Schlee |editor-first=Winfried |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-35647-6_20 |access-date=2024-11-04 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-35647-6_20 |isbn=978-3-031-35647-6 |editor2-last=Langguth |editor2-first=Berthold |editor3-last=De Ridder |editor3-first=Dirk |editor4-last=Vanneste |editor4-first=Sven|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> Its creators have used this model to explain certain aspects of the misophonia phenotype, such as that most people with misophonia do not present with peripheral [[hearing loss]] and that context (including whether a trigger is produced by oneself) plays a large role in response to a trigger sound.<ref name="Jastreboff_2023"/><ref name="Jastreboff_2024"/>

Although entirely speculative and not based on any empirical [[neuroscientific]] data on misophonia, the "neurophysiologic" model also postulates several putative neural mechanisms for the condition from a [[systems neuroscience]] perspective.<ref name="Jastreboff_2024"/> Namely, when processing a trigger stimulus, the brain's [[central auditory system]] is thought to have enhanced functional connections with its [[limbic]] and [[autonomic nervous system|autonomic control]] areas, and downstream overactivity of these areas is theorized to be responsible for the excessive emotional responses and certain physical symptoms of the condition, respectively.<ref name="Jastreboff_2023"/> These preliminary neuroscientific hypotheses form the basis of the Jastreboffs' signature intervention for sound tolerance conditions ([[Tinnitus Retraining Therapy]], an unproven combination of structured counseling and sound therapy originally developed for [[tinnitus]] and now available in modified form to treat misophonia).<ref name="Jastreboff_2014"/><ref name="Jastreboff_2024"/>

Notably, there has been relatively little empirical support for the central neuroscientific hypotheses of the neurophysiologic model. Although there has been a relative lack of [[neuroimaging]] research on misophonia thus far, [[functional connectivity]] between auditory cortical and [[limbic]] or [[autonomic nervous system|autonomic control]] areas is not typically increased either at rest or during the experience of trigger sound perception.<ref name="Neacsiu_2022"/> Though many of these same limbic and autonomic control areas may still be relevant in the [[pathophysiology]] of misophonia (with [[anterior insula]] being one of the most strongly implicated nodes thus far),<ref name="Neacsiu_2022"/> recent reviews of [[neuroimaging|human neuroimaging]] research in this condition<ref name="Neacsiu_2022"/><ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024">{{Cite journal |last1=Berger |first1=Joel I. |last2=Gander |first2=Phillip E. |last3=Kumar |first3=Sukhbinder |date=2024-08-26 |title=A social cognition perspective on misophonia |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |language=en |volume=379 |issue=1908 |article-number=20230257 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2023.0257 |issn=0962-8436 |pmc=11444241 |pmid=39005025}}</ref> indicate that '''(a)''' their activation may be driven by other pathways than simple auditory→limbic or auditory→limbic→autonomic hyper-connectivity and '''(b)''' additional structures outside of the Jastreboffs' model (such as premotor cortex)<ref name="Kumar_2021">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kumar S, Dheerendra P, Erfanian M, Benzaquén E, Sedley W, Gander PE, Lad M, Bamiou DE, Griffiths TD | title = The Motor Basis for Misophonia | journal = The Journal of Neuroscience | volume = 41 | issue = 26 | pages = 5762–5770 | date = June 2021 | pmid = 34021042 | pmc = 8244967 | doi = 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0261-21.2021 | doi-access = free }}</ref> may play a central role in this disorder. Other theorists have also criticized the "neurophysiologic" model for its vagueness and unwillingness to specify the specific neural structures and processes involved in the "[[limbic system]]" portion of the model, as well as its inability to account for non-sound trigger stimuli.

==="Action perception" (Berger–Gander–Kumar) model===

A more recently developed model of misophonia was published by neuroscientist Sukhbinder Kumar and colleagues at the [[University of Iowa]] in 2024.<ref name= "Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/> This model, not formally named by the authors but termed the "action perception" model by other researchers using it<ref name= "WilliamsDissertation_Ch5" /> (alternatively the Berger–Gander–Kumar model), sought to build on the perceived shortcomings of earlier models<ref name= "Noreña_2024">{{Cite journal |last=Norena |first=Arnaud |date= 2024-02-14 |title= Did Kant suffer from misophonia? |journal= Frontiers in Psychology |volume= 15 |article-number= 1242516 |doi= 10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1242516 |doi-access= free |issn= 1664-1078 |pmc= 10899398 |pmid= 38420172}}</ref><ref name= "Jastreboff_2014"/> by explicitly incorporating more up-to-date empirical findings in the [[behavioral science|behavioral]], [[clinical science|clinical]] and [[neuroimaging]] literature on misophonia; providing explanations for the presence of non-auditory (i.e., [[visual]]) and [[multisensory integration|multi-sensory]] trigger stimuli; and considering perspectives from [[social cognitive theory]] and [[social neuroscience]] in the broader theory. Although the action perception model is consistent with many of the findings in the misophonia neuroimaging literature, it was generated specifically to explain those findings and therefore represents something of a "[[just-so story]]" until its predictions can be empirically validated.<ref name= "Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/><ref name= "Borsboom_2021">{{Cite journal |last1= Borsboom |first1=Denny |last2= van der Maas |first2= Han L. J. |last3= Dalege |first3=Jonas |last4= Kievit |first4= Rogier A. |last5= Haig |first5= Brian D. |date= 2021-07-01 |title= Theory Construction Methodology: A Practical Framework for Building Theories in Psychology |url= https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1745691620969647 |journal= Perspectives on Psychological Science |language= en |volume= 16 |issue= 4 |pages= 756–766 |doi= 10.1177/1745691620969647 |pmid= 33593167 |issn= 1745-6916}}</ref><ref name= "Robinaugh_2021">{{Cite journal |last1= Robinaugh |first1= Donald J. |last2= Haslbeck |first2= Jonas M. B. |last3= Ryan |first3= Oisín |last4= Fried |first4= Eiko I. |last5= Waldorp |first5= Lourens J. |date= 2021-07-01 |title= Invisible Hands and Fine Calipers: A Call to Use Formal Theory as a Toolkit for Theory Construction |journal= Perspectives on Psychological Science |language= en |volume= 16 |issue= 4 |pages= 725–743 |doi= 10.1177/1745691620974697 |issn= 1745-6916 |pmc= 8273080 |pmid= 33593176}}</ref>

Based on what is known from neuroimaging and behavioral studies of misophonia, the action perception model conceptualizes the disorder as follows:<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/>
* [[Sensory information]] about any stimulus travels from the ear (eye in the case of visual information) through [[central auditory system|lemniscal/non-lemniscal auditory pathways]] (or [[visual system|analogous visual pathways]]) to arrive at and be processed by primary and higher-level [[auditory cortex]] ([[visual cortex]]).
* Information is transmitted from a [[sensory cortex]] (auditory or visual) to the (pre)[[motor cortex]] to form a motor representation of a given action (putatively related to the human "[[mirror neuron]]" system).<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/>
* '''Under pathological conditions (e.g., when an individual with misophonia hears a sound that "triggers" them):'''
** The strength or quality of the "motor representation" may be fundamentally different from that in non-misophonic people, as demonstrated by hyperactivity of regions responsible for creating these representations.<ref name="Kumar_2021"/><ref name="Kumar_2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kumar S, Tansley-Hancock O, Sedley W, Winston JS, Callaghan MF, Allen M, Cope TE, Gander PE, Bamiou DE, Griffiths TD | title = The Brain Basis for Misophonia | journal = Current Biology | volume = 27 | issue = 4 | pages = 527–533 | date = February 2017 | pmid = 28162895 | pmc = 5321671 | doi = 10.1016/j.cub.2016.12.048 | bibcode = 2017CBio...27..527K }}</ref>
** The aberrant motor representation conveys an abnormally strong signal to the (anterior) [[insular cortex]], which is then hyperactive relative to non-misophonic controls.<ref name="Kumar_2021"/>
** Although it is less clear whether this pathway is aberrant or hyperactive due to mixed/limited empirical findings,<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/> the insula communicates this signal to '''(a)''' the [[amygdala]] (putatively responsible for the extreme [[emotions|emotional responses]] during a misophonic reaction) and '''(b)''' [[autonomic nervous system|autonomic control centers]] such as the [[periaqueductal gray]] and several [[hypothalamic nuclei]] (putatively responsible for physiologic aspects of a misophonic reaction, such as changes in heart rate, [[skin conductance]], and potentially other subjective symptoms of being triggered).
* Though the action perception model denotes the "information flow" through the [[central nervous system]] as unidirectional, the authors note that more complex bidirectional interactions between the various [[Vertex (graph theory)|nodes]] of the implicated [[Large-scale brain network|brain network]] are likely.<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/>

The action perception model arguably represents a major advance over previous theoretical work in this area, particularly in its ability to explain the [[neuroimaging]] data on misophonia published before 2024, when the theory was first proposed.<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/> Additionally, by focusing on higher-order "motor representations" of objects or actions that are abstracted from their initial [[sensory information]] and represented in [[association cortex]] (i.e., [[motor cortex|(pre)motor]] and [[limbic]] areas), the model can be applied to both the auditory and non-auditory triggers of misophonia (i.e., [[misokinesia]]) just as easily.<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/> But the action perception model appears to apply only to misophonic reactions to human-generated trigger sounds.<ref name="Dozier_2023"/> The action perception model appears consistent with certain clinical features of misophonia, such as the extreme context-specificity of the condition, given that the ''perceived (even if incorrectly perceived) source of the sound''<ref name="Samermit_2022">{{Cite journal |last1=Samermit |first1=Patrawat |last2=Young |first2=Michael |last3=Allen |first3=Allison K. |last4=Trillo |first4=Hannah |last5=Shankar |first5=Sandhya |last6=Klein |first6=Abigail |last7=Kay |first7=Chris |last8=Mahzouni |first8=Ghazaleh |last9=Reddy |first9=Veda |last10=Hamilton |first10=Veronica |last11=Davidenko |first11=Nicolas |date=2022-07-22 |title=Development and Evaluation of a Sound-Swapped Video Database for Misophonia |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |volume=13 |article-number=890829 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2022.890829 |doi-access=free |issn=1664-1078 |pmc=9355709 |pmid=35936325}}</ref> and ''whether the source can be identified''<ref name="Savard_2022">{{Cite journal |last1=Savard |first1=Marie-Anick |last2=Sares |first2=Anastasia G. |last3=Coffey |first3=Emily B. J. |last4=Deroche |first4=Mickael L. D. |date=2022-05-26 |title=Specificity of Affective Responses in Misophonia Depends on Trigger Identification |journal=Frontiers in Neuroscience |volume=16 |article-number=879583 |doi=10.3389/fnins.2022.879583 |doi-access=free |issn=1662-453X |pmc=9179422 |pmid=35692416}}</ref> appear to be among the largest drivers of the severity of a given misophonic reaction.<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/> Last, although still largely speculative, the action perception model provides an explanation for the peculiar observation that many people with misophonia (46.7% of this population in a recent study by Kumar's group)<ref name="Ash_2024">{{Cite journal |last1=Ash |first1=Paris A. |last2=Benzaquén |first2=Ester |last3=Gander |first3=Phillip E. |last4=Berger |first4=Joel I. |last5=Kumar |first5=Sukhbinder |date=2024-01-01 |title=Mimicry in misophonia: A large-scale survey of prevalence and relationship with trigger sounds |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jclp.23605 |journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology |language=en |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=186–197 |doi=10.1002/jclp.23605 |pmid=37850971 |issn=0021-9762}}</ref> engage in mimicry (deliberate or unconscious imitation of the trigger sound). As the [[anterior insula]] is engaged when counter-imitating an action (i.e., performing the opposite of the imitated movement),<ref name="Campbell_2018">{{Cite journal |last1=Campbell |first1=Megan E.J. |last2=Mehrkanoon |first2=Steve |last3=Cunnington |first3=Ross |date=2018-03-01 |title=Intentionally not imitating: Insula cortex engaged for top-down control of action mirroring |journal=Neuropsychologia |language=en |volume=111 |pages=241–251 |doi=10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2018.01.037|pmid=29408525 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Kumar and colleagues theorize that this mimicry conveys an "error signal" that helps inhibit the hyperactive [[insular cortex]] involved in the triggering process, thereby reducing the intensity of the misophonic response.<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/><ref name="Ash_2024"/>

Despite its apparent success in explaining findings in the misophonia literature, the action perception model's predictions are largely untested, and many aspects of the model rely on empirical studies with substantial methodological limitations.<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/> The basic neural mechanisms of action perception, mimicry, and the role (if any) of the "human mirror neuron system" within a broader [[social cognition]] framework in non-clinical populations must be further explored.<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/> The role of other co-occurring conditions, particularly those such as [[autism]] that are known to both affect [[social cognition]] and cooccur with misophonia at exceptionally high rates,<ref name="WilliamsDissertation_Ch5"/><ref name="Williams_2021">{{Cite journal |last1=Williams |first1=Zachary J. |last2=He |first2=Jason L. |last3=Cascio |first3=Carissa J. |last4=Woynaroski |first4=Tiffany G. |date=February 2021 |title=A review of decreased sound tolerance in autism: Definitions, phenomenology, and potential mechanisms |journal=Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews |language=en |volume=121 |pages=1–17 |doi=10.1016/j.neubiorev.2020.11.030 |pmc=7855558 |pmid=33285160}}</ref> is also an area for future research to explore and test the model.<ref name="Berger_ActionPerception_2024"/> The evidence supporting the action perception model is essentially correlational, not causal;<ref name="Dozier_2023"/> that is, it is unclear whether motor representations cause misophonic reactions or misophonia is a primarily auditory experience sometimes accompanied by motor representations.

==Epidemiology==
Research is still being conducted on misophonia's global prevalence, and studies of misophonia's prevalence vary considerably.<ref name="Vitoratou_2023"/> Several studies have investigated misophonia prevalence in samples representative of national populations. In these studies, many people—33%,<ref name="Pfeiffer_2025"/> 79%,<ref name="Dixon_2024"/><ref name="Kilic_2021"/> or 96%<ref name="Vitoratou_2023"/>—reported negative reactions to at least one misophonia trigger sound. The prevalence of clinically significant levels of misophonia was much lower. An online representative study in the [[United Kingdom]] found 18% of participants reported a significant burden from misophonia.<ref name="Vitoratou_2023"/> This study has been cited in popular outlets, including [[BBC News|BBC]],<ref>{{Cite news |date=2023-03-23 |title=What sounds drive you crazy? |language=en-GB |work=BBC Newsround |url=https://www.bbc.com/newsround/65035879 |access-date=2023-06-14}}</ref> [[Medscape]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=About a Fifth of Us Are Hypersensitive to Sounds |url=https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/991451 |access-date=2023-06-14 |website=Medscape |language=en}}</ref> and [[Medical Xpress]].<ref>{{Cite web |author=Public Library of Science |title=Nearly 1 in 5 UK adults may have misophonia, experiencing significant negative responses to sounds |url=https://medicalxpress.com/news/2023-03-uk-adults-misophonia-experiencing-significant.html |access-date=2023-06-14 |website=medicalxpress.com |date=22 March 2023 |language=en}}</ref> A household interview study in [[Ankara]], [[Turkey]], reported a slightly lower prevalence of 13%.<ref name="Kilic_2021"/> A [[United States]] representative web-based panel study reported a misophonia prevalence of just 5%, but this study required participants to score in the clinical range on not one but two misophonia measures.<ref name="Dixon_2024"/> A [[Germany|German]] study in which participants filled out questionnaires during household visits reports a seemingly similar 5% prevalence,<ref name="Jakubovski_2022"/> but this is based on a single measure that in the U.S. study yielded a prevalence of 14%.<ref name="Dixon_2024"/> When the German study requires clinical criteria to be met on two measures, prevalence drops to only 2%.<ref name="Jakubovski_2022"/> A second German study, using a single measure, reported similar or slightly lower levels of clinical misophonia symptoms compared to the first German study.<ref name="Pfeiffer_2025">{{cite journal | vauthors=Pfeiffer E, Allroggen M, Sachser C | journal=Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology | title=The prevalence of misophonia in a representative population-based survey in Germany | volume=60 | issue=1 | pages=257–264 | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | date= January 2025 | issn=1433-9285 | doi=10.1007/s00127-024-02707-0 | pmid=38963546 | pmc=11790775 }}</ref>

Authors of both German studies discussed the possibility that misophonia may be less common in Germany than in countries like Turkey or the U.S. Methodological explanations for the studies' divergent results cannot be ruled out.<ref name="Jakubovski_2022"/><ref name="Pfeiffer_2025"/> Still, evidence does suggest misophonia is not specific to any one culture. For example, although these are not representative population studies, research has reported misophonia prevalences of 6% among [[China|Chinese]] university students<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Zhou X, Wu MS, Storch EA |title=Misophonia symptoms among Chinese university students: Incidence, associated impairment, and clinical correlates |journal=Journal of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders |date=July 2017 |volume=14 |pages=7–12 |doi=10.1016/j.jocrd.2017.05.001 }}</ref> and 24% among [[Iran]]ian university students.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Yektatalab S, Mohammadi A, Zarshenas L | title = The Prevalence of Misophonia and Its Relationship with Obsessive-compulsive Disorder, Anxiety, and Depression in Undergraduate Students of Shiraz University of Medical Sciences: A Cross-Sectional Study | journal = International Journal of Community Based Nursing and Midwifery | volume = 10 | issue = 4 | pages = 259–268 | date = October 2022 | pmid = 36274664 | pmc = 9579453 | doi = 10.30476/IJCBNM.2022.92902.1888 }}</ref>

Misophonia symptoms may vary along a continuous spectrum, with varying proportions of people experiencing few or no, mild, moderate, or severe symptoms.<ref name="Naylor_2021" /><ref name="Pfeiffer_2025"/> Accordingly, the consensus definition of misophonia recognises that misophonia severity and expression vary.<ref name="Swedo_2022"/>

Although some studies report the prevalence and severity of misophonia are similar across genders,<ref name="Jakubovski_2022"/><ref name="Pfeiffer_2025"/> others report female individuals are more likely to have misophonia than males.<ref name="Dixon_2024"/><ref name="Kilic_2021"/> At least among youth and adults, younger age may be related to higher levels of misophonia symptoms,<ref name="Dixon_2024"/><ref name="Kilic_2021"/><ref name="Vitoratou_2023"/><ref name="Pfeiffer_2025"/> though other studies find no relationship between age and misophonia.<ref name="Jakubovski_2022"/>

==Associated experiences==
There is some indication that misophonia may be related to the experience of [[ASMR|autonomous sensory meridian response]] (ASMR), or auto-sensory meridian response, a pleasant form of paresthesia, a tingling sensation that typically begins on the scalp and moves down the back of the neck and upper spine.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mahady A, Takac M, De Foe A | title = What is autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR)? A narrative review and comparative analysis of related phenomena | journal = Consciousness and Cognition | volume = 109 | article-number = 103477 | date = March 2023 | pmid = 36806854 | doi = 10.1016/j.concog.2023.103477 | s2cid = 256874981 | url = https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/27565896 }}</ref> ASMR is described as the opposite of what can be observed in reactions to specific audio stimuli in misophonia.<ref name="Rouw_2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Rouw R, Erfanian M | title = A Large-Scale Study of Misophonia | journal = Journal of Clinical Psychology | volume = 74 | issue = 3 | pages = 453–479 | date = March 2018 | pmid = 28561277 | doi = 10.1002/jclp.22500 | hdl-access = free | hdl = 11245.1/c9c45e84-3c70-407e-aa2f-782ccdb79791 | url = https://dare.uva.nl/personal/pure/en/publications/a-largescale-study-of-misophonia(c9c45e84-3c70-407e-aa2f-782ccdb79791).html }}</ref> Studies have reported high prevalence of ASMR in people with misophonia.<ref name="Jakubovski_2022"/><ref name="Rouw_2018"/> But one of these studies also reported that ASMR susceptibility may be negatively correlated with misophonia symptom severity.<ref name="Jakubovski_2022"/> Conversely, a general population study suggests that emotional reactions to videos designed to induce misophonia, ASMR, and [[frisson|musical chills]] are all positively related to one another.<ref name="Mednicoff_2024">{{cite journal | last1=Mednicoff | first1=Solena D. | last2=Barashy | first2=Sivan | last3=Vollweiler | first3=David J. | last4=Benning | first4=Stephen D. | last5=Snyder | first5=Joel S. | last6=Hannon | first6=Erin E. | journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences | title=Misophonia reactions in the general population are correlated with strong emotional reactions to other everyday sensory–emotional experiences | volume=379 | issue=1908 | article-number=20230253 | date= 2024 | doi=10.1098/rstb.2023.0253 | pmid=39005036 | pmc=11444238 }}</ref> Other research shows no relationship between ASMR and misophonia.<ref name="Möllmann_2023"/>

Misophonia also appears to be related to higher levels of sensory hyper-responsivity across multiple modalities.<ref name="Andermane_2023">{{cite journal | last1= Andermane| first1= Nora| last2= Bauer| first2= Mathilde| last3= Simner| first3= Julia| last4= Ward| first4= Jamie| journal= Journal of Clinical Psychology| title=A symptom network model of misophonia: From heightened sensory sensitivity to clinical comorbidity | date= 2023 | volume=79 | issue=10 | pages=2364–2387 | doi=10.1002/jclp.23552 | pmid=37341653 }}</ref><ref name="Rinaldi_traits_2022">{{cite journal | last1=Rinaldi | first1=L. J. | last2=Simner | first2=J. | last3=Koursarou | first3=S. | last4=Ward | first4=J. | journal=Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders | title=Autistic traits, emotion regulation, and sensory sensitivities in children and adults with Misophonia | date=21 June 2022 | volume=53 | issue=3 | pages=1162–1174 | issn= 1573-3432 | doi=10.1007/s10803-022-05623-x | pmid=35729298 | pmc=9986206 }}</ref><ref name="Wu_2014">{{cite journal | last1=Wu | first1=Monica S. | last2=Lewin | first2=Adam B. | last3=Murphy | first3=Tanya K. | last4=Storch | first4=Eric A. | journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology | title=Misophonia: Incidence, phenomenology, and clinical correlates in an undergraduate student sample | volume=70 | issue=10 | pages=994–1007 | date= 2014 | issn=1097-4679 | doi=10.1002/jclp.22098 | pmid=24752915 }}</ref> Further, in the auditory modality, misophonia also appears to be related to other forms of sound intolerance. Many people with hyperacusis experience co-occurring misophonia<ref name="Möllmann_2023"/><ref name="Jastreboff_2014"/><ref name="Andermane_2023"/> and hyperacusis and tinnitus impact are related to misophonia symptoms.<ref name="Aazh_2022">{{cite journal | last1=Aazh | first1=Hashir | last2=Erfanian | first2=Mercede | last3=Danesh | first3=Ali A. | last4=Moore | first4=Brian C. J. | journal=Frontiers in Neuroscience | title=Audiological and Other Factors Predicting the Presence of Misophonia Symptoms Among a Clinical Population Seeking Help for Tinnitus and/or Hyperacusis | volume=16 | article-number=900065 | date=5 July 2022 | issn=1662-453X | doi=10.3389/fnins.2022.900065 | pmid=35864982 | pmc=9294447 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

Moreover, several studies suggest that people with misophonia are more likely to have emotion regulation difficulties.<ref name="Möllmann_2023"/><ref name="Rinaldi_traits_2022"/><ref name="Cassiello_2020_ED">{{cite journal | last1=Cassiello-Robbins | first1=Clair | last2=Anand | first2=Deepika | last3=McMahon | first3=Kibby | last4=Guetta | first4=Rachel | last5=Trumbull | first5=Jacqueline | last6=Kelley | first6=Lisalynn | last7=Rosenthal | first7=M. Zachary | journal=Frontiers in Psychiatry | title=The mediating role of emotion regulation within the relationship between neuroticism and misophonia: A preliminary investigation | volume=11 | article-number=847 | date= 2020 | issn=1664-0640 | doi=10.3389/fpsyt.2020.00847 | pmid=33005154 | pmc=7485014 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Dixon_ED">{{cite journal | last1=Dixon | first1=Laura J. | last2=Sevier | first2=Carey J. | last3=Freshley | first3=Alexandra M. | journal=Journal of Psychiatric Research | title=Emotion dysregulation in misophonia: Findings from a nationally representative sample | volume=180 | pages=266–272 | publisher=Elsevier BV | date= December 2024 | issn=0022-3956 | doi=10.1016/j.jpsychires.2024.10.022 | pmid=39467402 }}</ref><ref name="Guetta_2022">{{cite journal | last1=Guetta | first1=Rachel E. | last2=Cassiello-Robbins | first2=Clair | last3=Trumbull | first3=Jacqueline | last4=Anand | first4=Deepika | last5=Rosenthal | first5=M. Zachary | journal=PLOS ONE | title=Examining emotional functioning in misophonia: The role of affective instability and difficulties with emotion regulation | volume=17 | issue=2 | article-number=e0263230 | date=11 February 2022 | issn=1932-6203 | doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0263230 | pmid=35148347 | pmc=8836307 | bibcode=2022PLoSO..1763230G | doi-access=free }}</ref> Misophonia has also been linked to behavioural impulsivity.<ref name="Abramovitch_2023">{{cite journal | last1=Abramovitch | first1=Amitai | last2=Herrera | first2=Tanya A. | last3=Etherton | first3=Joseph L. | journal=Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry | title=A neuropsychological study of misophonia | article-number=101897 | date= August 2023 | volume=82 | issn=0005-7916 | doi=10.1016/j.jbtep.2023.101897 | pmid=37657963 }}</ref>

Several studies also link misophonia to anxiety.<ref name="Cassiello_2020"/><ref name="Wu_2014"/><ref name="Aazh_2022"/><ref name="Guetta_2022"/><ref name="Abramovitch_2023"/><ref name="Ay_2024">{{cite journal | last1=Ay | first1=Ezgi | last2=Huviyetli | first2=Mert | last3=Çakmak | first3=Eda | journal=Frontiers in Psychology | title=The mediating role of anxiety in the relationship between misophonia and quality of life: findings from the validated Turkish version of MisoQuest | volume=15 | article-number=1361645 | date=16 April 2024 | issn=1664-1078 | doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1361645 | pmid=38689723 | pmc=11058809 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Higher levels of perfectionism have been reported in people with misophonia.<ref name="Jakubovski_2022"/>

Several studies suggest people with misophonia may show greater attention to detail.<ref name="Andermane_2023"/><ref name="Rinaldi_traits_2022"/><ref name="Simner_attention_2021">{{cite journal | last1=Simner | first1=J. | last2=Koursarou | first2=S. | last3=Rinaldi | first3=L.J. | last4=Ward | first4=J. | journal=Journal of Clinical and Experimental Neuropsychology | title=Attention, flexibility, and imagery in misophonia: Does attention exacerbate everyday disliking of sound? | volume=43 | pages=1006–1017 | publisher=Routledge | date= 2021 | issue=10 | issn=1380-3395 | doi=10.1080/13803395.2022.2056581 | pmid=35331082 }}</ref>

Misophonia has been linked to [[obsessive–compulsive disorder]].<ref name="Wu_2014"/><ref name="Rosenthal_phenotyping_2022">{{cite journal | last1=Rosenthal | first1=M. Zachary | last2=McMahon | first2=Kibby | last3=Greenleaf | first3=Anna S. | last4=Cassiello-Robbins | first4=Clair | last5=Guetta | first5=Rachel | last6=Trumbull | first6=Jacqueline | last7=Anand | first7=Deepika | last8=Frazer-Abel | first8=Emily S. | last9=Kelley | first9=Lisalynn | journal=Frontiers in Psychology | title=Phenotyping misophonia: Psychiatric disorders and medical health correlates | volume=13 | article-number=941898 | date=6 October 2022 | issn=1664-1078 | doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2022.941898 | pmid=36275232 | pmc=9583952 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Not-just-right experiences also appear to be more common in people with misophonia.<ref name="Jakubovski_2022"/>

==Society and culture==
People who experience misophonia have formed online support groups.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/09/06/health/06annoy.html |title=When a Chomp or a Slurp is a Trigger for Outrage | vauthors = Cohen J |date=5 September 2011|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=5 February 2012 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221220162932/https://www.nytimes.com/2011/09/06/health/06annoy.html |archive-date= 20 December 2022}}</ref><ref name="Plos2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Schröder A, Vulink N, Denys D | editor-first1 = Leonardo | editor-last1 = Fontenelle | title = Misophonia: diagnostic criteria for a new psychiatric disorder | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 8 | issue = 1 | article-number = e54706 | date = 23 January 2013 | pmid = 23372758 | pmc = 3553052 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0054706 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2013PLoSO...854706S }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Misophonia Peer Support Meetings |url=https://www.soquiet.org/groups |access-date=2025-01-20 |website=soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy |language=en-US}}</ref> Nonprofit organizations such as [[soQuiet]], [[Misophonia Hub]], and Teens for Education + Advocacy for Misophonia (TEAM) actively share resources for people affected by misophonia.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.soquiet.org/misophoniatools|title=Free Misophonia Tools & Resources|website=soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.teenmiso.org/resources|title=Resources|website=TEAM}}</ref> In 2025, [[Duke University]]'s Center for Misophonia and Emotion Regulation (CMER) partnered with the Italian Misophonia association, TEAM, [[Swansea University]], and others to host a research workshop called PRIMER for high school students to gain knowledge in the science of misophonia, conduct of human research, and project development.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://psychiatry.duke.edu/duke-center-misophonia-and-emotion-regulation|title=Duke Center for Misophonia and Emotion Regulation &#124; Duke Department of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences|website=psychiatry.duke.edu}}</ref>

In 2016, a documentary about the condition, ''Quiet Please'', was released.<ref>{{cite news| vauthors = Jeffries A |title=There's a New Film About Misophonia, Where People Get Enraged by Certain Sounds|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/theres-a-new-film-about-misophonia-where-people-are-enraged-by-certain-sounds/|work=Motherboard|date=17 June 2016|language=en-us|access-date=18 September 2020 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220701195101/https://www.vice.com/en/article/bmv7ez/theres-a-new-film-about-misophonia-where-people-are-enraged-by-certain-sounds |archive-date= 1 July 2022}}</ref>

In 2020, a team of misophonia researchers<ref name="Plos2013" /> received the [[Ig Nobel Prize]] in medicine "for diagnosing a long-unrecognized medical condition".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://improbable.com/ig/winners/|title=Past Ig Winners|date=1 August 2006|website=improbable.com}}</ref>

The 2022 film [[Tár]] depicts a conductor with misophonia.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-01-09 |title=Cate Blanchett Can't Imagine Her Life Without Lydia Tár |url=https://www.wmagazine.com/culture/cate-blanchett-lydia-tar-interview |access-date=2023-06-14 |website=W Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

In 2024, the misophonia advocacy organization soQuiet created [[World Misophonia Awareness Day]], to be held on July 9,<ref>{{Cite web |title= World Misophonia Awareness Day 2025: Why Misophonia Makes Everyday Sounds Feel Like An Attack—Here's What It Does To The Brain |url= https://www.healthandme.com/health-wellness/world-misophonia-awareness-day-2025-when-everyday-sounds-feel-like-an-attackheres-what-misophonia-is-article-152250616 |access-date= 2026-07-03 |website= Health and Me |language= en}}</ref> the birthday of Michelle Del Valle, a 17-year-old who took her own life due to her struggles with misophonia.<ref>{{Cite web |title= Misophonia Awareness Day - July 9th |url= https://www.misophoniaday.com/ |access-date= 2026-07-03 |website= World Misophonia Awareness Day {{!}} July 9th |language= en}}</ref> Many organizations, advocates, and individuals have used this awareness day to share information about misophonia, especially among medical professionals, and work to build community connections for people affected by misophonia.<ref>{{Cite web|title= Why World Misophonia Awareness Day Matters |url= https://www.misophoniaresearchfund.org/press/why-world-misophonia-awareness-day-matters |access-date= 2026-07-03 |website= www.misophoniaresearchfund.org |language= en}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Music therapy
======================================================================

{{Short description|Health profession}}
{{Infobox medical intervention
|  name        = Music therapy
|  image       = Louis Gallait - Power of Music - Walters 37134.jpg
|  caption     = ''Power of Music'' by [[Louis Gallait]]. A brother and sister resting before an old [[tomb]]. The brother is attempting to comfort his sibling by playing the violin, and she has fallen into a deep sleep, "oblivious of all grief, mental and physical".
|  ICD10       =
|  ICD9        = {{ICD9proc|93.84}}
|  MeshID      = D009147
|  other_codes =
}}

'''Music therapy''' is the use of music in a clinical setting to accomplish therapeutic goals.<ref name="About Music Therapy & AMTA" /> Music therapists are generally trained musicians who have completed an accredited music therapy program. Although established as a profession only relatively recently, the connection between music and therapy is not new.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Darnley-Smith |first1=Rachel |title=Music Therapy (Creative Therapies in Practice series) |last2=M Patey |first2=Helen |date=February 18, 2003  |publisher=Sage Publications Ltd. |location=London|isbn=978-0-7619-5777-5}}</ref>

Music therapy is a broad field, using music-based experiences to address client needs in one or more domains of human functioning: cognitive, academic, emotional/psychological, behavioral, communication, social, physiological (sensory, motor, pain, neurological and other physical systems), spiritual, or aesthetics.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book|last=Gaston|first=E. Thayer|title=Music in Therapy|publisher=The Macmillan Company|year=1968|editor-last=Gaston|editor-first=E. Thayer|location=New York|pages=7–29|chapter=Man and music}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Chase|first=Kristen M.|title=The Music Therapy Assessment Handbook|publisher=Southern Pen Publishers|year=2002|location=Columbus, MO}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Gfeller|first=Kate E.|title=An Introduction to Music Therapy: Theory and Practice|publisher=The American Music Therapy Association|year=2008|isbn=978-1-884914-20-1|editor-last=Davis|editor-first=William B.|edition=3|location=Silver Spring, MD|pages=41–75|chapter=Music: A human phenomenon and therapeutic tool|editor-last2=Gfeller|editor-first2=Kate E.|editor-last3=Thaut|editor-first3=Michael H.}}</ref> Music experiences are strategically designed to use the elements of music for therapeutic effects, including melody, harmony, key, mode, meter, rhythm, pitch/range, duration, timbre, form, texture, and instrumentation.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Bruscia|first=Kenneth E.|title=Improvisational models of music therapy|publisher=Charles C Thomas|year=1987|editor-last=Bruscia|editor-first=Kenneth E.|location=Springfield, IL|pages=465–496|chapter=IAP scales and criteria}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Schneck|first1=Daniel J.|title=The Music Effect: Music Physiology and Clinical Applications|last2=Berger|first2=Dorita S.|publisher=Jessica Kingsley Publishers|year=2006|isbn=978-1-84310-771-2|location=Philadelphia, PA}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Sarrazin|first=Natalie|url=https://milnepublishing.geneseo.edu/music-and-the-child/chapter/chapter-2/|title=Music and the Child|publisher=Open SUNY Textbooks|year=2016|isbn=978-1-942341-20-8|location=Milne Library|chapter=Music: Fundamentals and Educational Roots in the U.S.}}</ref>

Some common music therapy practices include developmental work (communication, motor skills, etc.) with individuals with special needs, [[songwriting]] and listening in reminiscence, orientation work with the elderly, processing and relaxation work, and rhythmic [[brainwave entrainment]] for physical rehabilitation in stroke survivors. Music therapy is used in medical hospitals, cancer centers, schools, alcohol and drug recovery programs, psychiatric hospitals, nursing homes, and correctional facilities.<ref name="About Music Therapy & AMTA">{{Cite web|last=American Music Therapy Association|title=About Music Therapy & AMTA|url=https://www.musictherapy.org/about/|access-date=January 2, 2021|website=About Music Therapy & AMTA}}</ref>

Music therapy is distinctive from musopathy, which relies on a more generic and non-cultural approach based on neural, physical, and other responses to the fundamental aspects of sound.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.dtnext.in/city/2019/12/30/musopathy-mapping-music-and-its-medicinal-benefits | title=Musopathy: Mapping music and its medicinal benefits | website=[[DT Next]] | date=December 31, 2019 }}</ref> Music therapy might also incorporate practices from sound healing, also known as sound immersion or sound therapy, which focuses on sound rather than song.<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal |last1=Crowe |first1=B. J. |last2=Scovel |first2=M. |date=1996-01-01 |title=An Overview of Sound Healing Practices: Implications for the Profession of Music Therapy |url=https://academic.oup.com/mtp/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/mtp/14.1.21 |journal=Music Therapy Perspectives |language=en |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=21–29 |doi=10.1093/mtp/14.1.21 |issn=0734-6875|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Sound healing describes the use of vibrations and frequencies for relaxation, meditation, and other claimed healing benefits.<ref>Gibson, David (2018). ''The Complete Guide to Sound Healing'' (2nd ed.), Sound of Light.</ref>  Unlike music therapy, sound healing is unregulated and an [[alternative therapy]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sound Healing Vs. Music Therapy {{!}} Sound Healing Research Foundation |url=https://soundhealingresearchfoundation.org/sound-healing-vs-music-therapy/ |access-date=2025-04-17 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":14" />

Music therapists use their techniques to help their patients in many areas, ranging from [[Psychological stress|stress relief]] before and after surgeries to [[Neuropathology|neuropathologies]] such as [[Alzheimer's disease]]. Studies on people diagnosed with mental health disorders such as anxiety, depression, and schizophrenia have associated some improvements in mental health with music therapy.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = McCaffrey T, Edwards J, Fannon D | date=2011|title=Is there a role for music therapy in the recovery approach in mental health? |journal=The Arts in Psychotherapy|volume=38|issue=3|pages=185–89|doi=10.1016/j.aip.2011.04.006| hdl=10344/3362|url=https://ulir.ul.ie/bitstream/10344/3362/2/McCaffrey_2011_music.pdf|hdl-access=free}}</ref> However, in many countries, including the United States, music therapists do not diagnose, so diagnosing mental disorders would not be within their scope of practice. [[National Institute for Health and Care Excellence|The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)]] has claimed that music therapy is an effective method in helping people with mental health issues, and more should be done to offer those in need of this type of help.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Is there a role for music therapy in the recovery approach in mental health?|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0197455611000438|journal=The Arts in Psychotherapy|year=2011|volume= 38| issue = 3|pages=185–189|doi=10.1016/j.aip.2011.04.006|last1=McCaffrey|first1=Tríona|last2=Edwards|first2=Jane|last3=Fannon|first3=Dominic|hdl=10344/3362|hdl-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Uses ==

=== Children and adolescents ===
Music therapy may be suggested for adolescent populations to help manage disorders usually diagnosed in adolescence, such as [[Mood disorder|mood]] and [[Anxiety disorder|anxiety]] disorders and [[eating disorder]]s, or unpleasant behaviors, including [[Suicide attempt|suicide attempts]], withdrawal from family, [[social isolation]] from peers, aggression, [[Runaway (dependent)|running away]], and [[substance abuse]].<ref name="Yinger">{{cite journal |last1=Swedberg Yinger |first1=Olivia |last2=Gooding |first2=Lori |date=July 2014 |title=Music Therapy and Music Medicine for Children and Adolescents |journal=Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Clinics |volume=23 |issue=3 |pages=535–53 |doi=10.1016/j.chc.2013.03.003 |pmid=24975624}}</ref><ref name="Keen">{{cite journal |last=Keen MSocSc |first=Alexander W. |date=March 2005 |title=Using music as a therapy tool to motivate troubled adolescents |journal=Social Work in Health Care |volume=39:3–4 |issue=3–4 |pages=361–73 |doi=10.1300/J010v39n03_09 |pmid=15774401 |s2cid=25035875}}</ref> Goals in treating adolescents with music therapy, especially for those at high risk, often include increased recognition and awareness of emotions and moods, improved decision-making skills, opportunities for creative self expression, decreased anxiety, increased self-confidence, improved self-esteem, and better listening skills.<ref>{{cite web |title=Music Therapy with High Risk Adolescents (PDF) |url=https://msu.edu/~msuamtas/scott_handout.pdf |access-date=August 23, 2018 |website=American Music Therapy Association, Michigan State University Chapter |publisher=Michigan State University}}</ref>

There is some evidence that, when combined with other types of rehabilitation, music therapy may contribute to the success rate of [[Sensory-motor coupling|sensorimotor]], cognitive, and communicative rehabilitation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=LaGasse |first1=A. Blythe |title=Music and Rehabilition: Neurological Approaches |last2=Thaut |first2=Michael H. |date=April 15, 2012 |journal=Music, Health, and Wellbeing |isbn=978-0-19-958697-4 |pages=153–63 |doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199586974.003.0012 |name-list-style=vanc}}</ref> For children and adolescents with major depressive or anxiety disorders, there is moderate to low quality evidence that music therapy added to the standard treatment, may reduce internalizing symptoms, and may be more effective than treatment without music therapy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aalbers |first1=Sonja |last2=Fusar-Poli |first2=Laura |last3=Freeman |first3=Ruth E. |last4=Spreen |first4=Marinus |last5=Ket |first5=Johannes Cf |last6=Vink |first6=Annemiek C. |last7=Maratos |first7=Anna |last8=Crawford |first8=Mike |last9=Chen |first9=Xi-Jing |date=November 2017 |title=Music therapy for depression |journal=The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |volume=2017 |issue=11 |article-number=CD004517 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD004517.pub3 |issn=1469-493X |pmc=6486188 |pmid=29144545 |hdl=10044/1/56028}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Geipel J, Koenig J, Hillecke TK, Resch F, Kaess M |date=January 2018 |title=Music-based interventions to reduce internalizing symptoms in children and adolescents: A meta-analysis |journal=Journal of Affective Disorders |volume=225 |pages=647–656 |doi=10.1016/j.jad.2017.08.035 |pmid=28889050}}</ref>

=== Premature infants ===
[[Preterm birth|Premature infants]] are those born at 37 weeks after conception or earlier. Offering musical therapy to premature infants while they are in the [[neonatal intensive care unit]] (NICU) aims to both mask unwanted auditory stimuli, stimulate infant development, and promote a calm environment for families. While there are no reported adverse effects from music therapy, the evidence supporting music therapy's beneficial effects for infants is weak as many of the clinical trials that have been performed either had mixed results or were poorly designed.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Haslbeck |first1=Friederike B |last2=Mueller |first2=Katharina |last3=Karen |first3=Tanja |last4=Loewy |first4=Joanne |last5=Meerpohl |first5=Joerg J |last6=Bassler |first6=Dirk |date=2023-09-07 |editor-last=Cochrane Neonatal Group |title=Musical and vocal interventions to improve neurodevelopmental outcomes for preterm infants |journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |language=en |volume=2023 |issue=9 |article-number=CD013472 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD013472.pub2 |pmc=10483930 |pmid=37675934}}</ref> There is no strong evidence to suggest that music therapy improves an infant's oxygen therapy, improves sucking, or improves development when compared to usual care.<ref name=":13" /> There is some weaker evidence that music therapy may decrease an infants' heart rate.<ref name=":13" /> There is no evidence to indicate that music therapy reduces anxiety in parents of preterm infants in the NICU or information to understand what type of music therapy may be more beneficial or how for how long.<ref name=":13" />

=== Medical disorders ===
Music may both motivate and provide a sense of distraction.<ref name="ReferenceB" /> Rhythmic stimuli has been found to help balance training for those with a brain injury.<ref name="ReferenceB" />

Singing is a form of rehabilitation for neurological impairments. Neurological impairments following a brain injury can be in the form of [[apraxia]] – loss to perform purposeful movements, [[dysarthria]], muscle control disturbances (due to damage of the central nervous system), [[aphasia]] (defect in expression causing distorted speech), or language comprehension. It is shown that patients with schizophrenia have altered feeling on major and minor chord.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Abe |first1=Daijyu |last2=Arai |first2=Makoto |last3=Itokawa |first3=Masanari |date=July 2017 |title=Music-evoked emotions in schizophrenia |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0920996416305874 |journal=Schizophrenia Research |language=en |volume=185 |pages=144–147 |doi=10.1016/j.schres.2016.12.013 |pmid=28017493 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Singing training has been found to improve lung, speech clarity, and coordination of speech muscles, thus, accelerating rehabilitation of such neurological impairments. For example, [[melodic intonation therapy]] is the practice of communicating with others by singing to enhance speech or increase speech production by promoting socialization, and emotional expression.<ref name="ReferenceB" /> After a stroke, music therapy may be a useful tool for the recovery of motor skills.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Magee WL, Clark I, Tamplin J, Bradt J |date=January 2017 |title=Music interventions for acquired brain injury |journal=The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |volume=1 |issue=1 |article-number=CD006787 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD006787.pub3 |pmc=6464962 |pmid=28103638}}</ref> Listening to music may improve heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure in those with [[coronary heart disease]] (CHD).<ref name="Bradt2013">{{cite journal |vauthors=Bradt J, Dileo C, Potvin N |date=December 2013 |title=Music for stress and anxiety reduction in coronary heart disease patients |journal=The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |volume=2021 |issue=12 |article-number=CD006577 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD006577.pub3 |pmc=8454043 |pmid=24374731 |s2cid=16861063}}</ref>  In addition, there is tentative evidence that music interventions led by a trained [[music therapist]] may have positive effects on psychological and physical outcomes in adults with cancer. The effectiveness of music therapy for children with cancer is not known.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bradt |first1=Joke |last2=Dileo |first2=Cheryl |last3=Myers-Coffman |first3=Katherine |last4=Biondo |first4=Jacelyn |date=October 12, 2021 |title=Music interventions for improving psychological and physical outcomes in people with cancer |url= |journal=The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |volume=2021 |issue=10 |article-number=CD006911 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD006911.pub4 |issn=1469-493X |pmc=8510511 |pmid=34637527}}</ref>

==== Autism ====
Music may help people with autism hone their motor and attention skills as well as healthy neurodevelopment of socio-communication and interaction skills. Music therapy may also contribute to improved selective attention, speech production, and language processing and acquisition in people with autism.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Janzen |first1=Thenille Braun |last2=Thaut |first2=Michael H. |year=2018 |title=Rethinking the role of music in the neurodevelopment of autism spectrum disorder |journal=Music & Science |volume=1 |page=205920431876963 |article-number=2059204318769639 |doi=10.1177/2059204318769639 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Music therapy may benefit the family as a whole. Some family members of children with autism claim that music therapy sessions have allowed their child to interact more with the family and the world. Music therapy is also beneficial in that it gives children an outlet to use outside of the sessions. Some children after participating in music therapy may want to keep making music long after the sessions end.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Thompson |first1=Grace |date=November 23, 2017 |title=Long-Term Perspectives of Family Quality of Life Following Music Therapy with Young Children on the Autism Spectrum |journal=Journal of Music Therapy |volume=54 |issue=4 |pages=432–59 |doi=10.1093/jmt/thx013 |pmid=29186566 |s2cid=4635448}}</ref>{{Primary source inline|date=April 2025}}

==== Dementia ====
{{main|Music therapy for Alzheimer's disease}}

{{More citations needed section|date=December 2020}}

Like many of the other disorders mentioned, some of the most common significant effects of dementia can be seen in social behaviors, leading to improvements in interaction, conversation, and other such skills. A study of over 330 subjects showed that music therapy produces highly significant improvements in social behaviors, overt behaviors like wandering and restlessness, reductions in agitated behaviors, and improvements to cognitive defects, measured with reality orientation and face recognition tests. The effectiveness of the treatment seems to be strongly dependent on the patient and the quality and length of treatment.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal |last1=Keough |first1=Laurie |date=October 1, 2017 |title=Assessment-Based Small-Group Music Therapy Programming for Individuals with Dementia and Alzheimer's Disease: A Multi-Year Clinical Project |journal=Music Therapy Perspectives |pages=181–189 |doi=10.1093/mtp/miw021}}</ref>{{Primary source inline|date=April 2025}}

A meta-study examined the proposed neurological mechanisms behind music therapy's effects on these patients.<ref name="Lu 2025 167–186">{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Li-Chin |last2=Lan |first2=Shao-Huan |last3=Lan |first3=Shou-Jen |last4=Hsieh |first4=Yen-Ping |date=2025 |title=Effectiveness of the Music Therapy in Dementia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials |journal=Dementia and Geriatric Cognitive Disorders |volume=54 |issue=3 |pages=167–186 |doi=10.1159/000542464 |issn=1421-9824 |pmid=39536719}}</ref> Many authors suspect that music has a soothing effect on the patient by affecting how noise is perceived: music renders noise familiar, or buffers the patient from overwhelming or extraneous noise in their environment. Others suggest that music acts like a mediator for social interactions, providing a vessel through which to interact with others without requiring much cognitive load.<ref name="ReferenceA" />{{Primary source inline|date=April 2025}}

==== Aphasia ====
{{main|Music therapy for non-fluent aphasia}}

Broca's aphasia, or non-fluent aphasia, is a language disorder caused by damage to Broca's area and surrounding regions in the left frontal lobe.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bates |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Wilson |first2=Stephen M. |last3=Saygin |first3=Ayse Pinar |last4=Dick |first4=Frederic |last5=Sereno |first5=Martin I. |last6=Knight |first6=Robert T. |last7=Dronkers |first7=Nina F. |date=April 21, 2003 |title=Voxel-based lesion–symptom mapping |journal=Nature Neuroscience |volume=6 |issue=5 |pages=448–450 |doi=10.1038/nn1050 |pmid=12704393 |s2cid=5134480}}</ref>{{Primary source inline|date=April 2025}} Those with non-fluent aphasia are able to understand language fairly well, they struggle with language production and syntax.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kolk |first1=Herman |last2=Heeschen |first2=Claus |date=May 1990 |title=Adaptation symptoms and impairment symptoms in Broca's aphasia |journal=Aphasiology |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=221–231 |doi=10.1080/02687039008249075}}</ref>

Neurologist [[Oliver Sacks]] studied neurological oddities in people, trying to understand how the brain works. He concluded that people with some type of frontal lobe damage often "produced not only severe difficulties with expressive language (aphasia) but a strange access of musicality with incessant whistling, singing and a passionate interest in music.
