'''Psychological trauma''' (also known as '''mental trauma''', '''psychiatric trauma''', '''emotional damage''', or '''psychotrauma''') is an emotional response caused by severe, distressing events, such as [[Major trauma|bodily injury]], [[Sexual assault|sexual violence]], or other threats to the life of the subject or their loved ones; indirect exposure, such as from watching television news, may be extremely distressing and can produce an involuntary and possibly overwhelming physiological [[stress response]], but does not always produce trauma.<ref name="DSM" /> Examples of distressing events include exposure to [[violence]], [[sexual assault]] or [[rape]], [[Child abuse|childhood abuse]], the death of a loved one, or [[Mass casualty incident|mass casualty events]] such as [[terrorist attacks]] or [[Natural disaster|natural disasters]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-09-03 |title=12 Very Common Examples of Trauma |url=https://ipseitycounselingclinic.com/2019/09/03/examples-of-trauma/ |access-date=2026-07-21 |website=Ipseity Counseling in Denver |language=en-US}}</ref>

Short-term reactions such as [[acute stress disorder|psychological shock]] and [[denial|psychological denial]] typically follow. Long-term reactions and effects include [[flashback (psychology)|flashbacks]], [[panic attacks]], [[insomnia]], [[nightmare disorder]], difficulties with [[interpersonal relationships]], [[emotional dysregulation]], [[post-traumatic stress disorder]] (PTSD), and [[brief psychotic disorder]]. Physical [[symptoms]] including [[migraines]], [[hyperventilation]], [[hyperhidrosis]], and [[nausea]] are often associated with or made worse by trauma.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.apa.org/topics/trauma|title=Trauma and Shock|work=American Psychological Association|access-date=21 March 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |chapter=Understanding the Impact of Trauma |title=Trauma-Informed Care in Behavioral Health Services |date=2014 |chapter-url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK207191/ }}</ref>

People react to similar events differently. Most who experience a potentially traumatic event do not become psychologically traumatized, though they may be distressed and experience suffering.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Storr CL, Ialongo NS, Anthony JC, Breslau N|year=2007|title=Childhood antecedents of exposure to traumatic events and post-traumatic stress disorder|journal=American Journal of Psychiatry|volume=164|issue=1|pages=119–25|pmid=17202553|doi=10.1176/ajp.2007.164.1.119}}</ref> Some will develop PTSD after exposure to a traumatic event, or series of events.<ref name="Karg_2014">{{cite book | quote = Among individuals who do develop post-traumatic stress after exposure to a traumatic event, some develop symptoms sufficient to meet the diagnostic criteria for PTSD | vauthors = Karg RS, Bose J, Batts KR, Forman-Hoffman VL, Liao D, Hirsch E, Pemberton MR, Colpe LJ, Hedden SL | display-authors = 6 | chapter = Past year mental disorders among adults in the United States: results from the 2008–2012 Mental Health Surveillance Study | title = CBHSQ Data Review | date = October 2014 | publisher = Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (US) | pmid = 27748100 | chapter-url = https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK379142/ }}</ref><ref name = "Forman-Hoffman_2016">{{cite book | vauthors = Forman-Hoffman VL, Bose J, Batts KR, Glasheen C, Hirsch E, Karg RS, Huang LN, Hedden SL | chapter = Correlates of lifetime exposure to one or more potentially traumatic events and subsequent posttraumatic stress among adults in the United States: results from the mental health surveillance study, 2008–2012. | title = CBHSQ data review | date = April 2016 | publisher = Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (US) | pmid = 27748101 | chapter-url = https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK390285/ }}</ref> This discrepancy in risk rate can be attributed to [[protective factor]]s some individuals have, that enable them to cope with difficult events, including temperamental and environmental factors, such as [[psychological resilience|resilience]] and willingness to seek help.<ref name="Wingo, Aliza P. 2014">{{cite journal|vauthors=Wingo, Aliza P, Ressler KJ, Bradley B |year=2014|title=Resilience characteristics mitigate tendency for harmful alcohol and illicit drug use in adults with a history of childhood abuse: A cross-sectional study of 2024 inner-city men and women|journal=Journal of Psychiatric Research|volume=51|pages=93–99|doi=10.1016/j.jpsychires.2014.01.007|pmid=24485848|pmc=4605671}}</ref>

[[Psychotraumatology]] is the study of psychological trauma.

==Signs and symptoms==
People who experience trauma often have problems and difficulties afterwards. The severity of these symptoms depends on formative year factors of the person affected, the types of trauma involved, and the support and treatment they receive from others. The range of reactions to trauma can be wide and varied, and differ in severity from person to person.<ref name="Carlson"/>

After a traumatic experience, a person may re-experience the trauma mentally and physically.  For example, the sound of a motorcycle engine may cause intrusive thoughts or a sense of re-experiencing a traumatic experience that involved a similar sound.  Sometimes a benign stimulus (e.g. noise from a motorcycle) may get connected in the mind with the traumatic experience.  This process is called traumatic coupling.<ref>{{Cite book| vauthors = Goulston M |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BlHgzUBOzbEC&q=%22traumatic+coupling%22&pg=PA39|title=Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder For Dummies|date=9 February 2011|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1-118-05090-3|page=39|language=en}}</ref>  In this process, the benign stimulus becomes a trauma reminder, also called a [[trauma trigger]].  These can produce uncomfortable and even painful feelings. Re-experiencing can damage people's sense of safety, self, [[self-efficacy]], as well as their ability to regulate emotions and navigate relationships. They may turn to [[psychoactive drug]]s, including [[alcohol (drug)|alcohol]], to try to escape or dampen the feelings. These triggers cause flashbacks, which are dissociative experiences where the person feels as though the events are reoccurring. Flashbacks can range from distraction to complete dissociation or loss of awareness of the current context. Re-experiencing of symptoms is a sign that the body and mind are actively struggling to cope with the traumatic experience.

Triggers and cues act as reminders of the trauma and can cause [[anxiety]] and other associated emotions.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Treatment (US) |first1=Center for Substance Abuse |title=Understanding the Impact of Trauma |date=2014 |publisher=Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (US) |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK207191/ |access-date=5 December 2022 |language=en}}</ref> Often the person can be completely unaware of what these triggers are. In many cases, this may lead a person with a traumatic disorder to engage in disruptive behaviors or self-destructive coping mechanisms, often without being fully aware of the nature or causes of their own actions. [[Panic attack]]s are an example of a psychosomatic response to such emotional triggers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Joscelyne |first1=Amy |last2=McLean |first2=Siobhan |last3=Drobny |first3=Juliette |last4=Bryant |first4=Richard A. |date=December 2012 |title=Fear of memories: the nature of panic in posttraumatic stress disorder |journal=European Journal of Psychotraumatology |volume=3 |issue=1 |article-number=19084 |doi=10.3402/ejpt.v3i0.19084 |pmc=3488113 |pmid=23130094}}</ref>

Consequently, intense feelings of anger may frequently surface, sometimes in inappropriate or unexpected situations, as danger may always seem to be present due to re-experiencing past events. Upsetting memories such as images, thoughts, or [[flashback (psychology)|flashback]]s may haunt the person, and [[nightmare]]s may be frequent.<ref name="Loyola">{{cite web|url=http://www.loyola.edu/campuslife/healthservices/counselingcenter/trauma.html|title=Loyola College in Maryland: Trauma and Post-traumatic Stress Disorder|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051028034430/http://www.loyola.edu/campuslife/healthservices/counselingcenter/trauma.html|archive-date=28 October 2005}}</ref> [[Insomnia]] may occur as lurking fears and insecurity keep the person vigilant and on the lookout for danger, both day and night. A messy personal financial scene, as well as debt, are common features in trauma-affected people.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Savoteur |date=13 January 2022 |title=The Effects of Trauma on Personal Finance » Savoteur |url=https://savoteur.com/effects-of-trauma-on-personal-finance/ |access-date=27 September 2022 |language=en-US}}</ref> Trauma does not only cause changes in one's daily functions, but could also lead to morphological changes.<ref>{{cite book  |date=2014 |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK207191/ |access-date=13 May 2023 |publisher=Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (US) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment (US)|title=Trauma-Informed Care in Behavioral Health Services|series=Treatment Improvement Protocol (TIP) Series, No. 57.|chapter=Chapter 3: Understanding the Impact of Trauma}}</ref> Such epigenetic changes can be passed on to the next generation, thus making genetics one of the components of psychological trauma.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yehuda |first1=Rachel |last2=Lehrner |first2=Amy |title=Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: putative role of epigenetic mechanisms: Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: putative role of epigenetic mechanisms |journal=World Psychiatry |date=October 2018 |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=243–257 |doi=10.1002/wps.20568 |pmid=30192087 |pmc=6127768 }}</ref> However, some people are born with or later develop protective factors that help lower their risk of psychological trauma.<ref name="Frommberger 2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Frommberger U, Angenendt J, Berger M | title = Post-traumatic stress disorder—a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge | journal = Deutsches Ärzteblatt International | volume = 111 | issue = 5 | pages = 59–65 | date = January 2014 | pmid = 24612528 | pmc = 3952004 | doi = 10.3238/arztebl.2014.0059 }}</ref>

Traumatic events are sometimes constantly experienced as if they were happening in the present, preventing the subject from gaining perspective on the experience. This can produce a pattern of prolonged periods of acute arousal punctuated by periods of physical and [[Occupational burnout|mental exhaustion]]. In time, [[emotional exhaustion]] may set in, leading to distraction, and clear thinking may be difficult or impossible. [[Emotional detachment]], as well as [[dissociation (psychology)|dissociation]] (depersonalization or derealization) can frequently occur. Dissociating from the painful emotion includes numbing all emotion, and the person may seem emotionally flat, preoccupied, distant, or cold. Exposure to and re-experiencing trauma can cause neurophysiological changes like slowed myelination, abnormalities in synaptic pruning, shrinking of the hippocampus, cognitive and affective impairment. This is significant in brain scan studies done regarding higher-order function assessment with children and youth who were in vulnerable environments.

Some traumatized people may feel permanently damaged when trauma symptoms do not go away and they do not believe their situation will improve. This can lead to feelings of despair, transient paranoid ideation,  loss of [[self-esteem]], profound [[emptiness]], suicidality, and frequently, [[Major depressive disorder|depression]]. If important aspects of the person's self and world understanding have been violated, the person may call their own identity into question.<ref name="Carlson">{{cite web |url=http://www.ncptsd.va.gov/facts/general/fs_effects.html |title=Effects of Traumatic Experiences: A National Center for PTSD Fact Sheet |access-date=9 December 2005 | vauthors = EB, Ruzek J |publisher=National Center for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051210194253/http://www.ncptsd.va.gov/facts/general/fs_effects.html |archive-date=10 December 2005 }}</ref>  Often despite their best efforts, traumatized parents may have difficulty assisting their child with emotion regulation, attribution of meaning, and containment of post-traumatic fear in the wake of the child's traumatization, leading to adverse consequences for the child.<ref name=Schechter/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Schechter DS, Coates SW, Kaminer T, Coots T, Zeanah CH, Davies M, Schonfeld IS, Marshall RD, Liebowitz MR, Trabka KA, McCaw JE, Myers MM | display-authors = 6 | title = Distorted maternal mental representations and atypical behavior in a clinical sample of violence-exposed mothers and their toddlers | journal = Journal of Trauma & Dissociation | volume = 9 | issue = 2 | pages = 123–47 | year = 2008 | pmid = 18985165 | pmc = 2577290 | doi = 10.1080/15299730802045666 | author2-link = Susan Coates | author1-link = Daniel Schechter }}</ref> In such instances, seeking counselling in appropriate mental health services is in the best interests of both the child and the parent(s).

Trauma is hard to speak of by those that experience it. The event in question might recur to them in a dream or another medium, but it is rare for them to speak of it.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pederson |first=Joshua |date=2014 |title=Speak, Trauma: Toward a Revised Understanding of Literary Trauma Theory |journal=Narrative |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=333–353 |doi=10.1353/nar.2014.0018 |jstor=24615578 }}</ref> It is with the aid of health professionals that re-visiting these memories can be easier.

==Causes==

===Situational trauma===
There are many causes for psychological trauma that can stem from various sources. Trauma can be caused by other humans, technological and [[Natural disaster|natural disasters]], [[war]], abuse, violence, vehicle collisions, or medical emergencies. An individual's response to psychological trauma can be varied based on the type of trauma, as well as socio-demographic and background factors.<ref name="Neria, Y. 2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Neria Y, Nandi A, Galea S | title = Post-traumatic stress disorder following disasters: a systematic review | journal = Psychological Medicine | volume = 38 | issue = 4 | pages = 467–80 | date = April 2008 | pmid = 17803838 | pmc = 4877688 | doi = 10.1017/S0033291707001353 }}</ref>

There are several behavioral responses commonly used towards stressors including the proactive, reactive, and passive responses. Proactive responses include attempts to address and correct a stressor before it has a noticeable effect on lifestyle. Reactive responses occur after the stress and possible trauma has occurred and is aimed more at correcting or minimizing the damage of a stressful event.  A passive response is often characterized by an emotional numbness or ignorance of a stressor.

There is also a distinction between trauma induced by recent situations and long-term trauma which may have been buried in the unconscious from past situations such as [[child abuse]]. Trauma is sometimes overcome through healing; in some cases this can be achieved by recreating or revisiting the origin of the trauma under more psychologically safe circumstances, such as with a [[Psychotherapy|therapist]]. More recently, awareness of the consequences of [[climate change]] is seen as a source of trauma as individuals contemplate future events as well as experience climate change related disasters. Emotional experiences within these contexts are increasing, and collective processing and engagement with these emotions can lead to increased resilience and [[post-traumatic growth]], as well as a greater sense of belongingness. These outcomes are protective against the devastating impacts of psychological trauma.<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Kieft J, Bendell J |year=2021|title=The responsibility of communicating difficult truths about climate influenced societal disruption and collapse: an introduction to psychological research |url= https://insight.cumbria.ac.uk/id/eprint/5950 |journal= Institute for Leadership and Sustainability (IFLAS) Occasional Papers |volume=7|pages=1–39}}</ref>

===Stress disorders===
{{main|Post-traumatic stress disorder|Complex post-traumatic stress disorder}}

All psychological traumas originate from stress, a physiological response to an unpleasant stimulus.<ref>{{cite book|isbn=978-0-205-23939-9|title=Physiology of Psychology| vauthors = Carlson N |publisher=Pearson Education Inc.|year=2013}}</ref> Long-term stress increases the risk of poor mental health and mental disorders, which can be attributed to secretion of glucocorticoids for a long period of time. Such prolonged exposure causes many physiological dysfunctions such as the suppression of the immune system and increase in blood pressure.<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Seyle H |title=The Stress of Life|journal=McGraw Hill|year=1976}}</ref> Not only does it affect the body physiologically, but a morphological change in the hippocampus also takes place. Studies have shown that extreme stress early in life can disrupt normal development of hippocampus and impact its functions in adulthood. Studies show a correlation between the size of hippocampus and one's susceptibility to stress disorders.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Brunson KL, Kramár E, Lin B, Chen Y, Colgin LL, Yanagihara TK, Lynch G, Baram TZ | display-authors = 6 | title = Mechanisms of late-onset cognitive decline after early-life stress | journal = The Journal of Neuroscience | volume = 25 | issue = 41 | pages = 9328–38 | date = October 2005 | pmid = 16221841 | pmc = 3100717 | doi = 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2281-05.2005 }}</ref> In times of war, psychological trauma has been known as shell shock or [[combat stress reaction]]. Psychological trauma may cause an [[acute stress reaction]] which may lead to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PTSD emerged as the label for this condition after the [[Vietnam War]] in which many veterans returned to their respective countries demoralized, and sometimes, addicted to psychoactive substances.

The symptoms of PTSD must persist for at least one month for diagnosis to be made. The main symptoms of PTSD consist of four main categories: trauma (i.e. intense fear), reliving (i.e. flashbacks), avoidance behavior (i.e. emotional numbing), and [[hypervigilance]] (i.e. continuous scanning of the environment for danger).<ref name="Frommberger 2014" /> Research shows that about 60% of the US population reported as having experienced at least one traumatic symptom in their lives, but only a small portion actually develops PTSD. There is a correlation between the risk of PTSD and whether or not the act was inflicted deliberately by the offender.<ref name="Frommberger 2014" /> Psychological trauma is treated with therapy and, if indicated, psychotropic medications.

The term ''continuous posttraumatic stress disorder'' (CTSD)<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Straker G |title=The continuous traumatic stress syndrome: The single therapeutic interview|journal=Psychology and Society|year=1987 |volume=8 |pages=48–78 |doi=10.17159//2309-8708/1987/n8a4 |doi-access=free }}</ref> was introduced into the trauma literature by Gill Straker (1987). It was originally used by South African clinicians to describe the effects of exposure to frequent, high levels of violence usually associated with civil conflict and political repression. The term is also applicable to the effects of exposure to contexts in which gang violence and crime are endemic as well as to the effects of ongoing exposure to life threats in high-risk occupations such as police, fire, and emergency services.

As one of the processes of treatment, confrontation with their sources of trauma plays a crucial role. While debriefing people immediately after a critical incident has not been shown to reduce incidence of PTSD, coming alongside people experiencing trauma in a supportive way has become standard practice.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = McNally RJ, Bryant RA, Ehlers A | title = Does Early Psychological Intervention Promote Recovery From Posttraumatic Stress? | journal = Psychological Science in the Public Interest | volume = 4 | issue = 2 | pages = 45–79 | date = November 2003 | pmid = 26151755 | doi = 10.1111/1529-1006.01421 }}</ref>

The impact of PTSD on children is to a degree unknown, but education on coping mechanisms has shown to improve the lives of children who have undergone a traumatic event.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lipovsky |first=Julie A. |date=1991 |title=Posttraumatic stress disorder in children |journal=Family and Community Health |volume=14 |issue=3 |pages=42–51 |jstor=44953202 }}</ref>

=== Moral injury ===
[[Moral injury]] is distress such as guilt or shame following a moral transgression. There are many other definitions, some based on different models of causality.<ref name="Hall-2022">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hall NA, Everson AT, Billingsley MR, Miller MB | title = Moral injury, mental health and behavioural health outcomes: A systematic review of the literature | journal = Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy | volume = 29 | issue = 1 | pages = 92–110 | date = January 2022 | pmid = 33931926 | doi = 10.1002/cpp.2607 }}</ref>{{Rp|page=2}} Moral injury is associated with [[post-traumatic stress disorder]] but is distinguished from it.<ref name="Hall-2022" />{{Rp|page=2,8}} Moral injury is associated with [[Guilt (emotion)|guilt]] and [[shame]] while PTSD is correlated with [[fear]] and [[anxiety]].<ref name="Hall-2022" />{{Rp|page=11}}
Moral injury can also cause more than just emotional pain. It can make people question their beliefs, lose trust in leaders or organizations, and feel disconnected from themselves.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Litz |first1=Brett T. |last2=Stein |first2=Nathan |last3=Delaney |first3=Eileen |last4=Lebowitz |first4=Leslie |last5=Nash |first5=William P. |last6=Silva |first6=Caroline |last7=Maguen |first7=Shira |title=Moral injury and moral repair in war veterans: A preliminary model and intervention strategy |journal=Clinical Psychology Review |date=December 2009 |volume=29 |issue=8 |pages=695–706 |doi=10.1016/j.cpr.2009.07.003 |pmid=19683376 }}</ref> It can also lead people to avoid others, hold themselves back, misuse substances, or experience thoughts of suicide.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Griffin |first1=Brandon J. |last2=Purcell |first2=Natalie |last3=Burkman |first3=Kristine |last4=Litz |first4=Brett T. |last5=Bryan |first5=Craig J. |last6=Schmitz |first6=Martha |last7=Villierme |first7=Claudia |last8=Walsh |first8=Jessica |last9=Maguen |first9=Shira |title=Moral Injury: An Integrative Review |journal=Journal of Traumatic Stress |date=June 2019 |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=350–362 |doi=10.1002/jts.22362 |pmid=30688367 }}</ref>

===Vicarious trauma===
Normally, hearing about or seeing a recording of an event, even if distressing, does not cause trauma; however, an exception is made to the diagnostic criteria for work-related exposures.<ref name="DSM">[[DSM-5]], Diagnostic Criteria for "Posttraumatic Stress Disorder" (309.81), criterion A: "Witnessing, in person, the event(s) as it occurred to others...does not apply to exposure through electronic media, television, movies, or pictures, unless this exposure is work related."</ref>  [[Vicarious trauma]] affects workers who witness their clients' trauma. It is more likely to occur in situations where trauma-related work is the norm rather than the exception. Listening with empathy to the clients generates feeling, and seeing oneself in clients' trauma may compound the risk for developing trauma symptoms.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2008/phac-aspc/H72-21-178-2000E.pdf|title=Guidebook on Vicarious Trauma: Recommended Solutions for Anti-Violence Workers|publisher=Health Canada}}</ref> Trauma may also result if workers witness situations that happen in the course of their work (e.g. violence in the workplace, reviewing violent video tapes.)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/dr-john-bradford-won-t-work-magnotta-case-because-of-ptsd-1.2571463|title=Russell Williams profiler won't work Magnotta case because of PTSD|publisher=CBC|date= 13 March 2014}}</ref>  Risk increases with exposure and with the absence of help-seeking protective factors and pre-preparation of preventive strategies. Individuals who have a personal history of trauma are also at increased risk for developing vicarious trauma.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kim J, Chesworth B, Franchino-Olsen H, Macy RJ | title = A Scoping Review of Vicarious Trauma Interventions for Service Providers Working With People Who Have Experienced Traumatic Events | journal = Trauma, Violence & Abuse | pages = 1437–1460 | date = March 2021 | volume = 23 | issue = 5 | pmid = 33685294 | pmc = 8426417 | doi = 10.1177/1524838021991310 }}</ref>  Vicarious trauma can lead workers to develop more negative views of themselves, others, and of the world as a whole, which can compromise their quality of life and ability to work effectively.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Molnar BE, Meeker SA, Manners K, Tieszen L, Kalergis K, Fine JE, Hallinan S, Wolfe JD, Wells MK | display-authors = 6 | title = Vicarious traumatization among child welfare and child protection professionals: A systematic review | journal = Child Abuse & Neglect | volume = 110 | issue = Pt 3 | article-number = 104679 | date = December 2020 | pmid = 32826062 | doi = 10.1016/j.chiabu.2020.104679 }}</ref>

== Theoretical models ==

=== Shattered assumptions theory ===
{{Main|Shattered assumptions theory}}
Janoff-Bulman theorises that people generally hold three fundamental assumptions about the world that are built and confirmed over years of experience: "the world is benevolent, the world is meaningful, and I am worthy."<ref name="Janoff">{{cite book |last1=Janoff-Bulman |first1=Ronnie |url=https://archive.org/details/shatteredassumpt00ronn |title=Shattered Assumptions |date=1992 |publisher=Free Press |location=New York |isbn=978-0-02-916015-2 |url-access=registration}}</ref> According to the shattered assumption theory, there are some extreme events that "shatter" an individual's worldviews by severely challenging and breaking assumptions about the world and ourself.<ref name="Brewin2">{{cite journal |last1=Brewin |first1=Chris |last2=Holmes |first2=Emily |date=2003 |title=Psychological theories of posttraumatic stress disorder |journal=Clinical Psychology Review |volume=23 |issue=3 |pages=339–376 |doi=10.1016/S0272-7358(03)00033-3 |pmid=12729677}}</ref> Once one has experienced such trauma, it is necessary for an individual to create new assumptions or modify their old ones to recover from the traumatic experience.<ref name="Janoff"/> Therefore, the negative effects of the trauma are simply related to our worldviews, and if we repair these views, we will recover from the trauma.<ref>{{cite book |last1=DePrince |first1=Anne |title=Loss of the Assumptive World: a theory of traumatic loss |last2=Freyd |first2=Jennifer |date=2002 |publisher=Brunner-Routledge |editor1-last=Kauffman |editor1-first=J |location=New York |pages=71–82 |author-link1=The harm of trauma: Pathological fear, shattered assumptions, or betrayal?}}</ref>

===In psychodynamics===
[[Psychodynamics|Psychodynamic]] viewpoints are controversial,<ref>{{Cite news |date=25 November 2007 |title=Freud Is Widely Taught at Universities, Except in the Psychology Department (Published 2007) |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/11/25/weekinreview/25cohen.html |access-date=1 January 2021 |vauthors=Cohen P}}</ref> but have been shown to have therapeutic utility.<ref>{{Cite web |date= |title=Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Brings Lasting Benefits through Self-Knowledge |url=https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2010/01/psychodynamic-therapy |access-date=1 January 2021 |publisher=[[American Psychological Association]]}}</ref>

French neurologist [[Jean-Martin Charcot]] argued in the 1890s that psychological trauma was the origin of all instances of the mental illness known as [[hysteria]]. Charcot's "traumatic hysteria" often manifested as paralysis that followed a physical trauma, typically years later after what Charcot described as a period of "incubation". [[Sigmund Freud]], Charcot's student and the father of [[psychoanalysis]], examined the concept of psychological trauma throughout his career. French psychologist [[Jean Laplanche]] has given a general description of Freud's understanding of trauma, which varied significantly over the course of Freud's career: "An event in the subject's life, defined by its intensity, by the subject's incapacity to respond adequately to it and by the upheaval and long-lasting effects that it brings about in the psychical organization".<ref name="Laplanche">{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/languageofpsycho00lapl/page/465 |title=The Language of Psycho-Analysis |vauthors=Laplanche J, Pontalis JB |publisher=W. W. Norton and Company |year=1967 |isbn=978-0-393-01105-0 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/languageofpsycho00lapl/page/465 465–9] |url-access=registration}}</ref>

The French psychoanalyst [[Jacques Lacan]] claimed that what he called "[[The Real]]" had a traumatic quality external to symbolization. As an object of anxiety, Lacan maintained that The Real is "the essential object which isn't an object any longer, but this something faced with which all words cease and all categories fail, the object of anxiety ''par excellence''".<ref name="Lacan">Lacan, J., ''The Seminar of Jacques Lacan: Book II: The Ego in Freud's Theory and in the Technique of Psychoanalysis 1954–1955'' | p.164 (W. W. Norton & Company, 1991), {{ISBN|978-0-393-30709-2}}</ref>

Fred Alford, citing the work of [[Object relations theory|object relations]] theorist [[Donald Winnicott]], uses the concept of inner other, and internal representation of the social world, with which one converses internally and which is generated through interactions with others. He posits that the inner other is damaged by trauma but can be repaired by conversations with others such as therapists. He relates the concept of the inner other to the work of [[Albert Camus]], viewing the inner other as that which removes the [[Absurdism|absurd]].<ref name="Alford_2016">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5v1jDAAAQBAJ&q=Fred+Alford++-+Trauma,+Culture,+and+PTSD&pg=PA107 |title=Trauma, Culture, and PTSD |vauthors=Alford CF |date=9 June 2016 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-137-57600-2 |language=en}}</ref> Alford notes how trauma damages trust in social relations due to fear of exploitation and argues that culture and social relations can help people recover from trauma.<ref name="Alford_2016" />{{Rp|49}}

[[Diana Fosha]], a pioneer of modern psychodynamic perspective, also argues that social relations can help people recover from trauma, but specifically refers to attachment theory and the attachment dynamic of the therapeutic relationship. Fosha states that the sense of emotional safety and co-regulation which occurs in a psychodynamically-oriented therapeutic relationship acts as the secure attachment where it is necessary to allow a client to experience and process through their trauma safely and effectively.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Fosha D |date=May 2006 |title=Quantum transformation in trauma and treatment: traversing the crisis of healing change |journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology |volume=62 |issue=5 |pages=569–83 |doi=10.1002/jclp.20249 |pmid=16523496}}</ref>

==Diagnosis==
{{refimprove|date=October 2025}}
As "trauma" adopted a more widely defined scope, [[Psychotraumatology]] as a field developed a more interdisciplinary approach. This is in part due to the field's diverse professional representation, including: psychologists, medical professionals, and lawyers. As a result, findings in this field are adapted for various applications, from individual psychiatric treatments to sociological large-scale trauma management. While the field has adopted a number of diverse methodological approaches, many pose their own limitations in practical application.

The experience and outcomes of psychological trauma can be assessed in a number of ways.<ref>{{Cite book | vauthors = Briere J, Scott C |title=Principles of Trauma Therapy: A Guide to Symptoms, Evaluation, and Treatment |publisher=SAGE Publications, Inc |location=California |year=2006 |pages=37–63 |isbn=978-0-7619-2921-5 }}</ref> Within the context of a clinical interview, the risk of imminent danger to the self or others is important to address but is not the focus of assessment. In most cases, it will not be necessary to involve contacting emergency services (e.g., medical, psychiatric, law enforcement) to ensure the individual's safety; members of the individual's [[social support]] network are much more critical.

Understanding and accepting the psychological state of an individual is paramount. There are many misconceptions of what it means for a traumatized individual to be in psychological crisis. These are times when an individual is in inordinate amounts of pain and incapable of self-comfort. If treated humanely and respectfully, the individual is less likely to resort to self harm. In these situations it is best to provide a supportive, caring environment and to communicate to the individual that no matter the circumstance, the individual will be taken seriously rather than being treated as delusional. It is vital for the assessor to understand that what is going on in the traumatized person's head is valid and real. If deemed appropriate, the assessing clinician may proceed by inquiring about both the traumatic event and the outcomes experienced (e.g., post-traumatic symptoms, dissociation, [[substance abuse]], somatic symptoms, psychotic reactions). Such inquiry occurs within the context of established [[rapport]] and is completed in an empathic, sensitive, and supportive manner. The clinician may also inquire about possible relational disturbance, such as alertness to interpersonal danger, [[Abandonment (emotional)|abandonment issues]], and the need for self-protection via interpersonal control. Through discussion of interpersonal relationships, the clinician is better able to assess the individual's ability to enter and sustain a clinical relationship.

During assessment, individuals may exhibit activation responses in which reminders of the traumatic event trigger sudden feelings (e.g., [[distress (medicine)|distress]], anxiety, [[anger]]), memories, or thoughts relating to the event. Because individuals may not yet be capable of managing this distress, it is necessary to determine how the event can be discussed in such a way that will not "retraumatize" the individual. It is also important to take note of such responses, as these responses may aid the clinician in determining the intensity and severity of possible post-traumatic stress as well as the ease with which responses are triggered. Further, the presence of possible avoidance responses. Avoidance responses may involve the absence of expected activation or emotional reactivity as well as the use of avoidance mechanisms (e.g., substance use, effortful avoidance of cues associated with the event, dissociation).

In addition to monitoring activation and avoidance responses, clinicians carefully observe the individual's strengths or difficulties with affect regulation (i.e., affect tolerance and affect modulation). Such difficulties may be evidenced by mood swings, brief yet intense [[depressive episode]]s, or [[self-mutilation]]. The information gathered through observation of affect regulation will guide the clinician's decisions regarding the individual's readiness to partake in various therapeutic activities.

Though assessment of psychological trauma may be conducted in an unstructured manner, assessment may also involve the use of a structured interview. Such interviews might include the [[Clinician Administered PTSD Scale|Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale]],<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Blake DD, Weathers FW, Nagy LM, Kaloupek DG, Gusman FD, Charney DS, Keane TM | title = The development of a Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale | journal = Journal of Traumatic Stress | volume = 8 | issue = 1 | pages = 75–90 | date = January 1995 | pmid = 7712061 | doi = 10.1002/jts.2490080106 }}</ref> Acute Stress Disorder Interview,<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Bryant RA, Harvey AG, Dang ST, Sackville T |date=1998|title=Assessing acute stress disorder: Psychometric properties of a structured clinical interview. |journal=Psychological Assessment|volume=10|issue=3|pages=215–220|doi=10.1037/1040-3590.10.3.215 }}</ref> Structured Interview for Disorders of Extreme Stress,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Pelcovitz D, van der Kolk B, Roth S, Mandel F, Kaplan S, Resick P | title = Development of a criteria set and a structured interview for disorders of extreme stress (SIDES) | journal = Journal of Traumatic Stress | volume = 10 | issue = 1 | pages = 3–16 | date = January 1997 | pmid = 9018674 | doi = 10.1002/jts.2490100103 }}</ref> [[SCID-D|Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Dissociative Disorders]] - Revised,<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Steinberg M | date = 1994 | title = Interviewer's guide to the structured clinical interview for DSM-IV dissociative disorders (SCID-D) | publisher = American Psychiatric Pub.| isbn = 978-1-58562-349-5 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=XDcgAX35QY8C&pg=PR5 }}</ref> and Brief Interview for post-traumatic Disorders.<ref>{{cite report | vauthors = Briere J | date = 1998 | title = Brief Interview for Posttraumatic Disorders (BIPD). | work = Unpublished psychological test | publisher = University of Southern California }}</ref>

Lastly, assessment of psychological trauma might include the use of self-administered psychological tests. Individual scores on such tests are compared to normative data in order to determine how the individual's level of functioning compares to others in a sample representative of the general population. Psychological testing might include the use of generic tests (e.g., [[MMPI-2]], [[MCMI-III]], SCL-90-R) to assess non-trauma-specific symptoms as well as difficulties related to personality. In addition, psychological testing might include the use of trauma-specific tests to assess post-traumatic outcomes. Such tests might include the post-traumatic Stress Diagnostic Scale,<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Foa EB | date = 1995 | title = PDS: Posttraumatic Stress Diagnostic Scale: manual | location = London | publisher = Pearson }}</ref> Davidson Trauma Scale,<ref name="Davidson-1997">{{cite journal | vauthors = Davidson JR, Book SW, Colket JT, Tupler LA, Roth S, David D, Hertzberg M, Mellman T, Beckham JC, Smith RD, Davison RM, Katz R, Feldman ME | title = Assessment of a new self-rating scale for post-traumatic stress disorder | journal = Psychological Medicine | volume = 27 | issue = 1 | pages = 153–60 | date = January 1997 | pmid = 9122295 | doi = 10.1017/s0033291796004229 }}</ref> Detailed Assessment of post-traumatic Stress,<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Briere J | date = 2001 | title = Detailed Assessment of Posttraumatic Stress: DAPS: Professional Manual | location = Lutz, FL | publisher = Psychological Assessment Resources }}{{isbn?}}{{pn|date=October 2026}}</ref> Trauma Symptom Inventory,<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Briere J | date = 1995 | title = Trauma Symptom Inventory professional manual | location = Odessa, FL | publisher = Psychological Assessment Resources }}{{isbn?}}{{pn|date=October 2026}}</ref> Trauma Symptom Checklist for Children,<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Briere J | date = 1996 | title = Trauma symptom checklist for children | location = Odessa, FL | publisher = Psychological Assessment Resources | pages = 253–8 }}{{isbn?}}</ref> Traumatic Life Events Questionnaire,<ref name="Kubany-2000">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kubany ES, Haynes SN, Leisen MB, Owens JA, Kaplan AS, Watson SB, Burns K | display-authors = 6 | title = Development and preliminary validation of a brief broad-spectrum measure of trauma exposure: the Traumatic Life Events Questionnaire | journal = Psychological Assessment | volume = 12 | issue = 2 | pages = 210–24 | date = June 2000 | pmid = 10887767 | doi = 10.1037/1040-3590.12.2.210 }}</ref> and Trauma-related Guilt Inventory.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kubany ES, Haynes SN, Abueg FR, Manke FP, Brennan JM, Stahura C | date = 1996 | title = Development and validation of the trauma-related guilt inventory (TRGI). | journal = Psychological Assessment | volume = 8 | issue = 4 | pages = 428–444 | doi = 10.1037/1040-3590.8.4.428 }}</ref>

Children are assessed through activities and therapeutic relationship, some of the activities are play genogram, sand worlds, coloring feelings, self and kinetic family drawing, symbol work, dramatic-puppet play, story telling, Briere's TSCC, etc.<ref name="GilATC">{{cite book| vauthors = Gil E |title=Helping Abused and Traumatized Children: Integrating Directive and Nondirective Approaches|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qe-E0CYLDqcC&pg=PA28|year=2011|publisher=Guilford Press|isbn=978-1-60918-474-2|pages=28, 59}}</ref>

===Definition===
The [[Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders|''Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition'' (DSM-5)]] defines trauma as the symptoms that occur following exposure to an event (i.e., traumatic event) that involves actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence.<ref name="DSM5">{{cite book|title=Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders | edition = 5th |publisher=American Psychiatric Association |year=2013 |isbn=978-0-89042-555-8 |location=Washington, DC |page=265}}</ref> This exposure could come in the form of experiencing the event or witnessing the event, or learning that an extreme violent or accidental event was experienced by a loved one.<ref name="DSM5" /> Trauma symptoms may come in the form of intrusive memories, dreams, or flashbacks; avoidance of reminders of the traumatic event; negative thoughts and feelings; or increased alertness or reactivity.<ref name="DSM5" /> [[Traumatic memories|Memories associated with trauma]] are typically explicit, coherent, and difficult to forget.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = McNally RJ | date = 2003 | title = Remembering Trauma | location = Cambridge, MA | publisher = Harvard University Press }}</ref> Due to the complexity of the interaction between traumatic event occurrence and trauma symptomatology, a person's distress response to aversive details of a traumatic event may involve intense fear or helplessness, but ranges according to the context.<ref name="DSM5" /> In children, trauma symptoms can be manifested in the form of disorganized or agitative behaviors.<ref>{{cite book |title=DSM-IV-TR|year=2000 |publisher=American Psychiatric Association |doi=10.1176/appi.books.9780890420249.dsm-iv-tr |isbn=0-89042-024-6 }}{{pn|date=October 2026}}</ref>

Trauma can be caused by a wide variety of events, but there are a few common aspects. There is frequently a violation of the person's core assumptions about the world and their [[human rights]], putting the person in a state of extreme [[confusion]] and insecurity. This is seen when institutions depended upon for survival violate, humiliate, [[Betrayal Trauma|betray]], or cause major losses or separations instead of evoking aspects like positive self worth, safe boundaries and personal freedom.<ref>{{cite book| vauthors = DePrince AP, Freyd JJ |year=2002|chapter=The Harm of Trauma: Pathological fear, shattered assumptions, or betrayal?|editor=J. Kauffman|chapter-url=http://pages.uoregon.edu/dynamic/jjf/articles/dpf02harm.pdf|title=Loss of the Assumptive World: a theory of traumatic loss|pages=71–82|location=New York|publisher=Brunner-Routledge}}</ref>

Psychologically traumatic experiences often involve [[physical trauma]] that threatens one's survival and sense of security.<ref>{{cite web|title=Emotional and Psychological Trauma|url=http://www.helpguide.org/mental/emotional_psychological_trauma.htm|work=Helpguide.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140913234027/http://www.helpguide.org/mental/emotional_psychological_trauma.htm|archive-date=13 September 2014}}</ref> Typical causes and dangers of psychological trauma include [[harassment]]; [[embarrassment]]; abandonment; abusive relationships; rejection; co-dependence; physical assault; [[sexual abuse]]; partner battery; [[employment discrimination]]; [[police brutality]]; [[corruption#Judicial corruption|judicial corruption]] and [[Judicial misconduct|misconduct]]; [[bullying]]; [[paternalism]]; [[domestic violence]]; [[indoctrination]]; being the victim of an [[alcoholism|alcoholic]] parent; the threat or the witnessing of violence (particularly in [[childhood]]); life-threatening [[medical condition]]s; and medication-induced trauma.<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Whitfield CL |title=Psychiatric drugs as agents of Trauma|journal= International Journal of Risk & Safety in Medicine|year=2010|volume=22|issue=4|pages=195–207 |doi=10.3233/JRS-2010-0508}}</ref> Catastrophic [[natural disaster]]s such as [[earthquake]]s and [[volcanic eruption]]s; large scale transportation accidents; [[Structure fire|house or domestic fire]]; [[motor collision]]; mass interpersonal violence like [[war]]; [[terrorist attack]]s or other mass victimization like [[sex trafficking]]; being taken as a hostage or being [[Kidnapping|kidnapped]] can also cause psychological trauma. Long-term exposure to situations such as extreme [[poverty]] or other forms of [[abuse]], such as [[verbal abuse]], exist independently of physical trauma but still generate psychological trauma.

Some theories suggest [[childhood trauma]] can increase one's risk for [[mental disorder]]s including [[post-traumatic stress disorder]] (PTSD),<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Ramos SM, Boyle GJ | chapter = Ritual and medical circumcision among Filipino boys: Evidence of post-traumatic stress disorder. | pages = 253–270 | veditors = Denniston GC, Hodges FM, Milos MF |title=Understanding circumcision: a multi-disciplinary approach to a multi-dimensional problem |date=2001 |publisher=Kluwer Academic/Plenum Publishers |location=New York |isbn=978-0306-46701-1}}</ref> depression, and substance abuse. [[Childhood trauma|Childhood adversity]] is associated with [[neuroticism]] during adulthood.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Jeronimus BF, Ormel J, Aleman A, Penninx BW, Riese H | title = Negative and positive life events are associated with small but lasting change in neuroticism | journal = Psychological Medicine | volume = 43 | issue = 11 | pages = 2403–15 | date = November 2013 | pmid = 23410535 | doi = 10.1017/s0033291713000159 }}</ref>
Parts of the brain in a growing child are developing in a sequential and hierarchical order, from least complex to most complex. The brain's neurons change in response to the constant external signals and stimulation, receiving and storing new information. This allows the brain to continually respond to its surroundings and promote survival. [[Sense#Five "traditional" senses|The five traditional signals]] (sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch) contribute to the developing brain structure and its function.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Perry BD | title = The cost of caring: Secondary traumatic stress and the impact of working with high-risk children and families. | publisher = The Child Trauma Academy | date = April 2003}}{{isbn?}}{{pn|date=October 2026}}</ref>
Infants and children begin to create internal representations of their external environment, and in particular, key attachment relationships, shortly after birth. Violent and [[victimization|victimizing]] attachment figures impact infants' and young children's internal representations.<ref name=Schechter>{{cite journal | vauthors = Schechter DS, Zygmunt A, Coates SW, Davies M, Trabka K, McCaw J, Kolodji A, Robinson J | display-authors = 6 | title = Caregiver traumatization adversely impacts young children's mental representations on the MacArthur Story Stem Battery | journal = Attachment & Human Development | volume = 9 | issue = 3 | pages = 187–205 | date = September 2007 | pmid = 18007959 | pmc = 2078523 | doi = 10.1080/14616730701453762 | author3-link = Susan Coates | author1-link = Daniel Schechter }}</ref> The more frequently a specific pattern of brain neurons is activated, the more permanent the internal representation associated with the pattern becomes.<ref name="Al-Krenawi-2009">{{cite journal | vauthors = Al-Krenawi A, Graham JR, Kanat-Maymon Y | title = Analysis of trauma exposure, symptomatology and functioning in Jewish Israeli and Palestinian adolescents | journal = The British Journal of Psychiatry | volume = 195 | issue = 5 | pages = 427–32 | date = November 2009 | pmid = 19880933 | doi = 10.1192/bjp.bp.108.050393 | doi-access = free }}</ref> This causes [[sensitization]] in the brain towards the specific neural network. Because of this sensitization, the neural pattern can be activated by decreasingly less external stimuli.
Child abuse tends to have the most complications, with long-term effects out of all forms of trauma, because it occurs during the most sensitive and critical stages of psychological development.<ref name="Wingo, Aliza P. 2014"/> It could lead to violent behavior, possibly as extreme as serial murder. For example, Hickey's Trauma-Control Model suggests that "[[childhood trauma]] for serial murderers may serve as a triggering mechanism resulting in an individual's inability to cope with the stress of certain events."<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Hickey EW | date = 2010 | title = Serial Murderers and Their Victims. | location = Blemont, CA | publisher = Wadsworth, Cengage Learning }}</ref>

Often, psychological aspects of trauma are overlooked even by health professionals: "If clinicians fail to look through a trauma lens and to conceptualize client problems as related possibly to current or past trauma, they may fail to see that trauma victims, young and old, organize much of their lives around repetitive patterns of reliving and warding off traumatic memories, reminders, and affects."<ref>{{cite web|title=The Effects of Psychological Trauma on Children and Adolescents|url=http://mentalhealth.vermont.gov/sites/dmh/files/report/cafu/DMH-CAFU_Psychological_Trauma_Moroz.pdf|date=30 June 2005| vauthors = Moroz KJ |publisher=Vermont Agency of Human Services|access-date=25 November 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101103231540/http://mentalhealth.vermont.gov/sites/dmh/files/report/cafu/DMH-CAFU_Psychological_Trauma_Moroz.pdf|archive-date=3 November 2010}}</ref> [[Biopsychosocial model]]s offer a broader view of health problems than [[Biomedicine|biomedical]] models.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kozlowska |first1=Kasia |title=Functional Somatic Symptoms in Children and Adolescents: A Stress-System Approach to Assessment and Treatment |last2=Scher |first2=Stephen |last3=Helgeland |first3=Helene |date=2020 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-030-46183-6 |series=Palgrave Texts in Counselling and Psychotherapy |location=Cham |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-46184-3 }}</ref>

== Effects ==
Evidence suggests that a majority of people who experience severe trauma in adulthood will experience personality changes. Personality changes include guilt, distrust, impulsiveness, aggression, avoidance, obsessive behavior, emotional numbness, loss of interest, hopelessness and altered self-perception.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Munjiza |first1=Jasna |last2=Law |first2=Vincent |last3=Crawford |first3=Mike J. |title=Lasting personality pathology following exposure to catastrophic trauma in adults: systematic review |journal=Personality and Mental Health |date=October 2014 |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=320–336 |doi=10.1002/pmh.1271 |pmid=25123294 }}</ref>

Trauma has profound lasting effects on the mind and the body with many victims of trauma citing an inability to have complete sensory perceptions or losing certain sensations in different parts of their body. This also translates to the numbing of emotions. People who have experienced trauma shut down parts of their bodies and mind in an attempt to cut themselves off from the trauma. Dr. Ruth Lanius did a study examining the brain activity of traumatized individuals, constructing them to think about nothing and saw that their ability to be self-aware was limited as only the [[posterior cingulate cortex]] of their brains lit up, whereas the "normal" individuals demonstrated the anterior and posterior cingulate cortexes, the medial and orbital prefrontal cortex, and in the insula all lighting up. Persistent trauma or even the thought of it leads to an inundation of a person's neurological system, limiting their ability to integrate sensory perceptions and be fully aware both internally and externally.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Van der Kolk |first1=Bessel A. |title=The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, and Body in the Healing of Trauma |date=2015 |publisher=Penguin Publishing Group |isbn=978-0-14-312774-1 |pages=91–94 }}</ref>

Psychological trauma can also lead to a condition known as Post traumatic Stress Disorder, which is defined as a condition developed by an individual who has experienced a highly traumatic or life-threatening event.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)? |url=https://www.psychiatry.org/patients-families/ptsd/what-is-ptsd |access-date=2026-07-21 }}</ref> Not all sufferers of psychological trauma develop P.T.S.D; 6% of individuals who experience trauma develop P.T.S.D, meaning a vast majority of individuals who suffer from a traumatic event do not develop the disorder.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder |url=https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/post-traumatic-stress-disorder-ptsd |access-date=2026-07-21 |website=National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) }}</ref> Psychological trauma is the main source of P.T.S.D, but P.T.S.D is not the cause of psychological trauma. Some side effects of P.T.S.D include intrusive memories of the traumatic event, re-occurring flashbacks, nightmares, and strong physical or emotional reactions to things that remind the individual of the traumatic event.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) - Symptoms and causes |url=https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/post-traumatic-stress-disorder/symptoms-causes/syc-20355967 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260711001116/https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/post-traumatic-stress-disorder/symptoms-causes/syc-20355967 |archive-date=2026-07-11 |access-date=2026-07-21 |work=Mayo Clinic |language=en}}</ref>

== Coping mechanisms ==
Coping mechanisms are widely used by individuals who have suffered from some kind of traumatic event. Coping is defined as the process of using certain thoughts or behaviors in order to relieve psychological distress.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Four Major Categories of Coping Mechanisms — Camellia Counseling - Trauma, Anxiety, & Depression Therapist, New Jersey |url=https://www.camellianj.com/blog/the-four-major-categories-of-coping-mechanisms |access-date=2026-07-21 |website=Camellia Counseling |date=26 August 2025 |language=en-US}}</ref> Some individuals unknowingly use coping mechanisms to ease the discomfort of [[psychological trauma]], while others purposely seek out solutions to help them cope with any psychological trauma they may be dealing with. While some coping mechanisms can greatly reduce psychological discomfort, there are certain kinds of coping mechanisms that can actually be harmful to the individual. 

There are four main types of coping:

* Problem-focused: A form of coping that prompts the individual to address and investigate the issue that is causing them stress.
* Emotion-focused: A form of coping that encourages the individual to look at the issue through a positive or humorous lens.
* Meaning-focused: A form of coping that focuses on finding a silver lining by applying personal values and beliefs to the traumatic event.
* Social Support: A form of coping that prompts the individual to rely on family and peers to ease discomfort.

Certain kinds of coping mechanisms can fall underneath two different strategies: adaptive coping and maladaptive coping. Adaptive coping mechanisms are recognized as healthy forms of coping, while maladaptive coping mechanisms are considered unhealthy and harmful. Some adaptive coping mechanisms include positive thinking, seeking support from others, accepting what happened, and finding healthy solutions for whatever the individual may be going through.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How We Cope: Adaptive & Maladaptive Coping Strategies |date=27 November 2023 |url=https://seaglassmentalhealth.com/how-we-cope-adaptive-maladaptive-coping-strategies/ }}{{rs|date=October 2026}}</ref> Some maladaptive coping mechanisms include substance abuse, physical or mental escape from the issue, self blame or criticism, and dangerous risk-taking.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Peterson |first=Ashley L. |date=2021-09-24 |title=What Is... Adaptive vs. Maladaptive Coping |url=https://mentalhealthathome.org/2021/09/24/adaptive-maladaptive-coping/ |access-date=2026-07-21 |website=Mental Health @ Home |language=en-US}}</ref> Maladaptive coping mechanisms may worsen psychological discomfort, so positive adaptive coping mechanisms are often taught to individuals during treatment for psychological trauma.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chaaya |first1=Roni |last2=Sfeir |first2=Michel |last3=Khoury |first3=Samar El |last4=Malhab |first4=Sandrella Bou |last5=Khoury-Malhame |first5=Myriam El |date=2025-04-21 |title=Adaptive versus maladaptive coping strategies: insight from Lebanese young adults navigating multiple crises |journal=BMC Public Health |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=1464 |doi=10.1186/s12889-025-22608-4 |doi-access=free |pmc=12010593 |pmid=40259293}}</ref>

==Treatment==
{{See also|Treatments for PTSD}}
A number of psychotherapy approaches have been designed with the treatment of trauma in mind—[[Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing|E.M.D.R]], [[progressive counting]],<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Jarecki K, Greenwald R |date=2016|title=Progressive counting with therapy clients with post-traumatic stress disorder: Three cases |journal=Counselling and Psychotherapy Research|language=en|volume=16|issue=1|pages=64–71|doi=10.1002/capr.12055|doi-access=free}}</ref> [[somatic experiencing]], [[biofeedback]], [[Internal Family Systems Model|Internal Family Systems Therapy]], and sensorimotor psychotherapy, and [[Emotional Freedom Techniques|Emotional Freedom Technique]] (EFT) etc. [[Trauma-informed care|Trauma informed care]] provides a framework for any person in any discipline or context to promote healing, or at least not re-traumatizing. A 2018 systematic review provided moderate evidence that Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (E.M.D.R) is effective in reducing P.T.S.D and depression symptoms, and it increases the likelihood of patients no longer meeting the criteria for P.T.S.D.<ref>{{cite report |last1=Forman-Hoffman |first1=Valerie |last2=Cook Middleton |first2=Jennifer |last3=Feltner |first3=Cynthia |last4=Gaynes |first4=Bradley N. |last5=Palmieri Weber |first5=Rachel |last6=Bann |first6=Carla |last7=Viswanathan |first7=Meera |last8=Lohr |first8=Kathleen N. |last9=Baker |first9=Claire |last10=Green |first10=Joshua |title=Psychological and Pharmacological Treatments for Adults With Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Systematic Review Update |date=17 May 2018 |doi=10.23970/ahrqepccer207 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Medications such as sertraline and paroxetine can be used to treat P.T.S.D, but are not recommended as a first-line treatment for the disorder.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rothbaum |first1=Barbara Olasov |last2=Watkins |first2=Laura E. |title=An Update on Psychotherapy for the Treatment of PTSD |journal=American Journal of Psychiatry |date=2025 |volume=182 |issue=5 |pages=424–437 |doi=10.1176/appi.ajp.20250110 |pmid=40308104 }}</ref>

There is a large body of empirical support for the use of [[cognitive behavioral therapy]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.abct.org/Information/?m=mInformation&fa=_WhatIsCBTpublic|title=What is Cognitive Behavior Therapy (CBT)?|publisher=Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies}}</ref><ref name="Schnurr-2007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Schnurr PP, Friedman MJ, Engel CC, Foa EB, Shea MT, Chow BK, Resick PA, Thurston V, Orsillo SM, Haug R, Turner C, Bernardy N | display-authors = 6 | title = Cognitive behavioral therapy for posttraumatic stress disorder in women: a randomized controlled trial | journal = JAMA | volume = 297 | issue = 8 | pages = 820–30 | date = February 2007 | pmid = 17327524 | doi = 10.1001/jama.297.8.820 | doi-access = free }}</ref> for the treatment of trauma-related symptoms,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.abct.org/Information/?m=mInformation&fa=fs_TRAUMA|title=ABCT Fact Sheets: Trauma|date=11 March 2021|publisher=Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies}}</ref> including [[posttraumatic stress disorder|post-traumatic stress disorder]]. [[Institute of Medicine]] guidelines identify cognitive behavioral therapies as the most effective treatments for P.T.S.D.<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Institute of Medicine | title = Treatment of posttraumatic stress disorder: An assessment of the evidence| location = Washington, DC | publisher = [[The National Academies Press]]|year= 2008}}</ref> Two of these cognitive behavioral therapies, prolonged exposure<ref name="McLean-2011">{{cite journal | vauthors = McLean CP, Foa EB | title = Prolonged exposure therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder: a review of evidence and dissemination | journal = Expert Review of Neurotherapeutics | volume = 11 | issue = 8 | pages = 1151–63 | date = August 2011 | pmid = 21797656 | doi = 10.1586/ern.11.94 }}</ref> and [[cognitive processing therapy]],<ref name="Resick-2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Resick PA, Galovski TE, Uhlmansiek MO, Scher CD, Clum GA, Young-Xu Y | title = A randomized clinical trial to dismantle components of cognitive processing therapy for posttraumatic stress disorder in female victims of interpersonal violence | journal = Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology | volume = 76 | issue = 2 | pages = 243–258 | date = April 2008 | pmid = 18377121 | pmc = 2967760 | doi = 10.1037/0022-006X.76.2.243 }}</ref> are being disseminated nationally by the Department of Veterans Affairs for the treatment of P.T.S.D.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treatment/overview/overview-treatment-research.asp|title=Overview of Psychotherapy for PTSD|publisher=U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs| vauthors = Hamblen JL, Schnurr PP, Rosenberg A, Eftekhari A }}</ref><ref name="Karlin-2010">{{cite journal | vauthors = Karlin BE, Ruzek JI, Chard KM, Eftekhari A, Monson CM, Hembree EA, Resick PA, Foa EB | display-authors = 6 | title = Dissemination of evidence-based psychological treatments for posttraumatic stress disorder in the Veterans Health Administration | journal = Journal of Traumatic Stress | volume = 23 | issue = 6 | pages = 663–73 | date = December 2010 | pmid = 21171126 | doi = 10.1002/jts.20588 }}</ref> A 2010 Cochrane review found that trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy was effective for individuals with acute traumatic stress symptoms when compared to waiting list and supportive counseling.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Roberts NP, Kitchiner NJ, Kenardy J, Bisson JI | title = Early psychological interventions to treat acute traumatic stress symptoms | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | issue = 3 | article-number = CD007944 | date = March 2010 | volume = 2012 | pmid = 20238359 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD007944.pub2 | doi-access = free | pmc = 11491193 }}</ref> Seeking Safety is another type of cognitive behavioral therapy that focuses on learning safe coping skills for co-occurring P.T.S.D and substance use problems.<ref name="Roberts_2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Roberts NP, Roberts PA, Jones N, Bisson JI | title = Psychological interventions for post-traumatic stress disorder and comorbid substance use disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis | journal = Clinical Psychology Review | volume = 38 | pages = 25–38 | date = June 2015 | pmid = 25792193 | doi = 10.1016/j.cpr.2015.02.007 }}</ref> While some sources highlight Seeking Safety as effective<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lenz |first1=A. Stephen |last2=Henesy |first2=Rachel |last3=Callender |first3=Karisse |title=Effectiveness of Seeking Safety for Co-Occurring Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Substance Use |journal=Journal of Counseling & Development |date=January 2016 |volume=94 |issue=1 |pages=51–61 |doi=10.1002/jcad.12061 }}</ref> with strong research support,<ref>{{cite web |title=Seeking Safety for PTSD with Substance Use Disorder |url=https://societyofclinicalpsychology.org/psychological-treatments-archive/seeking-safety-for-ptsd-with-substance-use-disorder/ |website=Society of Clinical Psychology |date=15 September 2025 }}</ref> others have suggested that it did not lead to improvements beyond usual treatment.<ref name="Roberts_2015" /> A review from 2014 showed that a combination of treatments involving [[dialectical behavior therapy]] (D.B.T), often used for borderline personality disorder, and [[exposure therapy]] is highly effective in treating psychological trauma.<ref name="Frommberger 2014"/> If, however, psychological trauma has caused [[dissociative disorders]] or [[complex PTSD|complex P.T.S.D]], [[Brief psychotic disorder|Brief Psychotic disorder]], the [[trauma model]] approach (also known as phase-oriented treatment of structural dissociation) has been proven to work better than the simple cognitive approach. Studies funded by pharmaceuticals have also shown that medications such as the new anti-depressants are effective when used in combination with other psychological approaches.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Steele K, van der Hart O, Nijenhuis ER | title = Phase-oriented treatment of structural dissociation in complex traumatization: overcoming trauma-related phobias | journal = Journal of Trauma & Dissociation | volume = 6 | issue = 3 | pages = 11–53 | year = 2005 | pmid = 16172081 | doi = 10.1300/J229v06n03_02 }}</ref> At present, the selective [[serotonin]] reuptake inhibitor (S.S.R.I) antidepressants sertraline (Zoloft) and paroxetine (Paxil) are the only medications that have been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the United States to treat P.T.S.D.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Krystal JH, Davis LL, Neylan TC, A Raskind M, Schnurr PP, Stein MB, Vessicchio J, Shiner B, Gleason TC, Huang GD | display-authors = 6 | title = It Is Time to Address the Crisis in the Pharmacotherapy of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Consensus Statement of the PTSD Psychopharmacology Working Group | journal = Biological Psychiatry | volume = 82 | issue = 7 | pages = e51–e59 | date = October 2017 | pmid = 28454621 | doi = 10.1016/j.biopsych.2017.03.007 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Other options for pharmacotherapy include serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (S.N.R.I) antidepressants and anti-psychotic medications, though none have been FDA approved.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Alexander W | title = Pharmacotherapy for Post-traumatic Stress Disorder In Combat Veterans: Focus on Antidepressants and Atypical Antipsychotic Agents | journal = P & T | volume = 37 | issue = 1 | pages = 32–8 | date = January 2012 | pmid = 22346334 | pmc = 3278188 }}</ref>

Trauma therapy allows processing trauma-related memories and allows growth towards more adaptive psychological functioning. It helps to develop positive coping instead of negative coping and allows the individual to integrate upsetting-distressing material (thoughts, feelings and memories) and to resolve these internally. It also aids in the growth of personal skills like resilience, ego regulation, empathy, etc.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Briere |first1=John N. |last2=Scott |first2=Catherine |title=Principles of Trauma Therapy: A Guide to Symptoms, Evaluation, and Treatment ( DSM-5 Update) |date=2014 |publisher=SAGE Publications |isbn=978-1-4833-5125-4 }}{{pn|date=October 2026}}</ref>

Processes involved in trauma therapy are:
* Psychoeducation: Information dissemination and educating in vulnerabilities and adoptable coping mechanisms.
* Emotional regulation: Identifying, countering, discriminating, grounding thoughts and emotions from internal construction to an external representation.
* Cognitive processing: Transforming negative perceptions and beliefs about self, others and environment to positive ones through cognitive reconsideration or re-framing.
* Trauma processing: Systematic desensitization, response activation and counter-conditioning, titrated extinction of emotional response, deconstructing disparity (emotional vs. reality state), resolution of traumatic material (in theory, to a state in which triggers no longer produce harmful distress and the individual is able to express relief.)
* Emotional processing: Reconstructing perceptions, beliefs and erroneous expectations, habituating new life contexts for auto-activated trauma-related fears, and providing crisis cards with coded emotions and appropriate cognition. (This stage is only initiated in pre-termination phase from clinical assessment and judgement of the mental health professional.)
* [[Gestalt therapy|Experiential]] processing: Visualization of achieved relief state and relaxation methods.

A number of complementary approaches to trauma treatment have been implicated as well, including yoga and meditation.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Pradhan B, Kluewer D'Amico J, Makani R, Parikh T | title = Nonconventional interventions for chronic post-traumatic stress disorder: Ketamine, repetitive trans-cranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and alternative approaches | journal = Journal of Trauma & Dissociation | volume = 17 | issue = 1 | pages = 35–54 | date = 10 July 2015 | pmid = 26162001 | doi = 10.1080/15299732.2015.1046101 }}</ref> There has been recent interest in developing [[trauma-sensitive yoga]] practices,<ref>{{Cite book| vauthors = Emerson D, Hopper E |title=Overcoming Trauma through Yoga|publisher=North Atlantic Books|year=2012|location=USA}}</ref> but the actual efficacy of yoga in reducing the effects of trauma needs more exploration.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Nguyen-Feng VN, Clark CJ, Butler ME | title = Yoga as an intervention for psychological symptoms following trauma: A systematic review and quantitative synthesis | journal = Psychological Services | volume = 16 | issue = 3 | pages = 513–523 | date = August 2019 | pmid = 29620390 | doi = 10.1037/ser0000191 }}</ref>

In health and social care settings, a [[Trauma-informed care|trauma informed approach]] means that care is underpinned by understandings of trauma and its far-reaching implications.<ref name="SAMHSA">{{cite web|title=SAMHSA's Concept of Trauma and Guidance for a Trauma-Informed Approach | publisher = SAMHSA Publications and Digital Products|url=https://store.samhsa.gov/product/SAMHSA-s-Concept-of-Trauma-and-Guidance-for-a-Trauma-Informed-Approach/SMA14-4884|access-date=23 June 2021 }}</ref> Trauma is widespread. For example, 26% of participants in the [[Adverse childhood experiences|Adverse Childhood Experiences]] (A.C.Es) study<ref>{{Cite web|date=21 May 2021|title=About the CDC-Kaiser ACE Study {{!}}Violence Prevention{{!}}Injury Center |url=https://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/aces/about.html|access-date=23 June 2021|website=CDC }}</ref> were survivors of one A.C.E and 12.5% were survivors of four or more A.C.Es. A trauma-informed approach acknowledges the high rates of trauma and means that care providers treat every person as if they might be a survivor of trauma.<ref name="SAMHSA" /> Measurement of the effectiveness of a universal trauma informed approach is in early stages <ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Boucher N, Darling-Fisher CS, Sinko L, Beck D, Granner J, Seng J | title = Psychometric Evaluation of the TIC Grade, a Self-Report Measure to Assess Youth Perceptions of the Quality of Trauma-Informed Care They Received | journal = Journal of the American Psychiatric Nurses Association | pages = 319–325 | date = September 2020 | volume = 28 | issue = 4 | pmid = 32907448 | pmc = 7943641 | doi = 10.1177/1078390320953896 }}</ref> and is largely based in theory and epidemiology.

Trauma informed teaching practice is an educative approach for migrant children from war-torn countries, who have typically experienced complex trauma, and the number of such children entering Canadian schools has led some school jurisdictions to consider new classroom approaches to assist these pupils.<ref name="Tweedie 2017 36–45">{{cite journal |last1=Tweedie |first1=M. Gregory |last2=Belanger |first2=Carla |last3=Rezazadeh |first3=Kimberley |last4=Vogel |first4=Karen |title=Trauma-informed Teaching Practice and Refugee Children: A Hopeful Reflection on Welcoming Our New Neighbours to Canadian Schools |journal=BC TEAL Journal |date=19 December 2017 |pages=36–45 Pages |doi=10.14288/bctj.v2i1.268 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Miles J, Bailey-McKenna MC |date=2017|title=Giving Refugee Students a Strong Head Start: The LEAD Program|journal=TESL Canada Journal|volume=33|pages=109–128|doi=10.18806/tesl.v33i0.1249|doi-access=free}}</ref> Along with complex trauma, these students often have experienced interrupted schooling due to the migration process, and as a consequence may have limited literacy skills in their first language.<ref>{{Cite journal | vauthors = Block K, Cross S, Riggs E, Gibbs L |date=2014 |title=Supporting schools to create an inclusive environment for refugee students|journal=International Journal of Inclusive Education|volume=18|issue=12|pages=1337–1355|doi=10.1080/13603116.2014.899636}}</ref> One study of a Canadian secondary school classroom, as told through journal entries of a student teacher, showed how Blaustein and Kinniburgh's ARC (attachment, regulation and competency) framework<ref>{{Cite book|title=Treating traumatic stress in children and adolescents: How to foster resilience through attachment, self-regulation, and competency| vauthors = Blaustein ME, Kinniburgh KM |publisher=Guilford Press|year=2010|location=New York}}{{isbn?}}{{pn|date=October 2026}}</ref> was used to support newly arrived refugee students from war zones.<ref name="Tweedie 2017 36–45" /> Tweedie et al. (2017) describe how key components of the ARC framework, such as establishing consistency in classroom routines; assisting students to identify and self-regulate emotional responses; and enabling student personal goal achievement, are practically applied in one classroom where students have experienced complex trauma. The authors encourage teachers and schools to avoid a deficit lens to view such pupils, and suggest ways schools can structure teaching and learning environments which take into account the extreme stresses these students have encountered.<ref name="Tweedie 2017 36–45" />

== Society and culture ==
Some people, and many [[self-help book]]s, use the word ''trauma'' broadly, to refer to any unpleasant experience, even if the affected person has a psychologically healthy response to the experience.<ref name="Cummins-2021" >{{Cite web| vauthors = Cummins E |date=18 October 2021|title=The Self-Help That No One Needs Right Now|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2021/10/trauma-books-wont-save-you/620421/|access-date=19 October 2021|website=The Atlantic|language=en}}</ref> This imprecise language may promote the [[medicalization]] of normal human behaviors (e.g., [[grief]] after a death) and make discussions of psychological trauma more complex, but it might also encourage people to respond with [[compassion]] to the distress and suffering of others.<ref name="Cummins-2021" />

While this may never be the intention, certain cultures and beliefs can lead to specific kinds of trauma. [[Religious trauma syndrome|Religious trauma]] is amongst one of the more common forms of psychological trauma, being defined as a negative experience one may have while within a faith-based community.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Religious trauma: Definition, signs, causes, and treatment |url=https://therapist.com/trauma/religious-trauma/ |access-date=2026-07-22 |website=therapist.com |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Religious trauma syndrome|Religious trauma]] is often gained by individuals who have been shamed or shunned by their community, discriminated against due to their race or gender, experienced fear-based teaching, or [[Physical abuse|physical]], [[Emotional abuse|emotional]], or [[Sexual abuse|sexual]] abuse.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Religious Trauma {{!}} 9+ Signs of Spiritual Abuse & How to Heal |url=https://www.sandstonecare.com/blog/religious-trauma/ |access-date=2026-07-22 |website=Sandstone Care |language=en-US}}</ref>

While some in society are more accepting of and open towards psychological trauma than others, there are certain groups who specifically struggle with psychological trauma. Men in particular often downplay their trauma, wanting to appear resilient after a traumatic experience, which may lead them to avoid seeking treatment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nomamiukor |first1=Faith O. |last2=Collazo |first2=Elizabeth N. |last3=Harper |first3=Kelly L. |last4=Neilson |first4=Elizabeth C. |last5=Ellis |first5=Amy E. |last6=Simiola |first6=Vanessa L. |last7=Cook |first7=Joan M. |last8=Livingston |first8=Nicholas A. |date=2025-12-15 |title=How masculinity and treatment impact posttraumatic stress disorder recovery in sexual minority men with sexual trauma: Findings from a randomized clinical trial |journal=Psychology of Sexual Orientation and Gender Diversity |doi=10.1037/sgd0000894 |pmc=12867092 |pmid=41641008}}</ref> Women are more likely to fall victim to traumatic events, and often internalize the effects in order to appear outwardly unaffected.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Clearwater |first=The Wave of |date=2025-10-14 |title=How Trauma Impacts Women |url=https://thewaveclearwater.com/how-trauma-impacts-women-differently-and-the-best-treatment-options-available/ |access-date=2026-07-22 |website=The Wave of Clearwater |language=en-US}}</ref> Non-conforming gendered individuals are also more susceptible to trauma due to acts of [[transphobia]] and [[homophobia]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Healthcare |first=Women's |date=2021-10-11 |title=Trauma-informed Care Part 2: Transgender and Gender Nonconforming Individuals |url=https://npwomenshealthcare.com/trauma-informed-care-part-2-transgender-and-gender-nonconforming-individuals/ |access-date=2026-07-22 |website=Women's Healthcare |language=en-US}}</ref>

Minority groups are commonly victims of traumatic events, often experiencing [[racial trauma]]. [[Racial trauma]] is any sort of physical or emotional harm an individual may experience due to acts of [[racism]] or [[discrimination]].<ref name="VA Racial Trauma">{{cite web |title=Racial Trauma |url=https://www.ptsd.va.gov/understand/types/racial_trauma.asp |website=Veterans Affairs }}</ref> Racial acts that may lead to psychological trauma include unfair treatment due to one's race, racist microagressions, being called slurs, or falling victim to violence or hate crimes.<ref name="VA Racial Trauma"/>
